abstract: Ictalurid catfish use a highly developed gustatory system to localize, track and acquire food from their aquatic environment. The neural organization of the gustatory system illustrates well the importance of the four fundamental ingredients (representation, architecture, search and knowledge) of an "intelligent" system. In addition, the "pipelined" design of architecture illustrates how a goal-directed system effectively utilizes interactive feedback from its environment. Anatomical analysis of neural networks involved in target-tracking indicated that reticular neurons within the medullary region of the brainstem, mediate connections between the gustatory (sensory) inputs and the motor outputs of the spinal cord. Electrophysiological analysis suggested that these neurons integrate selective spatio-temporal patterns of sensory input transduced through a rapidly adapting-type peripheral filter (responding tonically only to a continuously increasing stimulus concentration). The connectivity and response patterns of reticular cells and the nature of the peripheral taste response suggest a unique "gustation-seeking" fUnction of reticulospinal cells, which may enable a catfish to continuously track a stimulus source once its directionality has been computed.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how catfish use taste to locate and pursue food. It treats the gustatory system as a goal-directed processing architecture that continually interacts with its environment. Anatomical analysis identifies reticular neurons in the medullary brainstem as a link between taste-related sensory signals and spinal motor outputs.

Electrophysiological observations suggest that these neurons combine selected patterns of sensory input across space and time. The incoming signals pass through a rapidly adapting peripheral filter. According to the abstract, a sustained response occurs only when stimulus concentration continues increasing, tying ongoing sensory activity to how the chemical signal changes during tracking.

The authors interpret the connectivity and response patterns as evidence for a possible gustation-seeking function of reticulospinal cells. Once the direction of a stimulus source has been computed, these cells may help maintain pursuit through continuing environmental feedback. The proposed mechanism connects sensory filtering, neural integration, and movement, explaining how a processing pipeline could remain responsive while the animal is actively seeking food.
summary.tldr: Anatomical and physiological evidence suggests brainstem neurons help catfish sustain food tracking through taste-driven sensory feedback.

title: HOW THE CATFISH TRACKS ITS PREY: AN INTERACTIVE "PIPELINED" PROCESSING SYSTEM MAY DIRECT FORAGING VIA RETICULOSPINAL NEURONS

abstract: We discuss synthetic receptors for haptic sensing. These are based on magnetic field sensors (Hall effect structures) fabricated using standard CMOS technologies. These receptors, biased with a small permanent magnet can detect the presence of ferro or ferri-magnetic objects in the vicinity of the sensor. They can also detect the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field.
originalAbstract: We discuss synthetic receptors for haptic sensing. These are based on magnetic field sensors (Hall effect structures) fabricated using standard CMOS technologies. These receptors, biased with a small permanent magnet can detect the presence of ferro or ferri-magnetic objects in the vicinity of the sensor. They can also detect the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field.

paragraphs: The paper describes synthetic receptors intended for tactile and haptic sensing. Their sensing mechanism is magnetic: the receptors use Hall-effect structures fabricated with standard CMOS technology. The contribution connects a physical sensing element with integrated-circuit fabrication, presenting magnetic-field measurements as a basis for electronic receptors.

A small permanent magnet provides a bias field for the receptors. In this arrangement, they can detect nearby ferromagnetic or ferrimagnetic objects. The stated sensing capability is therefore tied to objects with those magnetic properties. The presence-detection function concerns objects in the sensor's vicinity, making proximity part of the proposed receptor's operation.

The receptors can also detect the magnitude and direction of a magnetic field. This gives the design a richer measurement capability than a simple indication that a suitable object is nearby: it can register both field strength and orientation. Together, these capabilities define the paper's proposal for haptic sensing through CMOS magnetic receptors and a small permanent magnet.
summary.tldr: CMOS Hall-effect receptors use a small permanent magnet to sense nearby magnetic objects and measure field magnitude and direction.

title: Electronic Receptors for Tactile/Haptic Sensing

paragraphs: This paper generalizes radial basis function networks so that individual units can represent oriented regions. The proposed oriented non-radial basis functions replace the Euclidean-distance expression inside a Gaussian exponent with a more general polynomial. This allows regions such as rotated hyperellipses, expanding the shapes available to each unit.

For hypersurface estimation, the authors state that this more flexible representation requires fewer hidden units and alleviates the dimensionality problem associated with kernel approximators. The key change is in what a single unit can express: its region can have directional structure, giving the network a richer building block for approximating a surface.

For images, hidden units correspond to features, and their parameters describe rotation, scaling, and translation. The paper argues that an image can consequently be represented with relatively few features. Transforming the whole image corresponds to transforming its individual features in the same way. This connection between feature parameters and image transformations motivates the proposed use of the representation for image coding, recognition, and analysis.
summary.tldr: Oriented basis functions represent directional features compactly and connect image transformations to explicit feature parameters.

title: Oriented Non-Radial Basis Functions for Image Coding and Analysis

abstract: Light adaptation (LA) allows cone vIslOn to remain functional between twilight and the brightest time of day even though, at anyone time, their intensity-response (I-R) characteristic is limited to 3 log units of the stimu(cid:173) lating light. One mechanism underlying LA, was localized in the outer seg(cid:173) ment of an isolated cone (1,2). We found that by adding annular illhmination, an I-R characteristic of a cone can be shifted along the intensity domain. Neural network involving feedback synapse from horizontal cells to cones is involved to be in register with ambient light level of the periphery. An equivalent electrical circuit with three different transmembrane channels leakage, photocurrent and feedback was used to model static behavior of a cone. SPICE simulation showed that interactions between feedback synapse and the light sensitive conductance in the outer segment can shift the I-R curves along the intensity domain, provided that phototransduction mechan(cid:173) ism is not saturated during maximally hyperpolarized light response.

paragraphs: The paper studies how cones remain useful across large changes in ambient illumination despite having a limited intensity-response range at any one time. The authors find that adding illumination around a cone's central stimulus shifts its response curve along the light-intensity axis. This suggests a role for surrounding illumination in setting the cone's operating range.

They investigate feedback from horizontal cells to cones as a mechanism for aligning sensitivity with peripheral light levels. To model a cone's static behavior, they construct an equivalent electrical circuit with leakage, photocurrent, and feedback channels. This provides a way to examine how the feedback synapse interacts with the cone's own light-sensitive conductance.

SPICE simulations show that those interactions can shift the intensity-response curve. The result depends on a stated condition: phototransduction must remain unsaturated during the maximally hyperpolarized light response. The model therefore offers a specific, conditional explanation for how retinal feedback can contribute to light adaptation alongside mechanisms located within the cone itself.
summary.tldr: A cone circuit model shows how horizontal-cell feedback can shift light sensitivity, provided phototransduction remains unsaturated.

title: Feedback Synapse to Cone and Light Adaptation

abstract: The occurence of chaos in recurrent neural networks is supposed to depend on the architecture and on the synaptic coupling strength. It is studied here for a randomly diluted architecture. By normalizing the variance of synaptic weights, we produce a bifurcation parameter, dependent on this variance and on the slope of the transfer function but independent of the connectivity, that allows a sustained activity and the occurence of chaos when reaching a critical value. Even for weak connectivity and small size, we find numerical results in accordance with the theoretical ones previously established for fully connected infinite sized networks. Moreover the route towards chaos is numerically checked to be a quasi-periodic one, whatever the type of the first bifurcation is (Hopf bifurcation, pitchfork or flip).

paragraphs: The paper investigates how recurrent neural networks develop sustained activity and chaos when connections are randomly removed. The problem is to understand how connection structure and synaptic coupling strength jointly influence dynamics. Random dilution allows the authors to study networks whose connectivity differs from the fully connected setting used in earlier theoretical results.

By normalizing synaptic weight variance, the authors construct a parameter governing changes in dynamical behavior. It depends on weight variance and the slope of the transfer function but is independent of connectivity. Reaching a critical value permits sustained activity and chaos, providing a way to compare dynamical transitions across different levels of connection density.

Numerical results agree with earlier theory for infinitely large, fully connected networks even when the studied networks are small and weakly connected. The simulations also show a quasi-periodic route toward chaos regardless of whether the first bifurcation is Hopf, pitchfork, or flip. Thus, differing initial instabilities can lead through the same reported type of progression toward chaotic dynamics.
summary.tldr: A connectivity-independent control parameter helps explain transitions to chaos in randomly diluted recurrent networks.

title: Destabilization and Route to Chaos in Neural Networks with Random Connectivity

abstract: We study the characteristics of learning with ensembles. Solving exactly the simple model of an ensemble of linear students, we find surprisingly rich behaviour. For learning in large ensembles, it is advantageous to use under-regularized students, which actu(cid:173) ally over-fit the training data. Globally optimal performance can be obtained by choosing the training set sizes of the students ap(cid:173) propriately. For smaller ensembles, optimization of the ensemble weights can yield significant improvements in ensemble generaliza(cid:173) tion performance, in particular if the individual students are sub(cid:173) ject to noise in the training process. Choosing students with a wide range of regularization parameters makes this improvement robust against changes in the unknown level of noise in the training data.

paragraphs: This paper examines how the best way to train an individual learner changes when it belongs to an ensemble. The authors solve a simple model containing linear learners exactly. That setting makes it possible to analyze how regularization, training-set size, and combination weights affect the ensemble's ability to generalize.

For large ensembles, the analysis favors learners with too little regularization, even though those learners overfit their training data. Choosing their training-set sizes appropriately can achieve globally optimal performance within the model. The result shows that optimizing each member in isolation need not produce the best combined predictor.

For smaller ensembles, adjusting the weights used to combine learners can substantially improve generalization, especially when training itself is noisy. Including learners with a broad range of regularization strengths makes this improvement robust to changes in an unknown training-data noise level. These findings establish several ensemble-design tradeoffs within the exactly solved linear setting, including circumstances in which individual overfitting is beneficial.
summary.tldr: An exact analysis of linear ensembles shows that overfitting members can improve the combined predictor under appropriate training choices.

title: Learning with ensembles: How overfitting can be useful

abstract: The choice of an input representation for a neural network can have a profound impact on its accuracy in classifying novel instances. However, neural networks are typically computationally expensive to train, making it difficult to test large numbers of alternative representations. This paper introduces fast quality measures for neural network representations, allowing one to quickly and ac(cid:173) curately estimate which of a collection of possible representations for a problem is the best. We show that our measures for ranking representations are more accurate than a previously published mea(cid:173) sure, based on experiments with three difficult, real-world pattern recognition problems.

paragraphs: The way information is represented at a neural network's input can strongly affect its accuracy on new examples. Choosing among representations is difficult when each candidate requires expensive training before its quality becomes clear. This paper addresses that selection problem by introducing fast measures of representation quality.

The measures estimate which candidate representation will be best for a given problem. Their purpose is to rank alternatives quickly and accurately, making it more practical to consider a collection of possible inputs. This places representation assessment earlier in the decision process, where it can help direct the costly work of neural-network training.

Experiments on three difficult real-world pattern-recognition problems show more accurate rankings than a previously published measure. The result supports the usefulness of inexpensive quality estimates for comparing representations. The contribution is specifically about predicting the relative usefulness of input choices: it provides a way to make a consequential design decision without relying solely on training a network for every alternative.
summary.tldr: Fast quality measures rank candidate neural-network input representations more accurately than an earlier measure on three real-world problems.

title: Rapid Quality Estimation of Neural Network Input Representations

abstract: We report on the development of the modular neural system "SEE(cid:173) EAGLE" for the visual guidance of robot pick-and-place actions. Several neural networks are integrated to a single system that vi(cid:173) sually recognizes human hand pointing gestures from stereo pairs of color video images. The output of the hand recognition stage is processed by a set of color-sensitive neural networks to determine the cartesian location of the target object that is referenced by the pointing gesture. Finally, this information is used to guide a robot to grab the target object and put it at another location that can be specified by a second pointing gesture. The accuracy of the cur(cid:173) rent system allows to identify the location of the referenced target object to an accuracy of 1 cm in a workspace area of 50x50 cm. In our current environment, this is sufficient to pick and place arbi(cid:173) trarily positioned target objects within the workspace. The system consists of neural networks that perform the tasks of image seg(cid:173) mentation, estimation of hand location, estimation of 3D-pointing direction, object recognition, and necessary coordinate transforms. Drawing heavily on the use of learning algorithms, the functions of all network modules were created from data examples only.

paragraphs: The paper presents SEE-EAGLE, a modular neural system that lets a person guide robot pick-and-place actions by pointing. It begins with stereo pairs of color video images and recognizes the person's hand gesture. The gesture is then used to identify the target object and determine its location in Cartesian coordinates.

Several networks divide the visual and geometric work among modules. Their tasks include image segmentation, hand localization, estimation of three-dimensional pointing direction, object recognition, and coordinate transformations. Color-sensitive networks help determine the position of the referenced object. The functions of all modules are learned from data examples, linking the stages into one operational system.

The robot uses the resulting position to grasp the object, while a second pointing gesture can specify where to place it. The reported localization accuracy is one centimeter within a 50 by 50 centimeter workspace. In the authors' environment, this is sufficient to pick and place objects at arbitrary positions within that area, demonstrating a complete path from human gesture to robotic action.
summary.tldr: SEE-EAGLE combines learned vision modules to turn human pointing gestures into robot pick-and-place actions with one-centimeter localization accuracy.

title: Visual gesture-based robot guidance with a modular neural system

abstract: A new reinforcement learning architecture for nonlinear control is proposed. A direct feedback controller, or the actor, is trained by a value-gradient based controller, or the tutor. This architecture enables both efficient use of the value function and simple computa(cid:173) tion for real-time implementation. Good performance was verified in multi-dimensional nonlinear control tasks using Gaussian soft(cid:173) max networks.
originalAbstract: A new reinforcement learning architecture for nonlinear control is proposed. A direct feedback controller, or the actor, is trained by a value-gradient based controller, or the tutor. This architecture enables both efficient use of the value function and simple computa(cid:173) tion for real-time implementation. Good performance was verified in multi-dimensional nonlinear control tasks using Gaussian soft(cid:173) max networks.

paragraphs: Nonlinear control requires a system to choose actions as its state changes, often with little time available for each decision. This paper proposes a reinforcement learning architecture that divides the task between two controllers. An actor supplies direct feedback control, while a tutor teaches the actor using information from a value function.

The tutor is a value-gradient controller: its guidance depends on how the value function changes with the system's state. The actor learns from that controller and provides a simpler route from feedback to action. This arrangement makes the value function useful for training while keeping the computation needed for real-time control simple.

The authors report good performance on multidimensional nonlinear control tasks using Gaussian softmax networks. The stated contribution is therefore both architectural and practical: value-based guidance and direct control occupy different roles within one learning system. The results support the possibility of using a more involved control calculation to train an actor suitable for repeated, time-sensitive decisions.
summary.tldr: A value-gradient tutor trains a direct-control actor, combining value-function guidance with simple real-time action computation.

title: Efficient Nonlinear Control with Actor-Tutor Architecture

abstract: Theories of cue combination suggest the possibility of constructing visual stimuli that evoke different patterns of neural activity in sensory areas of the brain, but that cannot be distinguished by any behavioral measure of perception. Such stimuli, if they exist, would be interesting for two reasons. First, one could know that none of the differences between the stimuli survive past the computations used to build the percepts. Second, it can be difficult to distinguish stimulus-driven components of measured neural activity from top-down components (such as those due to the interestingness of the stimuli). Changing the stimulus without changing the percept could be exploited to measure the stimulusdriven activity. Here we describe stimuli in which vertical and horizontal disparities trade during the construction of percepts of slanted surfaces, yielding stimulus equivalence classes. Equivalence class membership changed after a change of vergence eye posture alone, without changes to the retinal images. A formal correspondence can be drawn between these “perceptual metamers” and more familiar “sensory metamers” such as color metamers.

paragraphs: The paper explores perceptual metamers: different visual stimuli that yield equivalent percepts. Cue-combination theories suggest that stimuli could generate different sensory neural activity while being indistinguishable through behavioral measures of perception. If such stimuli exist, they could help identify which stimulus differences are lost during the construction of a percept.

The authors describe stimuli in which vertical and horizontal disparities trade off in the perception of slanted surfaces. Different combinations therefore form equivalence classes. Membership in these classes changes when vergence eye posture changes, even though the retinal images remain the same. The equivalence consequently depends on more than the images alone.

The paper draws a formal connection to sensory metamers, including color metamers. It also proposes a use for perceptually equivalent stimuli: changing sensory input while holding perception constant could help separate stimulus-driven neural activity from top-down influences. That experimental opportunity is presented as a possibility arising from the equivalence, alongside the reported interaction between disparity cues and eye posture.
summary.tldr: Different disparity combinations can produce equivalent surface-slant percepts, with equivalence changing when eye posture changes.

title: Perceptual Metamers in Stereoscopic Vision

abstract: A dynamic texture is a video model that treats a video as a sample from a spatio-temporal stochastic process, speciﬁcally a linear dynamical sys- tem. One problem associated with the dynamic texture is that it cannot model video where there are multiple regions of distinct motion. In this work, we introduce the layered dynamic texture model, which addresses this problem. We also introduce a variant of the model, and present the EM algorithm for learning each of the models. Finally, we demonstrate the efﬁcacy of the proposed model for the tasks of segmentation and syn- thesis of video.
originalAbstract: A dynamic texture is a video model that treats a video as a sample from a spatio-temporal stochastic process, speciﬁcally a linear dynamical sys- tem. One problem associated with the dynamic texture is that it cannot model video where there are multiple regions of distinct motion. In this work, we introduce the layered dynamic texture model, which addresses this problem. We also introduce a variant of the model, and present the EM algorithm for learning each of the models. Finally, we demonstrate the efﬁcacy of the proposed model for the tasks of segmentation and syn- thesis of video.

paragraphs: A dynamic texture models a video as a realization of a stochastic process evolving across space and time, specifically a linear dynamical system. The paper identifies a limitation of this representation: it cannot capture video containing multiple regions with distinct motion. Such video requires a model that can account for different motion patterns within the same sequence.

The authors introduce a layered dynamic texture model to address that problem. The layered formulation provides a way to represent multiple motion regions within the video model. They also develop a variant and present expectation-maximization algorithms for learning both formulations, supplying procedures for fitting the proposed representations from data.

The model is demonstrated on video segmentation and synthesis. These tasks examine complementary uses of the representation: separating a sequence into regions and generating video from a learned model. The reported efficacy supports the usefulness of the layered approach for handling distinct motions, while the learning algorithms make the proposed models operational for those tasks.
summary.tldr: Layered dynamic textures extend video modeling to multiple regions with distinct motion and support both segmentation and synthesis.

title: Layered Dynamic Textures

abstract: The classical Bayes rule computes the posterior model probability from the prior probability and the data likelihood. We generalize this rule to the case when the prior is a density matrix (symmetric positive definite and trace one) and the data likelihood a covariance matrix. The classical Bayes rule is retained as the special case when the matrices are diagonal. In the classical setting, the calculation of the probability of the data is an expected likelihood, where the expectation is over the prior distribution. In the generalized setting, this is replaced by an expected variance calculation where the variance is computed along the eigenvectors of the prior density matrix and the expectation is over the eigenvalues of the density matrix (which form a probability vector). The variances along any direction is determined by the covariance matrix. Curiously enough this expected variance calculation is a quantum measurement where the co-variance matrix specifies the instrument and the prior density matrix the mixture state of the particle. We motivate both the classical and the generalized Bayes rule with a minimum relative entropy principle, where the Kullbach-Leibler version gives the classical Bayes rule and Umegaki's quantum relative entropy the new Bayes rule for density matrices.

paragraphs: Ordinary Bayes updating combines prior probabilities with a data likelihood to obtain posterior probabilities. This paper extends that operation to matrix representations: the prior becomes a symmetric positive definite matrix with trace one, and the likelihood is represented by a covariance matrix. When both matrices are diagonal, the proposed rule reduces to classical Bayes updating.

The extension changes how the overall evidence is calculated. Instead of averaging likelihoods under prior probabilities, it averages variances measured along the prior matrix's eigenvectors. The corresponding eigenvalues supply the averaging weights, while the covariance matrix determines the variance in each direction. This gives the matrix construction a concrete interpretation in terms of directions and uncertainty.

The authors also connect this calculation to quantum measurement and derive both updating rules from a minimum relative entropy principle. Classical relative entropy yields ordinary Bayes updating, while quantum relative entropy yields the matrix rule. The contribution is therefore a unified mathematical motivation for a broader update operation that retains the familiar diagonal case.
summary.tldr: The paper generalizes Bayes updating to density matrices while recovering classical Bayes rule for diagonal matrices.

title: A Bayes Rule for Density Matrices

abstract: Many unsupervised learning problems can be expressed as a form of matrix factorization, reconstructing an observed data matrix as the product of two matrices of latent variables. A standard challenge in solving these problems is determining the dimensionality of the latent matrices. Nonparametric Bayesian matrix factorization is one way of dealing with this challenge, yielding a posterior distribution over possible factorizations of unbounded dimensionality. A drawback to this approach is that posterior estimation is typically done using Gibbs sampling, which can be slow for large problems and when conjugate priors cannot be used. As an alternative, we present a particle filter for posterior estimation in nonparametric Bayesian matrix factorization models. We illustrate this approach with two matrix factorization models and show favorable performance relative to Gibbs sampling.

A standard challenge in solving these problems is determining the dimensionality of the latent matrices. Nonparametric Bayesian matrix factorization is one way of dealing with this challenge, yielding a posterior distribution over possible factorizations of unbounded dimensionality. A drawback to this approach is that posterior estimation is typically done using Gibbs sampling, which can be slow for large problems and when conjugate priors cannot be used. As an alternative, we present a particle filter for posterior estimation in nonparametric Bayesian matrix factorization models. We illustrate this approach with two matrix factorization models and show favorable performance relative to Gibbs sampling.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization explains an observed data matrix as the product of two matrices of hidden variables. A recurring challenge is choosing the dimensionality of those hidden representations. Nonparametric Bayesian factorization addresses this by placing a posterior distribution over possible factorizations without imposing a fixed upper dimensionality in the model.

That flexibility creates an inference problem: the posterior must still be estimated computationally. Gibbs sampling is a typical choice, but it can become slow for large problems or when conjugate priors are unavailable. This paper proposes particle filtering as an alternative way to estimate the posterior in nonparametric Bayesian matrix factorization models.

The authors illustrate their approach with two factorization models and report favorable performance relative to Gibbs sampling. The contribution concerns how inference is performed within a flexible factorization framework, while retaining the ability to consider different latent dimensionalities. The reported comparisons support particle filtering as a useful alternative in the demonstrated models, particularly in light of the computational difficulties motivating the work.
summary.tldr: Particle filtering offers an alternative to Gibbs sampling for inferring Bayesian matrix factorizations with variable latent dimensionality.

title: Particle Filtering for Nonparametric Bayesian Matrix Factorization

abstract: Semi-supervised SVMs (S3 VM) attempt to learn low-density separators by maximizing the margin over labeled and unlabeled examples. The associated optimization problem is non-convex. To examine the full potential of S3 VMs modulo local minima problems in current implementations, we apply branch and bound techniques for obtaining exact, global ly optimal solutions. Empirical evidence suggests that the globally optimal solution can return excellent generalization performance in situations where other implementations fail completely. While our current implementation is only applicable to small datasets, we discuss variants that can potentially lead to practically useful algorithms.

Their optimization problem is nonconvex, so an implementation can settle at a local minimum. This creates a practical question: does poor performance reflect the learning objective or difficulty optimizing it?

The paper addresses that question with branch and bound, obtaining exact, globally optimal solutions. Solving the objective globally lets the authors examine what the model can achieve when local minima are removed from the explanation. The approach therefore serves as a way to investigate the potential of semi-supervised SVMs themselves.

The reported empirical evidence suggests that global solutions can generalize extremely well in situations where other implementations fail completely. This is a qualified finding about particular situations, rather than a guarantee that global optimization always gives good predictions. The current implementation handles only small datasets. The authors discuss variants that could potentially turn this diagnostic approach into practically useful algorithms.
summary.tldr: Exact optimization reveals that semi-supervised SVMs can perform well where local-search implementations fail, although the implementation handles only small datasets.

title: Branch and Bound for Semi-Supervised Support Vector Machines

abstract: We propose a new method for constructing hyperkenels and define two promising special cases that can be computed in closed form. These we call the Gaussian and Wishart hyperkernels. The former is especially attractive in that it has an interpretable regularization scheme reminiscent of that of the Gaussian RBF kernel. We discuss how kernel learning can be used not just for improving the performance of classification and regression methods, but also as a stand-alone algorithm for dimensionality reduction and relational or metric learning.

paragraphs: Kernel learning makes the choice of kernel part of the learning problem. This paper contributes a new method for constructing hyperkernels, which provide machinery for learning kernels themselves. The focus is on how that machinery can be specified in a usable form and how it can support several kinds of learning tasks.

The authors define two special cases, called Gaussian and Wishart hyperkernels, that can be computed in closed form. This gives explicit constructions for these cases. They single out the Gaussian hyperkernel because its regularization scheme has an interpretable character reminiscent of the familiar Gaussian radial basis function kernel.

The paper also broadens the role assigned to kernel learning. Beyond improving classification and regression methods, it discusses using kernel learning as a standalone approach to dimensionality reduction and relational or metric learning. In these uses, learning the representation of relationships is itself a goal. The stated contribution is the construction and interpretation of these hyperkernels, together with an account of their potential roles across these tasks.
summary.tldr: Gaussian and Wishart hyperkernels provide closed-form constructions for kernel learning and its broader representation-learning uses.

title: Gaussian and Wishart Hyperkernels

abstract: The locally linear embedding (LLE) is improved by introducing multiple linearly independent local weight vectors for each neighborhood. We characterize the reconstruction weights and show the existence of the linearly independent weight vectors at each neighborhood. The modiﬁed locally linear embedding (MLLE) proposed in this paper is much stable. It can retrieve the ideal embedding if MLLE is applied on data points sampled from an isometric manifold. MLLE is also compared with the local tangent space alignment (LTSA). Numerical examples are given that show the improvement and efﬁciency of MLLE.

The modiﬁed locally linear embedding (MLLE) proposed in this paper is much stable. It can retrieve the ideal embedding if MLLE is applied on data points sampled from an isometric manifold. MLLE is also compared with the local tangent space alignment (LTSA). Numerical examples are given that show the improvement and efﬁciency of MLLE.

paragraphs: Locally linear embedding constructs a lower-dimensional representation using local reconstruction relationships among neighboring data points. This paper modifies that approach by introducing multiple linearly independent weight vectors for each neighborhood. The change allows the embedding procedure to use several independent local reconstruction relationships within the same neighborhood.

The authors analyze the reconstruction weights and establish that the required independent vectors exist at each neighborhood. Their modified method, MLLE, is reported to be more stable. The paper also states a recovery property: MLLE can retrieve the ideal embedding when applied to points sampled from an isometric manifold, tying that result to a specific geometric condition on the data.

The method is compared with local tangent space alignment, and numerical examples demonstrate improvement and efficiency. The contribution combines a change to the information retained locally with analysis of when an ideal global representation can be recovered. The isometric-manifold condition belongs to that recovery statement; it should not be read as a claim that arbitrary datasets admit ideal recovery.
summary.tldr: MLLE improves embedding stability using multiple local weight vectors and can recover an ideal embedding under an isometric-manifold condition.

title: MLLE: Modified Locally Linear Embedding Using Multiple Weights

abstract: Bayesian models of multisensory perception traditionally address the problem of estimating an underlying variable that is assumed to be the cause of the two sen- sory signals. The brain, however, has to solve a more general problem: it also has to establish which signals come from the same source and should be integrated, and which ones do not and should be segregated. In the last couple of years, a few models have been proposed to solve this problem in a Bayesian fashion. One of these has the strength that it formalizes the causal structure of sensory signals. We ﬁrst compare these models on a formal level. Furthermore, we conduct a psy- chophysics experiment to test human performance in an auditory-visual spatial localization task in which integration is not mandatory. We ﬁnd that the causal Bayesian inference model accounts for the data better than other models. Keywords: causal inference, Bayesian methods, visual perception. 1 Multisensory perception In the ventriloquist illusion, a performer speaks without moving his/her mouth while moving a puppet’s mouth in synchrony with his/her speech. This makes the puppet appear to be speaking. This illusion was ﬁrst conceptualized as ”visual capture”, occurring when visual and auditory stimuli exhibit a small conﬂict ([1, 2]). Only recently has it been demonstrated that the phenomenon may be seen as a byproduct of a much more ﬂexible and nearly Bayes-optimal strategy ([3]), and therefore is part of a large collection of cue combination experiments showing such statistical near-optimality [4, 5]. In fact, cue combination has become the poster child for Bayesian inference in the nervous system. In previous studies of multisensory integration, two sensory stimuli are presented which act as cues about a single underlying source. For instance, in the auditory-visual localization experiment by Alais and Burr [3], observers were asked to envisage each presentation of a light blob and a sound click as a single event, like a ball hitting the screen. In many cases, however, the brain is not only posed with the problem of identifying the position of a common source, but also of determining whether there was a common source at all. In the on-stage ventriloquist illusion, it is indeed primar- ily the causal inference process that is being fooled, because veridical perception would attribute independent causes to the auditory and the visual stimulus. 1 To extend our understanding of multisensory perception to this more general problem, it is necessary to manipulate the degree of belief assigned to there being a common cause within a multisensory task. Intuitively, we expect that when two signals are very different, they are less likely to be per- ceived as having a common source. It is well-known that increasing the discrepancy or inconsistency between stimuli reduces the inﬂuence that they have on each other [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. In auditory- visual spatial localization, one variable that controls stimulus similarity is spatial disparity (another would be temporal disparity). Indeed, it has been reported that increasing spatial disparity leads to a decrease in auditory localization bias [1, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 2, 18, 19, 20, 21]. This decrease also correlates with a decrease in the reports of unity [19, 21]. Despite the abundance of experimental data on this issue, no general theory exists that can explain multisensory perception across a wide range of cue conﬂicts.

abstract: It is becoming increasingly evident that organisms acting in uncertain dynamical environments often employ exact or approximate Bayesian statistical calculations in order to continuously estimate the environmental state, integrate information from multiple sensory modalities, form predictions and choose actions. What is less clear is how these putative computations are implemented by cortical neural networks. An additional level of complexity is introduced because these networks observe the world through spike trains received from primary sensory afferents, rather than directly. A recent line of research has described mechanisms by which such computations can be implemented using a network of neurons whose activ- ity directly represents a probability distribution across the possible “world states”. Much of this work, however, uses various approximations, which severely re- strict the domain of applicability of these implementations. Here we make use of rigorous mathematical results from the theory of continuous time point process ﬁltering, and show how optimal real-time state estimation and prediction may be implemented in a general setting using linear neural networks. We demonstrate the applicability of the approach with several examples, and relate the required network properties to the statistical nature of the environment, thereby quantify- ing the compatibility of a given network with its environment.

paragraphs: An organism acting in a changing environment must continually estimate what is happening from uncertain sensory information. Neural networks face an additional challenge: their observations arrive as sequences of spikes. The paper asks how networks could use those events to carry out the Bayesian estimation and prediction computations attributed to perception and action.

The approach draws on mathematical results for continuous-time point-process filtering, a framework suited to observations arriving as discrete events over time. Using these results, the authors show how linear neural networks may implement optimal real-time state estimation and prediction in a general setting. This addresses restrictions associated with approximations used in earlier network implementations.

Several examples demonstrate the applicability of the construction. The analysis also connects the network properties required for these computations to the statistical properties of the environment. That connection provides a way to quantify how compatible a network is with its environment. The contribution is a mathematical implementation account, rather than evidence that cortical networks necessarily use this exact mechanism.
summary.tldr: Point-process filtering provides a mathematical route for linear neural networks to estimate and predict environmental states optimally from sensory spikes.

title: A neural network implementing optimal state estimation based on dynamic spike train decoding

abstract: Bartlett et al (2006) recently proved that a ground condition for convex surrogates, classification calibration, ties up the minimization of the surrogates and classification risks, and left as an important problem the algorithmic questions about the minimization of these surrogates. In this paper, we propose an algorithm which provably minimizes any classification calibrated surrogate strictly convex and differentiable --- a set whose losses span the exponential, logistic and squared losses ---, with boosting-type guaranteed convergence rates under a weak learning assumption. A particular subclass of these surrogates, that we call balanced convex surrogates, has a key rationale that ties it to maximum likelihood estimation, zero-sum games and the set of losses that satisfy some of the most common requirements for losses in supervised learning. We report experiments on more than 50 readily available domains of 11 flavors of the algorithm, that shed light on new surrogates, and the potential of data dependent strategies to tune surrogates.

paragraphs: Classification algorithms often optimize a surrogate loss in place of classification error itself. Classification calibration connects minimizing that surrogate to minimizing classification risk, but it does not by itself provide an efficient optimization algorithm. This paper addresses that algorithmic question for a broad class of calibrated losses.

The proposed method provably minimizes classification-calibrated surrogates that are strictly convex and differentiable. This class includes exponential, logistic, and squared losses. Its convergence guarantees are of a boosting type and depend on a weak learning assumption. These conditions matter because the optimization claim applies to the specified loss family and learning setting.

The authors also identify balanced convex surrogates, a subclass connected to maximum-likelihood estimation, zero-sum games, and common requirements for supervised losses. Experiments examine 11 variants of the algorithm across more than 50 domains. They explore new surrogates and the potential of tuning losses to the data, complementing the theoretical result with an investigation of how different loss choices behave in practice.
summary.tldr: A boosting-style algorithm provably minimizes a broad class of calibrated losses under a weak learning assumption.

title: On the Efficient Minimization of Classification Calibrated Surrogates

abstract: The hypothesis that high dimensional data tends to lie in the vicinity of a low dimensional manifold is the basis of a collection of methodologies termed Manifold Learning. In this paper, we study statistical aspects of the question of fitting a manifold with a nearly optimal least squared error. Given upper bounds on the dimension, volume, and curvature, we show that Empirical Risk Minimization can produce a nearly optimal manifold using a number of random samples that is {\it independent} of the ambient dimension of the space in which data lie. We obtain an upper bound on the required number of samples that depends polynomially on the curvature, exponentially on the intrinsic dimension, and linearly on the intrinsic volume. For constant error, we prove a matching minimax lower bound on the sample complexity that shows that this dependence on intrinsic dimension, volume and curvature is unavoidable. Whether the known lower bound of $O(\frac{k}{\eps^2} + \frac{\log \frac{1}{\de}}{\eps^2})$ for the sample complexity of Empirical Risk minimization on $k-$means applied to data in a unit ball of arbitrary dimension is tight, has been an open question since 1997 \cite{bart2}. Here $\eps$ is the desired bound on the error and $\de$ is a bound on the probability of failure. We improve the best currently known upper bound \cite{pontil} of $O(\frac{k^2}{\eps^2} + \frac{\log \frac{1}{\de}}{\eps^2})$ to $O\left(\frac{k}{\eps^2}\left(\min\left(k, \frac{\log^4 \frac{k}{\eps}}{\eps^2}\right)\right) + \frac{\log \frac{1}{\de}}{\eps^2}\right)$. Based on these results, we devise a simple algorithm for $k-$means and another that uses a family of convex programs to fit a piecewise linear curve of a specified length to high dimensional data, where the sample complexity is independent of the ambient dimension.

Both have sample complexity independent of ambient dimension, separating statistical data requirements from the number of coordinates used to represent observations.
summary.tldr: Under geometric bounds, nearly optimal manifold fitting needs samples governed by intrinsic geometry rather than ambient dimension.

title: Sample Complexity of Testing the Manifold Hypothesis

abstract: When software developers modify one or more files in a large code base, they must also identify and update other related files. Many file dependencies can be detected by mining the development history of the code base: in essence, groups of related files are revealed by the logs of previous workflows. From data of this form, we show how to detect dependent files by solving a problem in binary matrix completion. We explore different latent variable models (LVMs) for this problem, including Bernoulli mixture models, exponential family PCA, restricted Boltzmann machines, and fully Bayesian approaches. We evaluate these models on the development histories of three large, open-source software systems: Mozilla Firefox, Eclipse Subversive, and Gimp. In all of these applications, we find that LVMs improve the performance of related file prediction over current leading methods.

paragraphs: Changing a file in a large software project can require changes to other related files. Development histories contain clues about these relationships because past workflows record groups of files modified together. This paper uses those records to predict which additional files may be relevant when a developer begins a new change.

The authors formulate related-file detection as binary matrix completion. In this formulation, recorded file participation provides observed entries, and the learning problem is to infer missing relationships. They investigate several latent-variable approaches, including Bernoulli mixtures, exponential-family principal component analysis, restricted Boltzmann machines, and fully Bayesian models. These approaches use hidden structure to capture patterns in the historical records.

Evaluation covers the development histories of Mozilla Firefox, Eclipse Subversive, and Gimp. In all three applications, latent-variable models improve related-file prediction over the leading methods used for comparison. The findings support using patterns across earlier workflows to inform file recommendations, turning development history into evidence about which files tend to require coordinated attention.
summary.tldr: Latent-variable models predict related software files from development histories by treating the task as binary matrix completion.

title: Latent Variable Models for Predicting File Dependencies in Large-Scale Software Development

abstract: Spontaneous brain activity, as observed in functional neuroimaging, has been shown to display reproducible structure that expresses brain architecture and carries markers of brain pathologies. An important view of modern neuroscience is that such large-scale structure of coherent activity reflects modularity properties of brain connectivity graphs. However, to date, there has been no demonstration that the limited and noisy data available in spontaneous activity observations could be used to learn full-brain probabilistic models that generalize to new data. Learning such models entails two main challenges: i) modeling full brain connectivity is a difficult estimation problem that faces the curse of dimensionality and ii) variability between subjects, coupled with the variability of functional signals between experimental runs, makes the use of multiple datasets challenging. We describe subject-level brain functional connectivity structure as a multivariate Gaussian process and introduce a new strategy to estimate it from group data, by imposing a common structure on the graphical model in the population. We show that individual models learned from functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data using this population prior generalize better to unseen data than models based on alternative regularization schemes. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a cross-validated model of spontaneous brain activity. Finally, we use the estimated graphical model to explore the large-scale characteristics of functional architecture and show for the first time that known cognitive networks appear as the integrated communities of functional connectivity graph.

The number of relationships to estimate is large, and signals vary across both people and recording sessions. This paper asks whether information from a population can help build individual connectivity models that predict unseen data.

The authors describe each subject's functional connectivity through a multivariate Gaussian process. Their estimation strategy imposes a common graphical structure across the population, using that shared structure as a prior for subject-level models. These findings connect predictive validation with an interpretable organization of brain activity, supporting the usefulness of shared population structure for individual estimation.
summary.tldr: Sharing graphical structure across a population improves individual fMRI connectivity models' generalization and reveals communities corresponding to known cognitive networks.

title: Brain covariance selection: better individual functional connectivity models using population prior

abstract: In recent years semidefinite optimization has become a tool of major importance in various optimization and machine learning problems. In many of these problems the amount of data in practice is so large that there is a constant need for faster algorithms. In this work we present the first sublinear time approximation algorithm for semidefinite programs which we believe may be useful for such problems in which the size of data may cause even linear time algorithms to have prohibitive running times in practice. We present the algorithm and its analysis alongside with some theoretical lower bounds and an improved algorithm for the special problem of supervised learning of a distance metric.

paragraphs: Semidefinite programs are optimization problems used across machine learning and related areas. At very large data scales, even an algorithm whose running time grows linearly with the input can be expensive. This paper addresses that bottleneck by seeking approximate solutions with a running time that grows more slowly than the input size.

The authors present what they identify as the first sublinear-time approximation algorithm for semidefinite programs, together with an analysis of the algorithm. Approximation is central to the contribution: the stated result concerns obtaining an approximate answer efficiently. The paper also supplies theoretical lower bounds, placing the algorithmic development alongside results about limits on what computation can achieve.

A further contribution improves the algorithm for the particular task of supervised distance-metric learning. That specialization connects the general optimization result to a machine learning problem. The authors suggest that the approach may help when data volume makes even linear-time methods impractical; the abstract frames this practical usefulness as a possibility, rather than an experimentally established outcome.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a sublinear-time approximation algorithm for semidefinite programs and an improved specialization for distance-metric learning.

title: Approximating Semidefinite Programs in Sublinear Time

abstract: We consider the problem of Ising and Gaussian graphical model selection given n i.i.d. samples from the model. We propose an efficient threshold-based algorithm for structure estimation based known as conditional mutual information test. This simple local algorithm requires only low-order statistics of the data and decides whether two nodes are neighbors in the unknown graph. Under some transparent assumptions, we establish that the proposed algorithm is structurally consistent (or sparsistent) when the number of samples scales as n= Omega(J_{min}^{-4} log p), where p is the number of nodes and J_{min} is the minimum edge potential. We also prove novel non-asymptotic necessary conditions for graphical model selection.

Under some transparent assumptions, we establish that the proposed algorithm is structurally consistent (or sparsistent) when the number of samples scales as n= Omega(J_{min}^{-4} log p), where p is the number of nodes and J_{min} is the minimum edge potential. paragraphs: Recovering a graphical model from data means deciding which variable pairs have direct conditional relationships. In high dimensions, that decision must use limited samples and manageable computation. This paper proposes a local conditional-mutual-information test for selecting Ising and Gaussian graph structures.

The threshold-based algorithm relies only on low-order statistics and tests whether two nodes should be neighbors. Under stated structural assumptions, it consistently recovers the graph when the sample count scales as Ω(Jmin⁻⁴ log p), where p is the number of variables and Jmin is the smallest edge strength.

The authors also derive nonasymptotic necessary conditions for graphical-model selection. The contribution combines a simple estimator with both sufficient and limiting sample requirements. Its dependence on minimum edge strength is informative: weak interactions are harder to distinguish reliably, so logarithmic growth in the number of variables does not by itself determine the difficulty of recovery.
summary.tldr: Low-order conditional-mutual-information tests recover specified Ising and Gaussian graph families with explicit sample-complexity guarantees.

title: High-Dimensional Graphical Model Selection: Tractable Graph Families and Necessary Conditions

abstract: The object people perceive in an image can depend on its orientation relative to the scene it is in (its reference frame). For example, the images of the symbols $\times$ and $+$ differ by a 45 degree rotation. Although real scenes have multiple images and reference frames, psychologists have focused on scenes with only one reference frame. We propose an ideal observer model based on nonparametric Bayesian statistics for inferring the number of reference frames in a scene and their parameters. When an ambiguous image could be assigned to two conflicting reference frames, the model predicts two factors should influence the reference frame inferred for the image: The image should be more likely to share the reference frame of the closer object ({\em proximity}) and it should be more likely to share the reference frame containing the most objects ({\em alignment}). We confirm people use both cues using a novel methodology that allows for easy testing of human reference frame inference.

paragraphs: An object’s perceived identity can depend on the orientation against which it is interpreted. A cross, for example, can be read differently after rotation. Real scenes can contain several such reference frames, so understanding an ambiguous image requires deciding which surrounding orientation provides the appropriate context.

The authors propose an ideal observer model using nonparametric Bayesian statistics. It infers both how many reference frames a scene contains and the parameters describing them. This lets the model address scenes with multiple competing frames rather than assuming that every image belongs to a single shared frame.

For an image compatible with two conflicting frames, the model predicts two influences. Proximity favors the frame associated with a nearby object, while alignment favors the frame containing more objects. The findings support these specific predictions about how spatial context guides interpretation when an image is ambiguous.
summary.tldr: An ideal observer model predicts, and behavioral tests confirm, that proximity and alignment influence how people assign ambiguous images to reference frames.

title: An ideal observer model for identifying the reference frame of objects

abstract: An important way to make large training sets is to gather noisy labels from crowds of nonexperts. We propose a minimax entropy principle to improve the quality of these labels. Our method assumes that labels are generated by a probability distribution over workers, items, and labels. By maximizing the entropy of this distribution, the method naturally infers item confusability and worker expertise. We infer the ground truth by minimizing the entropy of this distribution, which we show minimizes the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the probability distribution and the unknown truth. We show that a simple coordinate descent scheme can optimize minimax entropy. Empirically, our results are substantially better than previously published methods for the same problem.

This paper proposes a minimax entropy principle for recovering better labels from that noisy information. Its model assumes a probability distribution over workers, items, and labels, so it can represent differences among annotators and among the examples they label.

The two parts of the principle play different roles. Maximizing entropy allows the method to infer worker expertise and item confusability. Minimizing entropy is then used to infer the underlying ground-truth labels. The authors show that this latter step minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the modeled distribution and the unknown truth.

A simple coordinate-descent procedure optimizes the resulting minimax objective. This gives the principle a concrete computational implementation, connecting its statistical interpretation to an algorithm for aggregating annotations. Empirically, the method substantially outperforms previously published approaches to the same problem. The results support jointly modeling who supplies a label and how confusing the labeled item is when estimating the underlying labels.
summary.tldr: Minimax entropy jointly models worker expertise and item confusability to infer more accurate labels from noisy crowdsourced annotations.

title: Learning from the Wisdom of Crowds by Minimax Entropy

abstract: We study large-scale, nonsmooth, nonconconvex optimization problems. In particular, we focus on nonconvex problems with \emph{composite} objectives. This class of problems includes the extensively studied convex, composite objective problems as a special case. To tackle composite nonconvex problems, we introduce a powerful new framework based on asymptotically \emph{nonvanishing} errors, avoiding the common convenient assumption of eventually vanishing errors. Within our framework we derive both batch and incremental nonconvex proximal splitting algorithms. To our knowledge, our framework is first to develop and analyze incremental \emph{nonconvex} proximal-splitting algorithms, even if we disregard the ability to handle nonvanishing errors. We illustrate our theoretical framework by showing how it applies to difficult large-scale, nonsmooth, and nonconvex problems.

paragraphs: The paper develops optimization methods for large problems whose objectives are both nonsmooth and nonconvex. It focuses on composite objectives, which combine multiple terms within one optimization problem. The framework also includes convex composite problems as a special case, placing familiar settings within a broader formulation.

A central feature is its treatment of computational errors that do not disappear asymptotically. Many analyses assume that errors eventually vanish; this framework explicitly accommodates persistent errors. That changes the conditions under which the authors develop and analyze proximal splitting methods, which organize optimization around the components of the objective.

Within the framework, the authors derive both batch and incremental algorithms. They identify the development and analysis of incremental nonconvex proximal splitting as novel to their knowledge, even apart from the treatment of nonvanishing errors. Applications to difficult large-scale, nonsmooth, nonconvex problems illustrate the framework. The contribution is an expanded analytical and algorithmic foundation for composite optimization under persistent inexactness, together with two styles of algorithm.
summary.tldr: A proximal splitting framework handles nonconvex composite objectives with persistent computational errors and yields batch and incremental algorithms.

title: Scalable nonconvex inexact proximal splitting

abstract: This paper aims to take a step forwards making the term ``intrinsic motivation'' from reinforcement learning theoretically well founded, focusing on curiosity-driven learning. To that end, we consider the setting where, a fixed partition P of a continuous space X being given, and a process \nu defined on X being unknown, we are asked to sequentially decide which cell of the partition to select as well as where to sample \nu in that cell, in order to minimize a loss function that is inspired from previous work on curiosity-driven learning. The loss on each cell consists of one term measuring a simple worst case quadratic sampling error, and a penalty term proportional to the range of the variance in that cell. The corresponding problem formulation extends the setting known as active learning for multi-armed bandits to the case when each arm is a continuous region, and we show how an adaptation of recent algorithms for that problem and of hierarchical optimistic sampling algorithms for optimization can be used in order to solve this problem. The resulting procedure, called Hierarchical Optimistic Region SElection driven by Curiosity (HORSE.C) is provided together with a finite-time regret analysis.

paragraphs: HORSE.C gives a mathematical formulation to a particular curiosity-driven learning problem. At each step, the learner must choose both a region and a location within that region at which to sample.

The objective assigns each region a loss with two components. One measures a worst-case quadratic sampling error, and the other penalizes the range of variance within the region. This makes the sampling goal explicit: decisions should improve performance according to that specified combination of error and variability. The formulation extends active learning for multi-armed bandits by treating each arm as a continuous region.

The proposed procedure combines adaptations of active-learning bandit algorithms with hierarchical optimistic sampling methods used in optimization. The authors provide a finite-time regret analysis for the resulting algorithm. Its significance is a theoretically analyzed sampling rule for this defined curiosity objective, tying the motivation for exploration to measurable performance over a finite period.
summary.tldr: HORSE.C formalizes curiosity-driven sampling across continuous regions and provides a hierarchical algorithm with finite-time regret analysis.

title: Hierarchical Optimistic Region Selection driven by Curiosity

abstract: The Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) is a popular density model that is also good for extracting features. A main source of tractability in RBM models is the model's assumption that given an input, hidden units activate independently from one another. Sparsity and competition in the hidden representation is believed to be beneficial, and while an RBM with competition among its hidden units would acquire some of the attractive properties of sparse coding, such constraints are not added due to the widespread belief that the resulting model would become intractable. In this work, we show how a dynamic programming algorithm developed in 1981 can be used to implement exact sparsity in the RBM's hidden units. We then expand on this and show how to pass derivatives through a layer of exact sparsity, which makes it possible to fine-tune a deep belief network (DBN) consisting of RBMs with sparse hidden layers. We show that sparsity in the RBM's hidden layer improves the performance of both the pre-trained representations and of the fine-tuned model.

paragraphs: Restricted Boltzmann machines model data distributions and learn useful features. Their computational tractability relies heavily on hidden units activating independently once an input is given. Introducing competition between those units could encourage sparse representations, but it also breaks the independence that makes ordinary RBMs convenient to compute with.

The paper shows that an existing dynamic programming algorithm can implement exact sparsity in the hidden layer. This makes a direct constraint on hidden activity computationally manageable, addressing the belief that such competition necessarily makes the model intractable. The approach brings an attractive property of sparse coding into the RBM setting through an explicit computational procedure.

The authors also show how derivatives can pass through a layer with exact sparsity. This enables fine-tuning a deep belief network built from RBMs with sparse hidden layers, extending the idea beyond isolated feature learning. They report improved performance for both pretrained representations and the fine-tuned model. The contribution therefore covers both enforcing sparse activity and training deeper models that contain it.
summary.tldr: Dynamic programming makes exact hidden-layer sparsity tractable in RBMs and supports fine-tuning deep networks built from them.

title: Cardinality Restricted Boltzmann Machines

abstract: How does the human visual system compute the speed of a coherent motion stimulus that contains motion energy in different spatiotemporal frequency bands? Here we propose that perceived speed is the result of optimal integration of speed information from independent spatiotemporal frequency tuned channels. We formalize this hypothesis with a Bayesian observer model that treats the channel activity as independent cues, which are optimally combined with a prior expectation for slow speeds. We test the model against behavioral data from a 2AFC speed discrimination task with which we measured subjects' perceived speed of drifting sinusoidal gratings with different contrasts and spatial frequencies, and of various combinations of these single gratings. We find that perceived speed of the combined stimuli is independent of the relative phase of the underlying grating components, and that the perceptual biases and discrimination thresholds are always smaller for the combined stimuli, supporting the cue combination hypothesis. The proposed Bayesian model fits the data well, accounting for perceptual biases and thresholds of both simple and combined stimuli. Fits are improved if we assume that the channel responses are subject to divisive normalization, which is in line with physiological evidence. Our results provide an important step toward a more complete model of visual motion perception that can predict perceived speeds for stimuli of arbitrary spatial structure.

paragraphs: A moving visual pattern can contain motion information at several spatial and temporal frequencies. This paper asks how the visual system combines those signals into one perceived speed. It proposes a Bayesian observer that treats frequency-tuned channels as independent cues and combines their information with a prior preference for slower motion.

The authors test the proposal using a two-alternative forced-choice speed-discrimination task. Participants view drifting sinusoidal gratings with different contrasts and spatial frequencies, along with combinations of those gratings. In the measured conditions, combined patterns produce smaller perceptual biases and discrimination thresholds, and their perceived speed does not depend on the relative phase of the component gratings.

The results support the cue-combination hypothesis and advance a broader account of motion perception, while prediction for arbitrary spatial structures remains the larger objective toward which the work contributes.
summary.tldr: Behavioral results support a Bayesian account in which independent frequency-tuned motion cues combine with a slow-speed prior to determine perceived speed.

title: Optimal integration of visual speed across different spatiotemporal frequency channels

abstract: Label propagation is one of the state-of-the-art methods for semi-supervised learning, which estimates labels by propagating label information through a graph. Label propagation assumes that data points (nodes) connected in a graph should have similar labels. Consequently, the label estimation heavily depends on edge weights in a graph which represent similarity of each node pair. We propose a method for a graph to capture the manifold structure of input features using edge weights parameterized by a similarity function. In this approach, edge weights represent both similarity and local reconstruction weight simultaneously, both being reasonable for label propagation. For further justification, we provide analytical considerations including an interpretation as a cross-validation of a propagation model in the feature space, and an error analysis based on a low dimensional manifold model. Experimental results demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach both in synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: Label propagation estimates unknown labels by spreading information through a graph connecting data points. Its usefulness depends heavily on the edge weights: strongly connected points are assumed to have similar labels. This paper focuses on adapting those weights so that the graph captures the manifold structure of the input features.

The authors parameterize edge weights with a similarity function and give each weight two simultaneous roles. It measures similarity between points and also serves as a local reconstruction weight. Linking these roles makes the graph reflect how nearby feature vectors relate to one another, supplying a structural basis for the connections used during propagation.

The paper offers an interpretation of the method as cross-validation of a propagation model in feature space. It also analyzes error under a low-dimensional manifold model. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. Together, the analysis and experiments support adapting the similarity graph through feature structure as a way to improve the foundation on which label propagation operates.
summary.tldr: Adapting graph weights to serve as both similarities and local reconstruction weights improves label propagation in the reported experiments.

title: Manifold-based Similarity Adaptation for Label Propagation

abstract: Motivated by the desire to extend fast randomized techniques to nonlinear $l_p$ regression, we consider a class of structured regression problems. These problems involve Vandermonde matrices which arise naturally in various statistical modeling settings, including classical polynomial fitting problems and recently developed randomized techniques for scalable kernel methods. We show that this structure can be exploited to further accelerate the solution of the regression problem, achieving running times that are faster than input sparsity''. We present empirical results confirming both the practical value of our modeling framework, as well as speedup benefits of randomized regression."

We present empirical results confirming both the practical value of our modeling framework, as well as speedup benefits of randomized regression."

paragraphs: Randomized methods can accelerate regression, and this paper investigates how to extend their benefits to structured nonlinear lₚ regression problems. The focus is on problems involving Vandermonde matrices. These matrices arise in polynomial fitting and in randomized techniques for making kernel methods scalable, connecting the analysis to several statistical modeling settings.

The main idea is to exploit the matrix's structure when accelerating the regression computation. Treating a structured matrix as a generic collection of entries can overlook opportunities supplied by its organization. The authors show that exploiting this organization produces running times faster than input sparsity, the benchmark associated with the number of nonzero entries in the matrix.

That speed claim is established for the structured regression problems considered in the paper. Empirical results support both the practical usefulness of the modeling framework and the speed benefits of randomized regression. The contribution is therefore a combination of structured modeling and faster computation: the same mathematical form that defines the regression problem also enables additional algorithmic savings.
summary.tldr: Exploiting Vandermonde structure accelerates randomized nonlinear regression beyond input-sparsity running times in the studied problem class.

title: Sketching Structured Matrices for Faster Nonlinear Regression

abstract: Pairwise clustering methods partition the data space into clusters by the pairwise similarity between data points. The success of pairwise clustering largely depends on the pairwise similarity function defined over the data points, where kernel similarity is broadly used. In this paper, we present a novel pairwise clustering framework by bridging the gap between clustering and multi-class classification. This pairwise clustering framework learns an unsupervised nonparametric classifier from each data partition, and search for the optimal partition of the data by minimizing the generalization error of the learned classifiers associated with the data partitions. We consider two nonparametric classifiers in this framework, i.e. the nearest neighbor classifier and the plug-in classifier. Modeling the underlying data distribution by nonparametric kernel density estimation, the generalization error bounds for both unsupervised nonparametric classifiers are the sum of nonparametric pairwise similarity terms between the data points for the purpose of clustering. Under uniform distribution, the nonparametric similarity terms induced by both unsupervised classifiers exhibit a well known form of kernel similarity. We also prove that the generalization error bound for the unsupervised plug-in classifier is asymptotically equal to the weighted volume of cluster boundary for Low Density Separation, a widely used criteria for semi-supervised learning and clustering. Based on the derived nonparametric pairwise similarity using the plug-in classifier, we propose a new nonparametric exemplar-based clustering method with enhanced discriminative capability, whose superiority is evidenced by the experimental results.

paragraphs: This paper connects clustering to classification by evaluating a proposed partition through a classifier learned from that partition. It seeks a partition whose associated classifier has low generalization error. This gives pairwise similarity a predictive interpretation: points should be grouped according to relationships that support distinguishing the resulting clusters.

The framework considers nearest-neighbor and plug-in classifiers, modeling the underlying distribution through kernel density estimation. Bounds on the classifiers’ generalization errors become sums of pairwise similarity terms.
