Using the derived plug-in similarity, the authors construct an exemplar-based clustering method and report experimental evidence of improved discrimination and performance. The contribution joins a theoretical account of similarity with a clustering procedure motivated by that account.
summary.tldr: Classifier generalization bounds yield clustering similarities that connect kernel methods, low-density separation, and exemplar-based clustering.

title: On a Theory of Nonparametric Pairwise Similarity for Clustering: Connecting Clustering to Classification

abstract: Learning accurate prior knowledge of natural images is of great importance for single image super-resolution (SR). Existing SR methods either learn the prior from the low/high-resolution patch pairs or estimate the prior models from the input low-resolution (LR) image. Specifically, high-frequency details are learned in the former methods. Though effective, they are heuristic and have limitations in dealing with blurred LR images; while the latter suffers from the limitations of frequency aliasing. In this paper, we propose to combine those two lines of ideas for image super-resolution. More specifically, the parametric sparse prior of the desirable high-resolution (HR) image patches are learned from both the input low-resolution (LR) image and a training image dataset. With the learned sparse priors, the sparse codes and thus the HR image patches can be accurately recovered by solving a sparse coding problem. Experimental results show that the proposed SR method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both subjective and objective image qualities.

Existing approaches learn this knowledge from paired low- and high-resolution patches or estimate it from the input image itself. The paper identifies difficulties with both: paired-patch methods can struggle with blurred inputs, while input-based estimation is affected by frequency aliasing.

The proposed approach combines these two information sources. It learns parametric sparse priors for the desired high-resolution patches using both the observed low-resolution image and a training image dataset. This lets the prior draw on the particular input while also incorporating information from external training images.

With those priors learned, the method solves a sparse coding problem to recover sparse codes and the corresponding high-resolution patches. Experiments report improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods in both subjective appearance and objective image quality. The findings support the paper’s central design choice: combining input-specific evidence and dataset knowledge when estimating the image prior used for reconstruction.
summary.tldr: The method improves image super-resolution by learning sparse priors jointly from the input image and an external training dataset.

title: Learning Parametric Sparse Models for Image Super-Resolution

abstract: Learning cooperative policies for multi-agent systems is often challenged by partial observability and a lack of coordination. In some settings, the structure of a problem allows a distributed solution with limited communication. Here, we consider a scenario where no communication is available, and instead we learn local policies for all agents that collectively mimic the solution to a centralized multi-agent static optimization problem. Our main contribution is an information theoretic framework based on rate distortion theory which facilitates analysis of how well the resulting fully decentralized policies are able to reconstruct the optimal solution. Moreover, this framework provides a natural extension that addresses which nodes an agent should communicate with to improve the performance of its individual policy.

Moreover, this framework provides a natural extension that addresses which nodes an agent should communicate with to improve the performance of its individual policy.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents can struggle when each sees only part of a problem and cannot coordinate directly. This paper considers the especially restrictive case in which agents have no communication available. It learns a separate local policy for each agent, aiming for their combined behavior to approximate the solution of a centralized multi-agent static optimization problem.

The main contribution is an information-theoretic framework built on rate-distortion theory. The framework analyzes how closely the decentralized policies can reconstruct the centralized optimum. This gives a way to reason about the quality of collective decisions when each decision must be produced from locally available information.

The same framework also supports an extension in which communication becomes a design choice. It addresses which other nodes an agent should communicate with to improve its own policy’s performance. Together, the two settings connect the quality achievable without communication to the potential value of particular communication partners, while keeping the centralized static solution as the reference for the original learning problem.
summary.tldr: A rate-distortion framework analyzes how well local, noncommunicating agents can collectively approximate a centralized solution.

title: Fully Decentralized Policies for Multi-Agent Systems: An Information Theoretic Approach

abstract: Discovering statistical structure from links is a fundamental problem in the analysis of social networks. Choosing a misspecified model, or equivalently, an incorrect inference algorithm will result in an invalid analysis or even falsely uncover patterns that are in fact artifacts of the model. This work focuses on unifying two of the most widely used link-formation models: the stochastic block model (SBM) and the small world (or latent space) model (SWM). Integrating techniques from kernel learning, spectral graph theory, and nonlinear dimensionality reduction, we develop the first statistically sound polynomial-time algorithm to discover latent patterns in sparse graphs for both models. When the network comes from an SBM, the algorithm outputs a block structure. When it is from an SWM, the algorithm outputs estimates of each node's latent position.

paragraphs: A network's links can reflect different kinds of hidden organization. The paper focuses on two widely used explanations: stochastic block models, which describe block structure, and small-world or latent-space models, which describe nodes through latent positions. Selecting an inappropriate model can lead an analysis to report patterns created by its own assumptions.

The authors develop a unified algorithm using techniques from kernel learning, spectral graph theory, and nonlinear dimensionality reduction. It is designed to discover latent structure in sparse graphs under either of the two model families. The abstract identifies it as the first statistically sound polynomial-time algorithm covering both settings.

The output depends on the network's generating model. For a stochastic block model, the algorithm returns blocks; for a small-world model, it estimates each node's latent position. This matters because the method can recover two different forms of organization within one framework. Its stated coverage is specifically these two model families, so the result does not establish correctness for every possible network-generating process.
summary.tldr: A unified polynomial-time algorithm recovers blocks or latent positions in sparse graphs generated by two major network models.

title: From which world is your graph

abstract: The focus in machine learning has branched beyond training classifiers on a single task to investigating how previously acquired knowledge in a source domain can be leveraged to facilitate learning in a related target domain, known as inductive transfer learning. Three active lines of research have independently explored transfer learning using neural networks. In weight transfer, a model trained on the source domain is used as an initialization point for a network to be trained on the target domain. In deep metric learning, the source domain is used to construct an embedding that captures class structure in both the source and target domains. In few-shot learning, the focus is on generalizing well in the target domain based on a limited number of labeled examples. We compare state-of-the-art methods from these three paradigms and also explore hybrid adapted-embedding methods that use limited target-domain data to fine tune embeddings constructed from source-domain data. We conduct a systematic comparison of methods in a variety of domains, varying the number of labeled instances available in the target domain (k), as well as the number of target-domain classes. We reach three principal conclusions: (1) Deep embeddings are far superior, compared to weight transfer, as a starting point for inter-domain transfer or model re-use (2) Our hybrid methods robustly outperform every few-shot learning and every deep metric learning method previously proposed, with a mean error reduction of 34% over state-of-the-art. (3) Among loss functions for discovering embeddings, the histogram loss (Ustinova & Lempitsky, 2016) is most robust. We hope our results will motivate a unification of research in weight transfer, deep metric learning, and few-shot learning.

summary.tldr: Adapting source-trained embeddings with limited target data improves few-shot transfer across the paper’s systematic comparisons.

title: Adapted Deep Embeddings: A Synthesis of Methods for k-Shot Inductive Transfer Learning

abstract: We study the sample complexity of learning one-hidden-layer convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with non-overlapping filters. We propose a novel algorithm called approximate gradient descent for training CNNs, and show that, with high probability, the proposed algorithm with random initialization grants a linear convergence to the ground-truth parameters up to statistical precision. Compared with existing work, our result applies to general non-trivial, monotonic and Lipschitz continuous activation functions including ReLU, Leaky ReLU, Sigmod and Softplus etc. Moreover, our sample complexity beats existing results in the dependency of the number of hidden nodes and filter size. In fact, our result matches the information-theoretic lower bound for learning one-hidden-layer CNNs with linear activation functions, suggesting that our sample complexity is tight. Our theoretical analysis is backed up by numerical experiments.

paragraphs: How much data is needed to recover the parameters of a convolutional network? This paper studies that question for networks with one hidden layer and non-overlapping filters. It proposes approximate gradient descent and analyzes both the speed of parameter recovery and the number of samples required.

Starting from random initialization, the algorithm converges linearly to the ground-truth parameters up to statistical precision, with high probability. The result covers general nontrivial activation functions that are monotonic and Lipschitz continuous, including ReLU, Leaky ReLU, Sigmoid, and Softplus. This broadens the activation functions covered by the analysis while retaining the specified network structure.

It also matches an information-theoretic lower bound for the linear-activation case, suggesting tight sample complexity. Numerical experiments support the theory. The lower-bound comparison is specifically to linear activations, so its broader significance is evidence of tightness rather than a separately established lower bound for every covered activation.
summary.tldr: Approximate gradient descent learns the studied one-hidden-layer CNNs with improved sample complexity and high-probability linear convergence up to statistical precision.

title: Tight Sample Complexity of Learning One-hidden-layer Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: This paper presents a new Unified pre-trained Language Model (UniLM) that can be fine-tuned for both natural language understanding and generation tasks. The model is pre-trained using three types of language modeling tasks: unidirectional, bidirectional, and sequence-to-sequence prediction. The unified modeling is achieved by employing a shared Transformer network and utilizing specific self-attention masks to control what context the prediction conditions on. UniLM compares favorably with BERT on the GLUE benchmark, and the SQuAD 2.0 and CoQA question answering tasks. Moreover, UniLM achieves new state-of-the-art results on five natural language generation datasets, including improving the CNN/DailyMail abstractive summarization ROUGE-L to 40.51 (2.04 absolute improvement), the Gigaword abstractive summarization ROUGE-L to 35.75 (0.86 absolute improvement), the CoQA generative question answering F1 score to 82.5 (37.1 absolute improvement), the SQuAD question generation BLEU-4 to 22.12 (3.75 absolute improvement), and the DSTC7 document-grounded dialog response generation NIST-4 to 2.67 (human performance is 2.65). The code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/microsoft/unilm.

UniLM brings these capabilities into a shared pretrained model that can be fine-tuned for either kind of task. Its pretraining combines unidirectional prediction, bidirectional prediction, and sequence-to-sequence prediction within one Transformer network.

The mechanism is to change self-attention masks, which control what context a prediction can access. Different masks let the shared network operate under the context restrictions required by the three training tasks. This provides a concrete way to combine multiple language modeling behaviors while retaining a common set of network parameters.

UniLM compares favorably with BERT on GLUE and the SQuAD 2.0 and CoQA question answering tasks. It also reports state-of-the-art results on five generation datasets spanning summarization, question answering, question generation, and document-grounded dialogue. For example, CNN/DailyMail summarization reaches 40.51 ROUGE-L, an absolute improvement of 2.04, and SQuAD question generation reaches 22.12 BLEU-4, improving by 3.75. These results show that the unified pretraining approach supports both understanding and varied forms of text generation.
summary.tldr: UniLM uses attention masks to train one Transformer for multiple language modeling tasks, supporting both understanding and generation.

title: Unified Language Model Pre-training for Natural Language Understanding and Generation

abstract: Geometric embeddings have recently received attention for their natural ability to represent transitive asymmetric relations via containment. Box embeddings, where objects are represented by n-dimensional hyperrectangles, are a particularly promising example of such an embedding as they are closed under intersection and their volume can be calculated easily, allowing them to naturally represent calibrated probability distributions. The benefits of geometric embeddings also introduce a problem of local identifiability, however, where whole neighborhoods of parameters result in equivalent loss which impedes learning. Prior work addressed some of these issues by using an approximation to Gaussian convolution over the box parameters, however this intersection operation also increases the sparsity of the gradient. In this work we model the box parameters with min and max Gumbel distributions, which were chosen such that the space is still closed under the operation of intersection. The calculation of the expected intersection volume involves all parameters, and we demonstrate experimentally that this drastically improves the ability of such models to learn.

paragraphs: Box embeddings represent objects as multidimensional rectangles. Containment naturally represents transitive asymmetric relationships, while intersections and easily computed volumes support probabilistic representations. These useful geometric properties also create a learning problem: whole neighborhoods of parameter values can produce the same loss, leaving optimization unable to distinguish nearby alternatives.

Earlier work addressed some of this local identifiability problem through an approximation to Gaussian convolution over box parameters, but its intersection operation also made gradients sparser. This paper instead models box parameters using minimum and maximum Gumbel distributions. The distributions are chosen so that intersecting boxes preserves the relevant family, retaining a key structural property of the representation.

With this construction, the expected intersection volume depends on all parameters. That provides a route for the learning objective to involve parameters that could otherwise receive little useful gradient information. Experiments demonstrate a drastic improvement in the models' ability to learn. The result connects the choice of probabilistic box parameterization directly to better optimization behavior.
summary.tldr: Gumbel-distributed box parameters preserve intersection structure while making expected intersection volumes involve all parameters, substantially improving learning experimentally.

title: Improving Local Identifiability in Probabilistic Box Embeddings

abstract: We revisit the problem of learning from untrusted batches introduced by Qiao and Valiant [QV17]. Recently, Jain and Orlitsky [JO19] gave a simple semidefinite programming approach based on the cut-norm that achieves essentially information-theoretically optimal error in polynomial time. Concurrently, Chen et al. [CLM19] considered a variant of the problem where μ is assumed to be structured, e.g. log-concave, monotone hazard rate, t-modal, etc. In this case, it is possible to achieve the same error with sample complexity sublinear in n, and they exhibited a quasi-polynomial time algorithm for doing so using Haar wavelets. In this paper, we find an appealing way to synthesize the techniques of [JO19] and [CLM19] to give the best of both worlds: an algorithm which runs in polynomial time and can exploit structure in the underlying distribution to achieve sublinear sample complexity. Along the way, we simplify the approach of [JO19] by avoiding the need for SDP rounding and giving a more direct interpretation of it through the lens of soft filtering, a powerful recent technique in high-dimensional robust estimation. We validate the usefulness of our algorithms in preliminary experimental evaluations.

paragraphs: Learning a distribution from untrusted batches requires coping with unreliable groups of observations. Prior approaches offered two useful properties separately: polynomial running time with essentially optimal error, and reduced sample requirements when the distribution has structure. The latter approach required quasi-polynomial running time. This paper combines these strengths in one algorithm.

The structural setting includes distribution families such as log-concave, monotone hazard rate, and distributions with a bounded number of modes. By synthesizing techniques from the two earlier approaches, the method exploits such structure to obtain sample complexity sublinear in n while keeping runtime polynomial. The improvement therefore concerns both data requirements and computational efficiency.

The paper also simplifies the semidefinite programming approach by removing the need for a rounding step. It interprets the method more directly through soft filtering, a technique from robust estimation. Preliminary experiments support the algorithms' usefulness. The main contribution remains the theoretical and algorithmic combination: structure can reduce the samples needed without retaining the earlier quasi-polynomial computational cost.
summary.tldr: The paper combines polynomial runtime with structure-dependent sublinear sample complexity for learning distributions from untrusted batches.

title: Learning Structured Distributions From Untrusted Batches: Faster and Simpler

abstract: Previous methods decompose blind super resolution (SR) problem into two sequential steps: \textit{i}) estimating blur kernel from given low-resolution (LR) image and \textit{ii}) restoring SR image based on estimated kernel. This two-step solution involves two independently trained models, which may not well compatible with each other. Small estimation error of the first step could cause severe performance drop of the second one. While on the other hand, the first step can only utilize limited information from LR image, which makes it difficult to predict highly accurate blur kernel. Towards these issues, instead of considering these two steps separately, we adopt an alternating optimization algorithm, which can estimate blur kernel and restore SR image in a single model. Specifically, we design two convolutional neural modules, namely \textit{Restorer} and \textit{Estimator}. \textit{Restorer} restores SR image based on predicted kernel, and \textit{Estimator} estimates blur kernel with the help of restored SR image. We alternate these two modules repeatedly and unfold this process to form an end-to-end trainable network. In this way, \textit{Estimator} utilizes information from both LR and SR images, which makes the estimation of blur kernel easier. More importantly, \textit{Restorer} is trained with the kernel estimated by \textit{Estimator}, instead of ground-truth kernel, thus \textit{Restorer} could be more tolerant to the estimation error of \textit{Estimator}. Extensive experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world images show that our model can largely outperform state-of-the-art methods and produce more visually favorable results at much higher speed. The source code will be publicly available.

That separation can create incompatibility: a small blur-estimation error can seriously damage restoration, while estimating blur from the low-resolution image alone provides limited information.

The paper combines a Restorer and an Estimator in one network. The Restorer uses the current blur estimate to reconstruct an image, and the Estimator uses that reconstruction to improve the blur estimate. Repeating and unfolding this alternating process creates an end-to-end trainable system in which each module helps the other.

The Estimator gains access to both low-resolution and restored images. Meanwhile, the Restorer trains with the Estimator’s actual predictions, which could make it more tolerant of estimation errors. Experiments on synthetic datasets and real images report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods, visually preferable outputs, and much higher speed. The results support learning the two coupled tasks together.
summary.tldr: An end-to-end network alternates blur estimation and image restoration, improving blind super-resolution quality and speed in the reported experiments.

title: Unfolding the Alternating Optimization for Blind Super Resolution

abstract: Various differentially private algorithms instantiate the exponential mechanism, and require sampling from the distribution $\exp(-f)$ for a suitable function $f$. When the domain of the distribution is high-dimensional, this sampling can be challenging. Using heuristic sampling schemes such as Gibbs sampling does not necessarily lead to provable privacy. When $f$ is convex, techniques from log-concave sampling lead to polynomial-time algorithms, albeit with large polynomials. Langevin dynamics-based algorithms offer much faster alternatives under some distance measures such as statistical distance. In this work, we establish rapid convergence for these algorithms under distance measures more suitable for differential privacy. For smooth, strongly-convex $f$, we give the first results proving convergence in R\'enyi divergence. This gives us fast differentially private algorithms for such $f$. Our techniques and simple and generic and apply also to underdamped Langevin dynamics.

paragraphs: Many differentially private algorithms use the exponential mechanism, which requires drawing samples from a distribution proportional to exp(−f). Sampling can be difficult in high dimensions. A sampling heuristic may produce plausible outputs without supplying the mathematical control needed to establish privacy, making the quality of its convergence guarantee consequential.

Langevin dynamics offers fast sampling methods, but convergence under a familiar distance measure does not automatically provide the guarantee most useful for differential privacy. This paper analyzes discretized Langevin methods using Rényi divergence. For smooth, strongly convex functions f, the authors establish rapid convergence and describe their results as the first convergence guarantees in that divergence.

These guarantees yield fast differentially private algorithms for functions satisfying the stated conditions. The techniques also apply to underdamped Langevin dynamics, extending the analysis to another form of the sampling process. The contribution therefore links computationally attractive samplers to a measure of distributional approximation suited to privacy analysis, rather than relying only on evidence that a sampler approaches its target in some other sense.
summary.tldr: Rényi-divergence convergence guarantees for Langevin sampling enable fast private algorithms when the target potential is smooth and strongly convex.

title: Faster Differentially Private Samplers via Rényi Divergence Analysis of Discretized Langevin MCMC

abstract: Despite its high search efficiency, differential architecture search (DARTS) often selects network architectures with dominated skip connections which lead to performance degradation. However, theoretical understandings on this issue remain absent, hindering the development of more advanced methods in a principled way. In this work, we solve this problem by theoretically analyzing the effects of various types of operations, e.g. convolution, skip connection and zero operation, to the network optimization. We prove that the architectures with more skip connections can converge faster than the other candidates, and thus are selected by DARTS. This result, for the first time, theoretically and explicitly reveals the impact of skip connections to fast network optimization and its competitive advantage over other types of operations in DARTS. Then we propose a theory-inspired path-regularized DARTS that consists of two key modules: (i) a differential group-structured sparse binary gate introduced for each operation to avoid unfair competition among operations, and (ii) a path-depth-wise regularization used to incite search exploration for deep architectures that often converge slower than shallow ones as shown in our theory and are not well explored during search. Experimental results on image classification tasks validate its advantages. Codes and models will be released.

paragraphs: Differentiable architecture search, or DARTS, can efficiently choose neural network structures, but often favors architectures dominated by skip connections and suffers degraded performance. This paper analyzes how convolutions, skip connections, and zero operations affect optimization. It proves that architectures with more skip connections can converge faster, explaining their competitive advantage during the search.

The proposed path-regularized DARTS uses two mechanisms informed by that analysis. A differentiable, group-structured sparse binary gate is assigned to each operation to avoid unfair competition among operations. A path-depth regularizer encourages exploration of deeper architectures, which the theory shows often converge more slowly than shallow ones and consequently receive insufficient exploration.

Image classification experiments validate advantages of the proposed method. The paper's central insight is that speed of optimization can influence which architecture wins the search, creating a preference for skip-heavy candidates. Its method addresses that preference through how operations compete and how depth is encouraged, connecting a theoretical explanation of search behavior to concrete changes in the search procedure.
summary.tldr: An analysis of skip connections' optimization advantage motivates gates and depth regularization that improve differentiable architecture search in image classification experiments.

title: Theory-Inspired Path-Regularized Differential Network Architecture Search

abstract: Training neural network models with discrete (categorical or structured) latent variables can be computationally challenging, due to the need for marginalization over large or combinatorial sets. To circumvent this issue, one typically resorts to sampling-based approximations of the true marginal, requiring noisy gradient estimators (e.g., score function estimator) or continuous relaxations with lower-variance reparameterized gradients (e.g., Gumbel-Softmax). In this paper, we propose a new training strategy which replaces these estimators by an exact yet efficient marginalization. To achieve this, we parameterize discrete distributions over latent assignments using differentiable sparse mappings: sparsemax and its structured counterparts. In effect, the support of these distributions is greatly reduced, which enables efficient marginalization. We report successful results in three tasks covering a range of latent variable modeling applications: a semisupervised deep generative model, a latent communication game, and a generative model with a bit-vector latent representation. In all cases, we obtain good performance while still achieving the practicality of sampling-based approximations.

We report successful results in three tasks covering a range of latent variable modeling applications: a semisupervised deep generative model, a latent communication game, and a generative model with a bit-vector latent representation. In all cases, we obtain good performance while still achieving the practicality of sampling-based approximations.

paragraphs: Neural models with discrete latent variables often need to sum over many possible hidden assignments during training. For structured variables, the number of assignments can grow combinatorially. Common workarounds approximate this sum through sampling or replace discrete choices with continuous relaxations, introducing the need for specialized gradient estimators.

This paper changes how the latent distribution is represented. Differentiable sparse mappings, including sparsemax and structured variants, assign nonzero probability to a much smaller set of possibilities. The model can then sum exactly over that reduced support. Exactness applies to the resulting sparse distribution: computational savings come from representing fewer active assignments, rather than approximating their sum through sampled assignments.

The authors evaluate the strategy in a semisupervised deep generative model, a latent communication game, and a generative model with bit-vector latent variables. They report good performance across all three while retaining the practicality associated with sampling-based approximations. The results show how a sparse probability representation can make exact marginalization usable in several forms of latent-variable learning.
summary.tldr: Sparse latent distributions make exact marginalization efficient by restricting the sum to assignments with nonzero probability.

title: Efficient Marginalization of Discrete and Structured Latent Variables via Sparsity

abstract: Metric learning is an important family of algorithms for classiﬁcation and similarity search, but the robustness of learned metrics against small adversarial perturbations is less studied. In this paper, we show that existing metric learning algorithms, which focus on boosting the clean accuracy, can result in metrics that are less robust than the Euclidean distance. To overcome this problem, we propose a novel metric learning algorithm to ﬁnd a Mahalanobis distance that is robust against adversarial perturbations, and the robustness of the resulting model is certiﬁable. Experimental results show that the proposed metric learning algorithm improves both certiﬁed robust errors and empirical robust errors (errors under adversarial attacks). Furthermore, unlike neural network defenses which usually encounter a trade-off between clean and robust errors, our method does not sacriﬁce clean errors compared with previous metric learning methods.

paragraphs: Metric learning adapts the notion of distance used for classification and similarity search. This paper asks whether learned distances remain reliable under small adversarial changes to their inputs. The authors show that methods emphasizing accuracy on unperturbed data can produce metrics that are less robust than ordinary Euclidean distance.

They propose an algorithm that learns a Mahalanobis distance with robustness as an explicit goal. The resulting model has certifiable robustness, providing a guarantee rather than relying only on observed behavior under selected attacks. This changes the learning objective from improving clean performance alone to constructing a distance that also supports protection against adversarial perturbations.

Experiments report improvements in both certified robust error and empirical error under adversarial attacks. The method also avoids sacrificing clean-data error relative to previous metric-learning methods in the reported comparisons. These findings show that the robustness weaknesses identified in conventional metric learning can be addressed while retaining clean performance, rather than assuming that a learned distance is automatically safer or more reliable.
summary.tldr: A certifiably robust metric-learning algorithm improves adversarial performance without sacrificing clean performance in the reported comparisons.

title: Provably Robust Metric Learning

abstract: Zero-shot semantic segmentation (ZSS) aims to classify pixels of novel classes without training examples available. Recently, most ZSS methods focus on learning the visual-semantic correspondence to transfer knowledge from seen classes to unseen classes at the pixel level. Yet, few works study the adverse effects caused by the noisy and outlying training samples in the seen classes. In this paper, we identify this challenge and address it with a novel framework that learns to discriminate noisy samples based on Bayesian uncertainty estimation. Specifically, we model the network outputs with Gaussian and Laplacian distributions, with the variances accounting for the observation noise as well as the uncertainty of input samples. Learning objectives are then derived with the estimated variances playing as adaptive attenuation for individual samples in training. Consequently, our model learns more attentively from representative samples of seen classes while suffering less from noisy and outlying ones, thus providing better reliability and generalization toward unseen categories. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through comprehensive experiments on multiple challenging benchmarks, and show that our method achieves significant accuracy improvement over previous approaches for large open-set segmentation.

summary.tldr: Uncertainty-based weighting reduces the influence of noisy seen-class samples and improves segmentation accuracy on unseen categories.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Learning for Zero-Shot Semantic Segmentation

abstract: We consider running multiple instances of multi-armed bandit (MAB) problems in parallel. A main motivation for this study are online recommendation systems, in which each of $N$ users is associated with a MAB problem and the goal is to exploit users' similarity in order to learn users' preferences to $K$ items more efficiently. We consider the adversarial MAB setting, whereby an adversary is free to choose which user and which loss to present to the learner during the learning process. Users are in a social network and the learner is aided by a-priori knowledge of the strengths of the social links between all pairs of users. It is assumed that if the social link between two users is strong then they tend to share the same action. The regret is measured relative to an arbitrary function which maps users to actions. The smoothness of the function is captured by a resistance-based dispersion measure $\Psi$. We present two learning algorithms, GABA-I and GABA-II, which exploit the network structure to bias towards functions of low $\Psi$ values. We show that GABA-I has an expected regret bound of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ln(NK/\Psi)\Psi KT})$ and per-trial time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(K\ln(N))$, whilst GABA-II has a weaker $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ln(N/\Psi)\ln(NK/\Psi)\Psi KT})$ regret, but a better $\mathcal{O}(\ln(K)\ln(N))$ per-trial time complexity. We highlight improvements of both algorithms over running independent standard MABs across users.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn recommendations for many users together when feedback can be adversarial. Each user has a separate multi-armed bandit problem: the learner chooses among items and receives limited feedback. An adversary can choose both which user appears and the losses presented. The learner also knows the strengths of social connections between users.

The central assumption is that strongly connected users tend to prefer the same action. The authors express this through a resistance-based measure of how smoothly a user-to-action assignment varies across the network. Their algorithms, GABA-I and GABA-II, favor assignments with low dispersion, allowing social structure to guide learning across users.

The two algorithms offer different trade-offs. GABA-I has the stronger expected regret guarantee, while GABA-II processes each interaction faster, particularly as the number of items grows. The analysis identifies improvements over learning independently for every user. Those benefits are expressed through the network dispersion measure, connecting the guarantees to how well users’ preferred actions align with their social links.
summary.tldr: Two bandit algorithms use social connections to share learning across users, with different trade-offs between regret guarantees and computation.

title: A Gang of Adversarial Bandits

abstract: We study k-median clustering under the sequential no-substitution setting. In this setting, a data stream is sequentially observed, and some of the points are selected by the algorithm as cluster centers. However, a point can be selected as a center only immediately after it is observed, before observing the next point. In addition, a selected center cannot be substituted later. We give the first algorithm for this setting that obtains a constant approximation factor on the optimal cost under a random arrival order, an exponential improvement over previous work. This is also the first constant approximation guarantee that holds without any structural assumptions on the input data. Moreover, the number of selected centers is only quasi-linear in k. Our algorithm and analysis are based on a careful cost estimation that avoids outliers, a new concept of a linear bin division, and a multi-scale approach to center selection.

paragraphs: The paper studies clustering when data arrive one point at a time and decisions cannot be revised. A point can become a cluster center only when it arrives, before the next point is seen. Once selected, a center cannot be replaced. These restrictions make it difficult to achieve a low clustering cost because early choices must be made without seeing the full dataset.

The proposed algorithm achieves a constant approximation to the optimal k-median cost when arrival order is random. Its guarantee requires no structural assumptions about the input data. Random arrival remains an explicit condition, however. The algorithm also selects a number of centers that is quasi-linear in k, so the guarantee allows more than exactly k selected centers.

The analysis combines cost estimates that avoid outliers, a new device called linear bin division, and center selection at multiple scales. The authors identify their constant-factor guarantee as the first in this setting and an exponential improvement over previous work. It shows that irreversible streaming decisions can still provide a strong approximation under random ordering.
summary.tldr: Under random arrival, an irreversible streaming clustering algorithm achieves a constant approximation using quasi-linearly many centers in k.

title: A Constant Approximation Algorithm for Sequential Random-Order No-Substitution k-Median Clustering

abstract: We consider the privacy-preserving machine learning (ML) setting where the trained model must satisfy differential privacy (DP) with respect to the labels of the training examples. We propose two novel approaches based on, respectively, the Laplace mechanism and the PATE framework, and demonstrate their effectiveness on standard benchmarks.While recent work by Ghazi et al. proposed Label DP schemes based on a randomized response mechanism, we argue that additive Laplace noise coupled with Bayesian inference (ALIBI) is a better fit for typical ML tasks. Moreover, we show how to achieve very strong privacy levels in some regimes, with our adaptation of the PATE framework that builds on recent advances in semi-supervised learning.We complement theoretical analysis of our algorithms' privacy guarantees with empirical evaluation of their memorization properties. Our evaluation suggests that comparing different algorithms according to their provable DP guarantees can be misleading and favor a less private algorithm with a tighter analysis.Code for implementation of algorithms and memorization attacks is available from https://github.com/facebookresearch/label_dp_antipodes.

paragraphs: The paper studies label differential privacy: the trained model must provide a formal privacy guarantee for the labels attached to training examples. This specifies which part of the training data is protected. The authors develop two approaches and examine both their theoretical privacy guarantees and their behavior on standard benchmarks.

The first approach, ALIBI, combines additive Laplace noise with Bayesian inference. The authors argue that this combination suits typical machine-learning tasks better than the randomized-response mechanisms used in recent label-privacy methods. The second adapts the PATE framework using advances in semi-supervised learning. That adaptation can achieve very strong privacy levels in some regimes, a qualification central to the claim.

The evaluation also investigates memorization, providing an empirical perspective alongside formal guarantees. It suggests that ranking algorithms solely by their proven differential-privacy bounds can be misleading: a tighter analysis can make an algorithm look preferable even when empirical evaluation suggests weaker privacy. The contribution therefore includes both new learning methods and a warning about treating the tightness of a privacy analysis as a complete comparison of algorithms.
summary.tldr: Two label-private learning methods show promising results while highlighting that formal privacy bounds alone can give misleading algorithm comparisons.

title: Antipodes of Label Differential Privacy: PATE and ALIBI

abstract: We prove analogues of the popular bounded difference inequality (also called McDiarmid's inequality) for functions of independent random variables under sub-gaussian and sub-exponential conditions. Applied to vector-valued concentration and the method of Rademacher complexities these inequalities allow an easy extension of uniform convergence results for PCA and linear regression to the case potentially unbounded input- and output variables.
originalAbstract: We prove analogues of the popular bounded difference inequality (also called McDiarmid's inequality) for functions of independent random variables under sub-gaussian and sub-exponential conditions. paragraphs: Concentration inequalities describe how tightly a random quantity stays around its typical value. The familiar bounded difference inequality provides such control for functions of independent random inputs when changes in individual inputs have bounded effects. This paper proves related inequalities under sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential conditions, extending the available tools beyond that bounded setting.

The key distinction is between requiring strict bounds and controlling the probability of unusually large values. Sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential conditions provide forms of tail control, allowing potentially unbounded variables while still restricting their fluctuations. Independence remains part of the setting studied here, so the contribution does not remove all structural assumptions about the data.

The authors apply the inequalities to vector-valued concentration and Rademacher complexity, a tool used to study generalization. These applications extend uniform convergence results for principal component analysis and linear regression to potentially unbounded inputs and outputs. The significance is theoretical: established ways of relating sample behavior to population behavior can continue to work under these broader, explicitly controlled tail conditions.
summary.tldr: New concentration inequalities extend uniform convergence tools for PCA and linear regression to potentially unbounded data with controlled tails.

title: Concentration inequalities under sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential conditions

abstract: We develop a new primitive for stochastic optimization: a low-bias, low-cost estimator of the minimizer $x_\star$ of any Lipschitz strongly-convex function $f$. In particular, we use a multilevel Monte-Carlo approach due to Blanchet and Glynn to turn any optimal stochastic gradient method into an estimator of $x_\star$ with bias $\delta$, variance $O(\log(1/\delta))$, and an expected sampling cost of $O(\log(1/\delta))$ stochastic gradient evaluations. As an immediate consequence, we obtain cheap and nearly unbiased gradient estimators for the Moreau envelope of any Lipschitz convex function. We demonstrate the potential of our estimator through four applications. First, we develop a method for minimizing the maximum of $N$ functions, improving on recent results and matching a lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Second and third, we recover state-of-the-art rates for projection-efficient and gradient-efficient optimization using simple algorithms with a transparent analysis. Finally, we show that an improved version of our estimator would yield a nearly linear-time, optimal-utility, differentially-private non-smooth stochastic optimization method.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization often needs an approximate solution as a component inside a larger algorithm. This paper develops an estimator of the minimizer of a Lipschitz, strongly convex function that combines low bias with low expected computational cost. The distinction matters because a cheap approximation can still introduce systematic error into subsequent computations.

Using multilevel Monte Carlo, the method transforms an optimal stochastic gradient procedure into an estimator with bias δ. Its variance and expected number of stochastic gradient evaluations both scale as O(log(1/δ)). An immediate application produces inexpensive, nearly unbiased gradient estimates for the Moreau envelope, a smoothed representation of a Lipschitz convex function.

The authors use this estimator to improve optimization of the maximum of N functions, matching a lower bound up to logarithmic factors. They also recover leading rates for projection-efficient and gradient-efficient optimization with simple algorithms. A final implication is explicitly conditional: an improved estimator would enable nearly linear-time, optimal-utility private nonsmooth stochastic optimization. That prospective application is distinct from the guarantees achieved by the current estimator.
summary.tldr: A multilevel Monte Carlo estimator reduces optimization bias at logarithmic expected sampling cost and supports several efficient optimization algorithms.

title: Stochastic Bias-Reduced Gradient Methods

abstract: Many black-box optimization tasks arising in high-stakes applications require risk-averse decisions. The standard Bayesian optimization (BO) paradigm, however, optimizes the expected value only. We generalize BO to trade mean and input-dependent variance of the objective, both of which we assume to be unknown a priori. In particular, we propose a novel risk-averse heteroscedastic Bayesian optimization algorithm (RAHBO) that aims to identify a solution with high return and low noise variance, while learning the noise distribution on the fly. To this end, we model both expectation and variance as (unknown) RKHS functions, and propose a novel risk-aware acquisition function. We bound the regret for our approach and provide a robust rule to report the final decision point for applications where only a single solution must be identified. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RAHBO on synthetic benchmark functions and hyperparameter tuning tasks.

paragraphs: Optimizing an uncertain black-box objective can require balancing strong average outcomes against variability. Standard Bayesian optimization targets the expected value, but this paper also considers noise variance that changes with the input. Both the expected objective and its variance are assumed unknown before optimization begins.

The proposed algorithm, RAHBO, seeks a solution with high return and low noise variance while learning the noise distribution during the search. It models the expectation and variance as unknown functions in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. A risk-aware acquisition function then guides which inputs to evaluate, making variability part of the search criterion.

The authors establish a regret bound and provide a robust rule for reporting a final decision when an application requires one selected solution. Experiments on synthetic benchmark functions and hyperparameter tuning demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness. The work connects risk-sensitive search with final selection, so that the concern for variable outcomes is reflected in both stages of the optimization process.
summary.tldr: RAHBO learns unknown input-dependent noise while optimizing a trade-off between high expected return and low variance.

title: Risk-averse Heteroscedastic Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) produce high-quality images but are challenging to train. They need careful regularization, vast amounts of compute, and expensive hyper-parameter sweeps. We make significant headway on these issues by projecting generated and real samples into a fixed, pretrained feature space. Motivated by the finding that the discriminator cannot fully exploit features from deeper layers of the pretrained model, we propose a more effective strategy that mixes features across channels and resolutions. Our Projected GAN improves image quality, sample efficiency, and convergence speed. It is further compatible with resolutions of up to one Megapixel and advances the state-of-the-art Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) on twenty-two benchmark datasets. Importantly, Projected GANs match the previously lowest FIDs up to 40 times faster, cutting the wall-clock time from 5 days to less than 3 hours given the same computational resources.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks can produce high-quality images, but training them can require substantial computation, careful regularization, and expensive parameter searches. This paper changes the information presented to the discriminator by projecting both real and generated images into the feature space of a fixed pretrained model.

Simply using pretrained features leaves some of their value untapped: the authors find that the discriminator does not fully exploit deeper features. Their solution mixes features across channels and resolutions. This changes how the pretrained representation is made available to the discriminator, helping it use information that the straightforward projection approach does not effectively exploit.

Projected GAN improves image quality, sample efficiency, and convergence speed in the reported evaluations. It supports resolutions up to one megapixel and improves the best reported Fréchet Inception Distance on twenty-two benchmark datasets. Matching previous best FID results takes up to forty times less time, including a reduction from five days to under three hours with the same computational resources.
summary.tldr: Projected GAN mixes fixed pretrained features across channels and resolutions to improve image generation and reach prior best FID results up to forty times faster.

title: Projected GANs Converge Faster

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent with backpropagation is the workhorse of artificial neural networks. It has long been recognized that backpropagation fails to be a biologically plausible algorithm. Fundamentally, it is a non-local procedure---updating one neuron's synaptic weights requires knowledge of synaptic weights or receptive fields of downstream neurons. This limits the use of artificial neural networks as a tool for understanding the biological principles of information processing in the brain. Lillicrap et al. (2016) propose a more biologically plausible "feedback alignment" algorithm that uses random and fixed backpropagation weights, and show promising simulations. In this paper we study the mathematical properties of the feedback alignment procedure by analyzing convergence and alignment for two-layer networks under squared error loss. In the overparameterized setting, we prove that the error converges to zero exponentially fast, and also that regularization is necessary in order for the parameters to become aligned with the random backpropagation weights. Simulations are given that are consistent with this analysis and suggest further generalizations. These results contribute to our understanding of how biologically plausible algorithms might carry out weight learning in a manner different from Hebbian learning, with performance that is comparable with the full non-local backpropagation algorithm.

paragraphs: Standard backpropagation updates a neuron's weights using information about downstream weights. This nonlocal dependence makes it difficult to interpret as a biological learning mechanism. Feedback alignment instead uses fixed random weights to carry information backward.

The paper studies the mathematics of feedback alignment in two-layer networks trained with squared error loss. It separates two questions: whether the prediction error approaches zero, and whether learned parameters become aligned with the random feedback weights.

In the overparameterized setting considered, the authors prove that the error decreases to zero exponentially fast. They also show that regularization is necessary for parameter alignment in their analysis. These results distinguish successful error reduction from the separate property of alignment with the feedback pathway.

Simulations agree with the analysis and suggest possible generalizations. The findings contribute to understanding how a more biologically plausible learning procedure could achieve performance comparable to full backpropagation. The formal conclusions concern the stated network, loss, and overparameterized setting; the suggested extensions go beyond what those proofs establish.
summary.tldr: For overparameterized two-layer networks, feedback alignment achieves exponentially vanishing error, while parameter alignment requires regularization in the analyzed setting.

title: Convergence and Alignment of Gradient Descent with Random Backpropagation Weights

abstract: We consider the estimation of treatment effects in settings when multiple treatments are assigned over time and treatments can have a causal effect on future outcomes. We propose an extension of the double/debiased machine learning framework to estimate the dynamic effects of treatments and apply it to a concrete linear Markovian high-dimensional state space model and to general structural nested mean models. Our method allows the use of arbitrary machine learning methods to control for the high dimensional state, subject to a mean square error guarantee, while still allowing parametric estimation and construction of confidence intervals for the dynamic treatment effect parameters of interest. Our method is based on a sequential regression peeling process, which we show can be equivalently interpreted as a Neyman orthogonal moment estimator. This allows us to show root-n asymptotic normality of the estimated causal effects.

Our method allows the use of arbitrary machine learning methods to control for the high dimensional state, subject to a mean square error guarantee, while still allowing parametric estimation and construction of confidence intervals for the dynamic treatment effect parameters of interest. paragraphs: When treatments are assigned repeatedly over time, a treatment can influence outcomes that occur later. This paper extends double/debiased machine learning to estimate these dynamic causal effects. The aim is to combine flexible modeling of a high-dimensional evolving state with interpretable treatment-effect parameters and confidence intervals.

The method uses a sequential regression peeling process. The authors show that this procedure can also be understood as a Neyman orthogonal moment estimator, providing the connection to debiased estimation. Machine learning methods can be chosen flexibly to control for the high-dimensional state, subject to a mean-square-error guarantee. That qualification is part of the framework’s support for statistical inference.

The authors apply the approach to a linear Markovian high-dimensional state-space model and to general structural nested mean models. They establish root-n asymptotic normality for the estimated causal effects, a statistical result that supports confidence-interval construction. The contribution is a way to retain parametric inference for dynamic treatment effects while using machine learning to handle the more complex state variables surrounding treatment decisions.
summary.tldr: A sequential debiasing method enables dynamic treatment-effect inference while allowing machine learning to model high-dimensional states under an error guarantee.

title: Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Dynamic Treatment Effects

abstract: In this paper, we study the nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization problem on decentralized setting. The minimax problems are attracting increasing attentions because of their popular practical applications such as policy evaluation and adversarial training. As training data become larger, distributed training has been broadly adopted in machine learning tasks. Recent research works show that the decentralized distributed data-parallel training techniques are specially promising, because they can achieve the efficient communications and avoid the bottleneck problem on the central node or the latency of low bandwidth network. However, the decentralized minimax problems were seldom studied in literature and the existing methods suffer from very high gradient complexity. To address this challenge, we propose a new faster decentralized algorithm, named as DM-HSGD, for nonconvex minimax problems by using the variance reduced technique of hybrid stochastic gradient descent. We prove that our DM-HSGD algorithm achieves stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexity of $O(\kappa^3 \epsilon^{-3})$ for decentralized stochastic nonconvex-strongly-concave problem to search an $\epsilon$-stationary point, which improves the exiting best theoretical results. Moreover, we also prove that our algorithm achieves linear speedup with respect to the number of workers. Our experiments on decentralized settings show the superior performance of our new algorithm.

The minimax problems are attracting increasing attentions because of their popular practical applications such as policy evaluation and adversarial training. Recent research works show that the decentralized distributed data-parallel training techniques are specially promising, because they can achieve the efficient communications and avoid the bottleneck problem on the central node or the latency of low bandwidth network. However, the decentralized minimax problems were seldom studied in literature and the existing methods suffer from very high gradient complexity. We prove that our DM-HSGD algorithm achieves stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexity of $O(\kappa^3 \epsilon^{-3})$ for decentralized stochastic nonconvex-strongly-concave problem to search an $\epsilon$-stationary point, which improves the exiting best theoretical results. Moreover, we also prove that our algorithm achieves linear speedup with respect to the number of workers. Our experiments on decentralized settings show the superior performance of our new algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems where one set of variables is minimized while another is maximized, with computation distributed across workers without a central coordinator. Its specific setting is nonconvex in the minimizing variables and strongly concave in the maximizing variables. Such problems arise in applications including policy evaluation and adversarial training.

The proposed algorithm, DM-HSGD, uses a variance-reduction technique based on hybrid stochastic gradient descent. The aim is to reduce the number of stochastic gradient evaluations needed to make progress. This addresses a computational weakness of existing decentralized minimax methods while retaining the communication advantages that motivate decentralized training.

The authors prove a stochastic first-order oracle complexity of O(κ³ε⁻³) for reaching an ε-stationary point, improving the previous best theoretical result cited in the abstract. This is a guarantee about approximate stationarity rather than global optimality. They also prove linear speedup with the number of workers. Experiments in decentralized settings support the algorithm’s performance advantages.
summary.tldr: DM-HSGD improves theoretical gradient complexity for decentralized nonconvex–strongly-concave minimax optimization and provides linear speedup with the number of workers.

title: A Faster Decentralized Algorithm for Nonconvex Minimax Problems

abstract: We study the Stochastic Shortest Path (SSP) problem in which an agent has to reach a goal state in minimum total expected cost. In the learning formulation of the problem, the agent has no prior knowledge about the costs and dynamics of the model. She repeatedly interacts with the model for $K$ episodes, and has to minimize her regret. In this work we show that the minimax regret for this setting is $\widetilde O(\sqrt{ (B_\star^2 + B_\star) |S| |A| K})$ where $B_\star$ is a bound on the expected cost of the optimal policy from any state, $S$ is the state space, and $A$ is the action space. This matches the $\Omega (\sqrt{ B_\star^2 |S| |A| K})$ lower bound of Rosenberg et al. [2020] for $B_\star \ge 1$, and improves their regret bound by a factor of $\sqrt{|S|}$. For $B_\star < 1$ we prove a matching lower bound of $\Omega (\sqrt{ B_\star |S| |A| K})$. Our algorithm is based on a novel reduction from SSP to finite-horizon MDPs. To that end, we provide an algorithm for the finite-horizon setting whose leading term in the regret depends polynomially on the expected cost of the optimal policy and only logarithmically on the horizon.
originalAbstract: We study the Stochastic Shortest Path (SSP) problem in which an agent has to reach a goal state in minimum total expected cost. In the learning formulation of the problem, the agent has no prior knowledge about the costs and dynamics of the model. She repeatedly interacts with the model for $K$ episodes, and has to minimize her regret. In this work we show that the minimax regret for this setting is $\widetilde O(\sqrt{ (B_\star^2 + B_\star) |S| |A| K})$ where $B_\star$ is a bound on the expected cost of the optimal policy from any state, $S$ is the state space, and $A$ is the action space. This matches the $\Omega (\sqrt{ B_\star^2 |S| |A| K})$ lower bound of Rosenberg et al. [2020] for $B_\star \ge 1$, and improves their regret bound by a factor of $\sqrt{|S|}$. For $B_\star < 1$ we prove a matching lower bound of $\Omega (\sqrt{ B_\star |S| |A| K})$. Our algorithm is based on a novel reduction from SSP to finite-horizon MDPs. To that end, we provide an algorithm for the finite-horizon setting whose leading term in the regret depends polynomially on the expected cost of the optimal policy and only logarithmically on the horizon.

paragraphs: In stochastic shortest-path learning, an agent repeatedly tries to reach a goal at minimum expected total cost without initially knowing action costs or environment dynamics. The paper studies regret over K episodes: the extra cost incurred while learning compared with optimal behavior. Its main result identifies the worst-case achievable rate in terms of problem size and optimal-policy cost.

The upper bound scales, up to logarithmic factors, as the square root of (B² + B) times the number of states, actions, and episodes. Here B bounds the optimal policy's expected cost from any state. For B at least one, the result matches an existing lower bound up to logarithmic factors and improves the previous upper bound by a square-root-of-state-count factor. For smaller B, the paper proves a matching lower bound.

The algorithm reduces shortest-path learning to finite-horizon decision problems. A supporting algorithm makes the leading regret term depend polynomially on optimal expected cost but only logarithmically on the horizon. This connects the learning guarantee more closely to cost while controlling horizon dependence.
summary.tldr: A reduction to finite-horizon learning yields stochastic shortest-path regret bounds matching lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

title: Minimax Regret for Stochastic Shortest Path

abstract: We present an oracle-efficient algorithm for boosting the adversarial robustness of barely robust learners. Barely robust learning algorithms learn predictors that are adversarially robust only on a small fraction $\beta \ll 1$ of the data distribution. Our proposed notion of barely robust learning requires robustness with respect to a ``larger'' perturbation set; which we show is necessary for strongly robust learning, and that weaker relaxations are not sufficient for strongly robust learning. Our results reveal a qualitative and quantitative equivalence between two seemingly unrelated problems: strongly robust learning and barely robust learning.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness concerns whether predictions withstand permitted changes to an input. This paper asks whether strong robustness can be obtained from learning algorithms whose predictors are robust on only a small fraction of the data distribution. It calls these starting algorithms barely robust learners.

The authors present an oracle-efficient boosting algorithm that strengthens such learners. A crucial qualification concerns which changes the starting learner must withstand: its robustness must hold for a larger perturbation set. The initial requirement therefore combines limited coverage of the data distribution with robustness against a broader set of input changes. Robustness on a small fraction alone is not the condition used by the result.

The paper shows that the larger-set requirement is necessary for strongly robust learning and that weaker relaxations do not suffice. Its main finding is a qualitative and quantitative equivalence between strong robust learning and this particular form of barely robust learning. This provides a way to characterize the weaker learning capability needed for boosting, while identifying why simply weakening the robustness requirement further would fail.
summary.tldr: Barely robust learners can be boosted to strong robustness under a larger-perturbation-set requirement that the paper shows is necessary.

title: Boosting Barely Robust Learners: A New Perspective on Adversarial Robustness

abstract: Neural rendering can be used to reconstruct implicit representations of shapes without 3D supervision. However, current neural surface reconstruction methods have difficulty learning high-frequency geometry details, so the reconstructed shapes are often over-smoothed. We develop HF-NeuS, a novel method to improve the quality of surface reconstruction in neural rendering. We follow recent work to model surfaces as signed distance functions (SDFs). First, we offer a derivation to analyze the relationship between the SDF, the volume density, the transparency function, and the weighting function used in the volume rendering equation and propose to model transparency as a transformed SDF. Second, we observe that attempting to jointly encode high-frequency and low-frequency components in a single SDF leads to unstable optimization. We propose to decompose the SDF into base and displacement functions with a coarse-to-fine strategy to increase the high-frequency details gradually. Finally, we design an adaptive optimization strategy that makes the training process focus on improving those regions near the surface where the SDFs have artifacts. Our qualitative and quantitative results show that our method can reconstruct fine-grained surface details and obtain better surface reconstruction quality than the current state of the art. Code available at https://github.com/yiqun-wang/HFS.

paragraphs: Neural rendering can reconstruct shapes without direct 3D supervision, but the resulting surfaces often lose fine geometric detail. HF-NeuS addresses this oversmoothing using a signed distance function, a representation that describes a surface through distances to it. The method targets both how this representation connects to rendering and how it is optimized.

The authors analyze the relationships between the signed distance function, density, transparency, and rendering weights, then model transparency through a transformed signed distance function. They also identify unstable optimization when one function must learn coarse structure and fine detail together. Their solution separates base geometry from displacement and gradually introduces higher-frequency detail through coarse-to-fine learning.

An adaptive optimization strategy further concentrates training on regions near the surface where artifacts remain. Together, these choices organize learning around increasingly detailed geometry and targeted corrections. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations show finer reconstructed surface details and better reconstruction quality than the state-of-the-art methods considered in the paper.
summary.tldr: HF-NeuS reconstructs finer surfaces by separating coarse geometry from detail and concentrating optimization near surface artifacts.

title: HF-NeuS: Improved Surface Reconstruction Using High-Frequency Details

abstract: Backdoor learning is an emerging and vital topic for studying deep neural networks' vulnerability (DNNs). Many pioneering backdoor attack and defense methods are being proposed, successively or concurrently, in the status of a rapid arms race. However, we find that the evaluations of new methods are often unthorough to verify their claims and accurate performance, mainly due to the rapid development, diverse settings, and the difficulties of implementation and reproducibility. Without thorough evaluations and comparisons, it is not easy to track the current progress and design the future development roadmap of the literature. To alleviate this dilemma, we build a comprehensive benchmark of backdoor learning called BackdoorBench. It consists of an extensible modular-based codebase (currently including implementations of 8 state-of-the-art (SOTA) attacks and 9 SOTA defense algorithms) and a standardized protocol of complete backdoor learning. We also provide comprehensive evaluations of every pair of 8 attacks against 9 defenses, with 5 poisoning ratios, based on 5 models and 4 datasets, thus 8,000 pairs of evaluations in total. We present abundant analysis from different perspectives about these 8,000 evaluations, studying the effects of different factors in backdoor learning. All codes and evaluations of BackdoorBench are publicly available at https://backdoorbench.github.io.

paragraphs: Research on neural-network backdoor attacks and defenses develops rapidly, but evaluating progress is difficult when implementations and experimental settings vary. The paper argues that incomplete comparisons make it hard to verify reported performance or understand how new methods relate to existing ones. BackdoorBench addresses this evaluation problem with shared infrastructure.

The benchmark combines an extensible, modular codebase with a standardized protocol for backdoor learning. Its reported implementation includes eight attack methods and nine defense methods. The evaluation covers attack-defense pairings across five poisoning ratios, five models, and four datasets, with the abstract reporting 8,000 evaluation pairs in total.

The authors analyze these evaluations from several perspectives to study how different factors affect backdoor learning. The contribution is therefore both a collection of implementations and a common experimental basis for comparing them. Publicly available code and evaluations support reproducibility and further investigation, while the modular design provides a way to incorporate additional methods as the research area develops.
summary.tldr: BackdoorBench standardizes implementations and evaluations of backdoor attacks and defenses to make comparisons more reproducible.

title: BackdoorBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark of Backdoor Learning

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in long horizon and sparse reward tasks is notoriously difficult and requires a lot of training steps. A standard solution to speed up the process is to leverage additional reward signals, shaping it to better guide the learning process.In the context of language-conditioned RL, the abstraction and generalisation properties of the language input provide opportunities for more efficient ways of shaping the reward.In this paper, we leverage this idea and propose an automated reward shaping method where the agent extracts auxiliary objectives from the general language goal. These auxiliary objectives use a question generation (QG) and a question answering (QA) system: they consist of questions leading the agent to try to reconstruct partial information about the global goal using its own trajectory.When it succeeds, it receives an intrinsic reward proportional to its confidence in its answer. This incentivizes the agent to generate trajectories which unambiguously explain various aspects of the general language goal.Our experimental study using various BabyAI environments shows that this approach, which does not require engineer intervention to design the auxiliary objectives, improves sample efficiency by effectively directing the exploration.

paragraphs: An agent pursuing a long-term goal may receive little feedback until it succeeds, making useful behavior difficult to discover. EAGER addresses this sparse-reward problem in reinforcement learning guided by language. It uses the language goal to automatically construct auxiliary objectives that provide additional feedback during exploration.

A question-generation system creates questions about parts of the overall goal. A question-answering system then tries to recover the relevant information using the agent's own trajectory. When it succeeds, the agent receives an intrinsic reward proportional to confidence in the answer. This encourages behavior whose trajectory clearly reveals aspects of the requested goal, connecting the additional rewards to the instruction the agent is supposed to follow.

Experiments across several BabyAI environments show improved sample efficiency through more effective exploration. The auxiliary objectives do not require an engineer to design them individually. The result supports using question generation and answering as an automatic bridge from a broad language instruction to more frequent learning signals.
summary.tldr: EAGER turns language goals into automatically generated questions and rewards trajectories that answer them, improving sample efficiency in BabyAI.

title: EAGER: Asking and Answering Questions for Automatic Reward Shaping in Language-guided RL

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) can be used to improve future performance by leveraging historical data. There exist many different algorithms for offline RL, and it is well recognized that these algorithms, and their hyperparameter settings, can lead to decision policies with substantially differing performance. This prompts the need for pipelines that allow practitioners to systematically perform algorithm-hyperparameter selection for their setting. Critically, in most real-world settings, this pipeline must only involve the use of historical data. Inspired by statistical model selection methods for supervised learning, we introduce a task- and method-agnostic pipeline for automatically training, comparing, selecting, and deploying the best policy when the provided dataset is limited in size. In particular, our work highlights the importance of performing multiple data splits to produce more reliable algorithm-hyperparameter selection. While this is a common approach in supervised learning, to our knowledge, this has not been discussed in detail in the offline RL setting. We show it can have substantial impacts when the dataset is small. Compared to alternate approaches, our proposed pipeline outputs higher-performing deployed policies from a broad range of offline policy learning algorithms and across various simulation domains in healthcare, education, and robotics. This work contributes toward the development of a general-purpose meta-algorithm for automatic algorithm-hyperparameter selection for offline RL.
