title: PASS: Path-selective State Space Model for Event-based Recognition

abstract: Motivated by the need to identify new and clinically relevant categories of lung disease, we propose a novel clustering with constraints method using a Dirichlet process mixture of Gaussian processes in a variational Bayesian nonparametric framework. We claim that individuals should be grouped according to biological and/or genetic similarity regardless of their level of disease severity; therefore, we introduce a new way of looking at subtyping/clustering by recasting it in terms of discovering associations of individuals to disease trajectories (i.e., grouping individuals based on their similarity in response to environmental and/or disease causing variables). The nonparametric nature of our algorithm allows for learning the unknown number of meaningful trajectories. Additionally, we acknowledge the usefulness of expert guidance by providing for their input using must-link and cannot- link constraints. These constraints are encoded with Markov random fields. We also provide an efficient variational approach for performing inference on our model.

paragraphs: Motivated by lung-disease subtyping, the paper proposes grouping people according to shared biological or genetic patterns rather than their current disease severity. It reframes clustering as associating individuals with disease trajectories: people belong together when they respond similarly to environmental or disease-causing variables.

The model uses a Dirichlet process mixture of Gaussian processes within a variational Bayesian nonparametric framework. Its nonparametric structure allows it to learn an unknown number of meaningful trajectories. This makes the number of groups part of the learning problem, while the trajectory perspective allows individuals at different severity levels to be associated with a similar underlying response pattern.

Experts can guide the clustering through must-link and cannot-link constraints, which are encoded using Markov random fields. The authors also provide an efficient variational inference procedure. The contribution is a combination of trajectory-based grouping, a learned number of groups, and explicit expert input, aimed at discovering clinically relevant categories of disease.
summary.tldr: A constrained nonparametric Gaussian-process mixture groups individuals by disease-response trajectories while learning the number of groups.

title: Nonparametric Mixture of Gaussian Processes with Constraints

abstract: Training machine learning models sometimes needs to be done on large amounts of data that exceed the capacity of a single machine, motivating recent works on developing algorithms that train in a distributed fashion. This paper proposes an efficient box-constrained quadratic optimization algorithm for distributedly training linear support vector machines (SVMs) with large data. Our key technical contribution is an analytical solution to the problem of computing the optimal step size at each iteration, using an efficient method that requires only O(1) communication cost to ensure fast convergence. With this optimal step size, our approach is superior to other methods by possessing global linear convergence, or, equivalently, O(\log(1/ε)) iteration complexity for an epsilon-accurate solution, for distributedly solving the non-strongly-convex linear SVM dual problem. Experiments also show that our method is significantly faster than state-of- the-art distributed linear SVM algorithms including DSVM-AVE, DisDCA and TRON.

paragraphs: Training a linear support vector machine can require more data than a single machine can hold. This paper addresses distributed training through the model's dual optimization problem, a quadratic objective with bounds on its variables. The goal is to make progress toward the solution efficiently while coordinating computation across machines.

The central contribution is an analytical way to compute the optimal step size at each iteration. Its communication cost is O(1), so this particular calculation requires only constant communication. The step-size result is paired with a global linear convergence guarantee even though the linear SVM dual problem is not strongly convex.

Linear convergence means the iteration requirement grows as O(log(1/ε)) for an ε-accurate solution. This gives a precise account of how the method approaches higher accuracy. Experiments also report substantially faster training than the distributed SVM algorithms compared in the paper. Together, the results connect a low-communication step-size calculation to both a convergence guarantee and observed training speed.
summary.tldr: An optimal step-size calculation with constant communication enables globally linearly convergent distributed training of linear SVMs.

title: Distributed Box-Constrained Quadratic Optimization for Dual Linear SVM

abstract: Interactive querying of a database degrades the privacy level. In this paper we answer the fundamental question of characterizing the level of privacy degradation as a function of the number of adaptive interactions and the differential privacy levels maintained by the individual queries. Our solution is complete: the privacy degradation guarantee is true for every privacy mechanism, and further, we demonstrate a sequence of privacy mechanisms that do degrade in the characterized manner. The key innovation is the introduction of an operational interpretation (involving hypothesis testing) to differential privacy and the use of the corresponding data processing inequalities. Our result improves over the state of the art and has immediate applications to several problems studied in the literature.
originalAbstract: Interactive querying of a database degrades the privacy level. In this paper we answer the fundamental question of characterizing the level of privacy degradation as a function of the number of adaptive interactions and the differential privacy levels maintained by the individual queries. Our solution is complete: the privacy degradation guarantee is true for every privacy mechanism, and further, we demonstrate a sequence of privacy mechanisms that do degrade in the characterized manner. The key innovation is the introduction of an operational interpretation (involving hypothesis testing) to differential privacy and the use of the corresponding data processing inequalities. Our result improves over the state of the art and has immediate applications to several problems studied in the literature.

paragraphs: Repeated queries to a database can weaken privacy, even when each query individually satisfies differential privacy. The issue becomes especially important for adaptive interactions, where later queries can depend on earlier responses. This paper characterizes the resulting privacy degradation using the number of interactions and the privacy levels of the individual queries.

The authors establish a guarantee that holds for every privacy mechanism covered by the characterization. They also exhibit a sequence of mechanisms that attains the characterized degradation. These two parts make the result tight: the bound protects against all mechanisms in scope, and an example shows that it cannot generally be strengthened.

The key analytical step is to interpret differential privacy operationally through hypothesis testing and use the associated data-processing inequalities. This supplies a way to reason about how privacy changes as outputs are combined and used adaptively. The result improves previous guarantees and has immediate applications to several problems in the literature. Its importance is precise accounting of cumulative privacy loss under repeated interaction.
summary.tldr: The paper tightly characterizes cumulative differential-privacy degradation under adaptive queries using a hypothesis-testing interpretation.

title: The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy

abstract: In this work, we investigate the accelerated proximal gradient method for nonconvex programming (APGnc). The method compares between a usual proximal gradient step and a linear extrapolation step, and accepts the one that has a lower function value to achieve a monotonic decrease. In specific, under a general nonsmooth and nonconvex setting, we provide a rigorous argument to show that the limit points of the sequence generated by APGnc are critical points of the objective function. Then, by exploiting the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz (KL) property for a broad class of functions, we establish the linear and sub-linear convergence rates of the function value sequence generated by APGnc. We further propose a stochastic variance reduced APGnc (SVRG-APGnc), and establish its linear convergence under a special case of the KL property. We also extend the analysis to the inexact version of these methods and develop an adaptive momentum strategy that improves the numerical performance.

The method compares between a usual proximal gradient step and a linear extrapolation step, and accepts the one that has a lower function value to achieve a monotonic decrease. In specific, under a general nonsmooth and nonconvex setting, we provide a rigorous argument to show that the limit points of the sequence generated by APGnc are critical points of the objective function. Then, by exploiting the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz (KL) property for a broad class of functions, we establish the linear and sub-linear convergence rates of the function value sequence generated by APGnc. We further propose a stochastic variance reduced APGnc (SVRG-APGnc), and establish its linear convergence under a special case of the KL property. We also extend the analysis to the inexact version of these methods and develop an adaptive momentum strategy that improves the numerical performance.

paragraphs: Momentum can change how an optimization method moves, but understanding its behavior is harder when the objective is nonsmooth and nonconvex. This paper studies accelerated proximal gradient for nonconvex programming, called APGnc. At each iteration, it compares a standard proximal gradient candidate with a linear extrapolation candidate and accepts the one with the lower objective value.

This selection produces a monotonic decrease in the objective. The authors prove that limit points of the generated sequence are critical points under their general nonsmooth, nonconvex setting. They then use the Kurdyka–Lojasiewicz property to establish linear and sublinear rates for objective values across a broad class of functions. These guarantees concern critical points, without asserting global optimality.

The paper also introduces a stochastic variance-reduced version and proves linear convergence under a special case of that property. Further analysis covers inexact versions of the methods. An adaptive momentum strategy improves numerical performance, connecting the convergence analysis to a practical choice about how aggressively to extrapolate.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional convergence guarantees for proximal gradient methods that compare momentum steps against ordinary updates.

title: Convergence Analysis of Proximal Gradient with Momentum for Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: In conventional ODE modelling coefficients of an equation driving the system state forward in time are estimated. However, for many complex systems it is practically impossible to determine the equations or interactions governing the underlying dynamics. In these settings, parametric ODE model cannot be formulated. Here, we overcome this issue by introducing a novel paradigm of nonparametric ODE modelling that can learn the underlying dynamics of arbitrary continuous-time systems without prior knowledge. We propose to learn non-linear, unknown differential functions from state observations using Gaussian process vector fields within the exact ODE formalism. We demonstrate the model’s capabilities to infer dynamics from sparse data and to simulate the system forward into future.
originalAbstract: In conventional ODE modelling coefficients of an equation driving the system state forward in time are estimated. However, for many complex systems it is practically impossible to determine the equations or interactions governing the underlying dynamics. In these settings, parametric ODE model cannot be formulated. Here, we overcome this issue by introducing a novel paradigm of nonparametric ODE modelling that can learn the underlying dynamics of arbitrary continuous-time systems without prior knowledge. We propose to learn non-linear, unknown differential functions from state observations using Gaussian process vector fields within the exact ODE formalism. We demonstrate the model’s capabilities to infer dynamics from sparse data and to simulate the system forward into future.

paragraphs: Conventional differential-equation modeling begins with an equation for how a system changes and then estimates its coefficients. For complex systems, choosing that equation can be the main obstacle: the relevant interactions may be unknown. This paper moves the learning problem from estimating coefficients in a chosen equation to estimating the unknown dynamics themselves.

The authors use Gaussian process vector fields to learn nonlinear differential functions from observations of system states. These functions describe how the state changes over continuous time. The method retains the exact ordinary differential equation formalism while using a nonparametric representation, so the governing functional form does not need to be specified in advance.

The demonstrations show that the model can infer dynamics from sparse observations and simulate the system into the future. These capabilities connect learning the underlying rule of change with predicting a trajectory. The paper presents a broad modeling paradigm for unknown continuous-time dynamics, with empirical demonstrations of sparse-data inference and forward simulation.
summary.tldr: Gaussian process vector fields learn unknown continuous-time dynamics from state observations and support forward simulation within an ODE model.

title: Learning unknown ODE models with Gaussian processes

abstract: We describe two efficient, and exact, algorithms for computing Bellman updates in robust Markov decision processes (MDPs). The first algorithm uses a homotopy continuation method to compute updates for L1-constrained s,a-rectangular ambiguity sets. It runs in quasi-linear time for plain L1-norms and also generalizes to weighted L1-norms. The second algorithm uses bisection to compute updates for robust MDPs with s-rectangular ambiguity sets. This algorithm, when combined with the homotopy method, also has a quasi-linear runtime. Unlike previous methods, our algorithms compute the primal solution in addition to the optimal objective value, which makes them useful in policy iteration methods. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed methods are over 1,000 times faster than Gurobi, a state-of-the-art commercial optimization package, for small instances, and the performance gap grows considerably with problem size.
originalAbstract: We describe two efficient, and exact, algorithms for computing Bellman updates in robust Markov decision processes (MDPs). The first algorithm uses a homotopy continuation method to compute updates for L1-constrained s,a-rectangular ambiguity sets. It runs in quasi-linear time for plain L1-norms and also generalizes to weighted L1-norms. The second algorithm uses bisection to compute updates for robust MDPs with s-rectangular ambiguity sets. This algorithm, when combined with the homotopy method, also has a quasi-linear runtime. Unlike previous methods, our algorithms compute the primal solution in addition to the optimal objective value, which makes them useful in policy iteration methods. paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes evaluate decisions while accounting for uncertainty represented by ambiguity sets. Their Bellman updates are a central computational step. This paper develops two exact algorithms that make those updates efficient for particular ambiguity-set structures, addressing the computation directly rather than replacing it with an approximate update.

The first algorithm uses homotopy continuation for L1-constrained state-action rectangular sets. It has quasi-linear running time for ordinary L1 norms and also extends to weighted L1 norms. The second uses bisection for state-rectangular sets; combined with the homotopy method, it also achieves quasi-linear runtime. Both return a primal solution as well as the optimal objective value, which supports their use in policy iteration.

Experiments report speedups of more than 1,000 times over Gurobi on small instances, with the gap increasing substantially as problems grow. These are empirical comparisons for the evaluated problems. Together with exactness and the runtime results, they show how exploiting the specified uncertainty structures can substantially reduce the cost of robust planning.
summary.tldr: Two exact algorithms accelerate robust Bellman updates for specified ambiguity sets and return solutions useful for policy iteration.

title: Fast Bellman Updates for Robust MDPs

abstract: Amortized variational inference (AVI) replaces instance-specific local inference with a global inference network. While AVI has enabled efficient training of deep generative models such as variational autoencoders (VAE), recent empirical work suggests that inference networks can produce suboptimal variational parameters. We propose a hybrid approach, to use AVI to initialize the variational parameters and run stochastic variational inference (SVI) to refine them. Crucially, the local SVI procedure is itself differentiable, so the inference network and generative model can be trained end-to-end with gradient-based optimization. This semi-amortized approach enables the use of rich generative models without experiencing the posterior-collapse phenomenon common in training VAEs for problems like text generation. Experiments show this approach outperforms strong autoregressive and variational baselines on standard text and image datasets.
originalAbstract: Amortized variational inference (AVI) replaces instance-specific local inference with a global inference network. While AVI has enabled efficient training of deep generative models such as variational autoencoders (VAE), recent empirical work suggests that inference networks can produce suboptimal variational parameters. We propose a hybrid approach, to use AVI to initialize the variational parameters and run stochastic variational inference (SVI) to refine them. Crucially, the local SVI procedure is itself differentiable, so the inference network and generative model can be trained end-to-end with gradient-based optimization. This semi-amortized approach enables the use of rich generative models without experiencing the posterior-collapse phenomenon common in training VAEs for problems like text generation. Experiments show this approach outperforms strong autoregressive and variational baselines on standard text and image datasets.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders often use a shared inference network to produce variational parameters for each input. This amortized approach makes training efficient, but the network’s output can be suboptimal for an individual example. The paper addresses that problem by combining shared inference with local refinement.

The inference network first supplies an initial set of variational parameters. Stochastic variational inference then improves those parameters for the particular input. Crucially, the refinement procedure is differentiable, allowing gradients to pass through the local optimization. The inference network and generative model can therefore be trained together with the refinement included in the learning process.

The authors report that this semi-amortized approach supports rich generative models without the posterior-collapse problem common in VAE training for tasks such as text generation. Experiments outperform strong autoregressive and variational baselines on standard text and image datasets. The results support learning an initialization and refining it jointly, so the shared network’s first estimate need not be the final inference result.
summary.tldr: Semi-amortized VAEs refine inference-network outputs through differentiable local optimization, improving reported text and image results while avoiding posterior collapse.

title: Semi-Amortized Variational Autoencoders

abstract: We propose a method of moments (MoM) algorithm for training large-scale implicit generative models. Moment estimation in this setting encounters two problems: it is often difficult to define the millions of moments needed to learn the model parameters, and it is hard to determine which properties are useful when specifying moments. To address the first issue, we introduce a moment network, and define the moments as the network’s hidden units and the gradient of the network’s output with respect to its parameters. To tackle the second problem, we use asymptotic theory to highlight desiderata for moments – namely they should minimize the asymptotic variance of estimated model parameters – and introduce an objective to learn better moments. The sequence of objectives created by this Method of Learned Moments (MoLM) can train high-quality neural image samplers. On CIFAR-10, we demonstrate that MoLM-trained generators achieve significantly higher Inception Scores and lower Frechet Inception Distances than those trained with gradient penalty-regularized and spectrally-normalized adversarial objectives. These generators also achieve nearly perfect Multi-Scale Structural Similarity Scores on CelebA, and can create high-quality samples of 128x128 images.

Moment estimation in this setting encounters two problems: it is often difficult to define the millions of moments needed to learn the model parameters, and it is hard to determine which properties are useful when specifying moments. To address the first issue, we introduce a moment network, and define the moments as the network’s hidden units and the gradient of the network’s output with respect to its parameters. To tackle the second problem, we use asymptotic theory to highlight desiderata for moments – namely they should minimize the asymptotic variance of estimated model parameters – and introduce an objective to learn better moments. The sequence of objectives created by this Method of Learned Moments (MoLM) can train high-quality neural image samplers. On CIFAR-10, we demonstrate that MoLM-trained generators achieve significantly higher Inception Scores and lower Frechet Inception Distances than those trained with gradient penalty-regularized and spectrally-normalized adversarial objectives. These generators also achieve nearly perfect Multi-Scale Structural Similarity Scores on CelebA, and can create high-quality samples of 128x128 images.

paragraphs: Training large implicit generative models with the method of moments requires many useful statistical properties to match. Choosing those properties manually is difficult, especially when millions are needed. This paper introduces the Method of Learned Moments, or MoLM, to construct and improve the moments through a separate neural network.

The moment network supplies moments from its hidden units and from gradients of its output with respect to its parameters. To guide their learning, the authors use asymptotic theory: useful moments should reduce the asymptotic variance of estimated model parameters. This turns moment selection into a learned objective with a statistical motivation.

On CIFAR-10, MoLM-trained generators achieve significantly better Inception Scores and Frechet Inception Distances than generators trained with the specified gradient-penalty and spectral-normalization adversarial objectives. The authors also report nearly perfect Multi-Scale Structural Similarity Scores on CelebA and high-quality 128-by-128 samples. These findings support learned moments as an effective training approach for the evaluated neural image generators.
summary.tldr: MoLM learns statistically motivated moments for training implicit image generators and reports improvements over specified adversarial training objectives.

title: Learning Implicit Generative Models with the Method of Learned Moments

abstract: In this work, we demonstrate universal multi-party poisoning attacks that adapt and apply to any multi-party learning process with arbitrary interaction pattern between the parties. More generally, we introduce and study $(k,p)$-poisoning attacks in which an adversary controls $k\in[m]$ of the parties, and for each corrupted party $P_i$, the adversary submits some poisoned data $T’_i$ on behalf of $P_i$ that is still "$(1-p)$-close" to the correct data $T_i$ (e.g., $1-p$ fraction of $T’_i$ is still honestly generated).We prove that for any "bad" property $B$ of the final trained hypothesis $h$ (e.g., $h$ failing on a particular test example or having "large" risk) that has an arbitrarily small constant probability of happening without the attack, there always is a $(k,p)$-poisoning attack that increases the probability of $B$ from $\mu$ to by $\mu^{1-p \cdot k/m} = \mu + \Omega(p \cdot k/m)$. Our attack only uses clean labels, and it is online, as it only knows the the data shared so far.
originalAbstract: In this work, we demonstrate universal multi-party poisoning attacks that adapt and apply to any multi-party learning process with arbitrary interaction pattern between the parties. More generally, we introduce and study $(k,p)$-poisoning attacks in which an adversary controls $k\in[m]$ of the parties, and for each corrupted party $P_i$, the adversary submits some poisoned data $T’_i$ on behalf of $P_i$ that is still "$(1-p)$-close" to the correct data $T_i$ (e.g., $1-p$ fraction of $T’_i$ is still honestly generated).We prove that for any "bad" property $B$ of the final trained hypothesis $h$ (e.g., $h$ failing on a particular test example or having "large" risk) that has an arbitrarily small constant probability of happening without the attack, there always is a $(k,p)$-poisoning attack that increases the probability of $B$ from $\mu$ to by $\mu^{1-p \cdot k/m} = \mu + \Omega(p \cdot k/m)$. Our attack only uses clean labels, and it is online, as it only knows the the data shared so far.

paragraphs: The paper studies poisoning in learning systems where multiple parties contribute data through potentially arbitrary interaction patterns. Its attack model gives an adversary control over k of m parties while requiring each corrupted contribution to remain close to its honest version. The parameter p describes the permitted amount of corruption.

The theoretical result concerns a bad property of the final trained hypothesis that already occurs with an arbitrarily small constant probability mu without an attack. The authors prove that an attack exists that increases this probability to mu raised to the power 1−pk/m. The result links the achievable increase to both the corruption allowance and the fraction of controlled parties.

The attacks use clean labels and operate online, knowing only the data shared so far. Their generality covers arbitrary interaction patterns within the stated multiparty model. The guarantee concerns amplification of an existing failure probability under the specified control and closeness conditions. It demonstrates that these constraints still permit a broad theoretical vulnerability across multiparty learning processes.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that constrained, online, clean-label poisoning can amplify existing failure probabilities across arbitrary multiparty interaction patterns.

title: Universal Multi-Party Poisoning Attacks

abstract: We provide the first mathematically complete derivation of the Nystr{ö}m method for low-rank approximation of indefinite kernels and propose an efficient method for finding an approximate eigendecomposition of such kernel matrices. Building on this result, we devise highly scalable methods for learning in reproducing kernel Krein spaces. The devised approaches provide a principled and theoretically well-founded means to tackle large scale learning problems with indefinite kernels. The main motivation for our work comes from problems with structured representations (e.g., graphs, strings, time-series), where it is relatively easy to devise a pairwise (dis)similarity function based on intuition and/or knowledge of domain experts. Such functions are typically not positive definite and it is often well beyond the expertise of practitioners to verify this condition. The effectiveness of the devised approaches is evaluated empirically using indefinite kernels defined on structured and vectorial data representations.
originalAbstract: We provide the first mathematically complete derivation of the Nystr{ö}m method for low-rank approximation of indefinite kernels and propose an efficient method for finding an approximate eigendecomposition of such kernel matrices. Building on this result, we devise highly scalable methods for learning in reproducing kernel Krein spaces. The devised approaches provide a principled and theoretically well-founded means to tackle large scale learning problems with indefinite kernels. The main motivation for our work comes from problems with structured representations (e.g., graphs, strings, time-series), where it is relatively easy to devise a pairwise (dis)similarity function based on intuition and/or knowledge of domain experts. Such functions are typically not positive definite and it is often well beyond the expertise of practitioners to verify this condition. The effectiveness of the devised approaches is evaluated empirically using indefinite kernels defined on structured and vectorial data representations.

paragraphs: For structured objects such as graphs, strings, and time series, domain knowledge can suggest useful pairwise similarities or dissimilarities. Those functions may not satisfy positive definiteness, a mathematical condition required by familiar kernel formulations. Checking that condition can itself be difficult for practitioners, motivating methods that work directly with indefinite kernels.

The paper provides what the authors describe as the first mathematically complete derivation of Nyström low-rank approximation for indefinite kernels. It also introduces an efficient method for approximating the eigendecomposition of the resulting kernel matrices. These results form the foundation for scalable learning methods in reproducing kernel Krein spaces.

The importance of the construction is that it connects practical, domain-informed similarity functions with a principled large-scale learning approach. The authors evaluate effectiveness empirically using indefinite kernels on both structured and vector representations. The contribution combines a theoretical basis for the approximation with learning methods designed to make indefinite-kernel problems computationally manageable at larger scales.
summary.tldr: A principled low-rank approximation of indefinite kernels enables scalable learning with domain-informed similarities on structured and vector data.

title: Scalable Learning in Reproducing Kernel Krein Spaces

abstract: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) can model complex marginal densities as well as complex mappings. Non-Gaussian marginals are essential for modelling real-world data, and can be generated from the DGP by incorporating uncorrelated variables to the model. Previous work in the DGP model has introduced noise additively, and used variational inference with a combination of sparse Gaussian processes and mean-field Gaussians for the approximate posterior. Additive noise attenuates the signal, and the Gaussian form of variational distribution may lead to an inaccurate posterior. We instead incorporate noisy variables as latent covariates, and propose a novel importance-weighted objective, which leverages analytic results and provides a mechanism to trade off computation for improved accuracy. Our results demonstrate that the importance-weighted objective works well in practice and consistently outperforms classical variational inference, especially for deeper models.
originalAbstract: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) can model complex marginal densities as well as complex mappings. Non-Gaussian marginals are essential for modelling real-world data, and can be generated from the DGP by incorporating uncorrelated variables to the model. Previous work in the DGP model has introduced noise additively, and used variational inference with a combination of sparse Gaussian processes and mean-field Gaussians for the approximate posterior. Additive noise attenuates the signal, and the Gaussian form of variational distribution may lead to an inaccurate posterior. We instead incorporate noisy variables as latent covariates, and propose a novel importance-weighted objective, which leverages analytic results and provides a mechanism to trade off computation for improved accuracy. Our results demonstrate that the importance-weighted objective works well in practice and consistently outperforms classical variational inference, especially for deeper models.

paragraphs: Deep Gaussian processes can represent complicated mappings and marginal distributions. Incorporating uncorrelated variables allows them to generate non-Gaussian marginals, which matter for modeling real-world data. The paper revisits how these variables enter the model and how the resulting posterior is approximated during inference.

Earlier approaches described in the abstract add noise directly and use sparse Gaussian processes together with mean-field Gaussian posterior approximations. Additive noise attenuates the signal, while the Gaussian approximation may inaccurately represent the posterior. The proposed method instead treats noisy variables as latent covariates, incorporating them as unobserved inputs to the model.

The authors also introduce an importance-weighted variational objective that uses analytic results and offers a way to exchange additional computation for improved accuracy. Their reported results consistently favor this objective over classical variational inference, particularly in deeper models. The contribution combines a change in how uncertainty enters the model with a more accurate inference objective, and the experiments indicate that this combination works well in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Latent noise covariates and an importance-weighted objective improve deep Gaussian process inference in reported experiments, especially for deeper models.

title: Deep Gaussian Processes with Importance-Weighted Variational Inference

abstract: A recent line of research termed "unlabeled sensing" and "shuffled linear regression" has been exploring under great generality the recovery of signals from subsampled and permuted measurements; a challenging problem in diverse fields of data science and machine learning. In this paper we introduce an abstraction of this problem which we call "homomorphic sensing". Given a linear subspace and a finite set of linear transformations we develop an algebraic theory which establishes conditions guaranteeing that points in the subspace are uniquely determined from their homomorphic image under some transformation in the set. As a special case, we recover known conditions for unlabeled sensing, as well as new results and extensions. On the algorithmic level we exhibit two dynamic programming based algorithms, which to the best of our knowledge are the first working solutions for the unlabeled sensing problem for small dimensions. One of them, additionally based on branch-and-bound, when applied to image registration under affine transformations, performs on par with or outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets.

In this paper we introduce an abstraction of this problem which we call "homomorphic sensing". Given a linear subspace and a finite set of linear transformations we develop an algebraic theory which establishes conditions guaranteeing that points in the subspace are uniquely determined from their homomorphic image under some transformation in the set. paragraphs: Recovering a signal becomes difficult when its measurements have been subsampled or rearranged, leaving their correspondence uncertain. This paper introduces homomorphic sensing as an abstraction of problems such as unlabeled sensing and shuffled linear regression. It asks when a transformed observation still uniquely identifies the original signal.

The theoretical setting consists of a known linear subspace and a finite collection of linear transformations. The authors develop algebraic conditions guaranteeing that a point in the subspace is uniquely determined by its image under some transformation from that collection. The framework recovers established conditions for unlabeled sensing while also producing new results and extensions.

The paper also presents two algorithms based on dynamic programming for unlabeled sensing in small dimensions. One combines dynamic programming with branch and bound. Applied to image registration under affine transformations, that algorithm matches or exceeds leading methods on benchmark datasets. The work thus connects conditions for unique recovery with algorithms, while explicitly locating the unlabeled sensing solutions in the small dimensional setting.
summary.tldr: Homomorphic sensing gives algebraic guarantees for recovering signals under uncertain linear transformations and algorithms for small dimensional unlabeled sensing.

title: Homomorphic Sensing

abstract: This work focuses on the estimation of multiple change-points in a time-varying Ising model that evolves piece-wise constantly. The aim is to identify both the moments at which significant changes occur in the Ising model, as well as the underlying graph structures. For this purpose, we propose to estimate the neighborhood of each node by maximizing a penalized version of its conditional log-likelihood. The objective of the penalization is twofold: it imposes sparsity in the learned graphs and, thanks to a fused-type penalty, it also enforces them to evolve piece-wise constantly. Using few assumptions, we provide two change-points consistency theorems. Those are the first in the context of unknown number of change-points detection in time-varying Ising model. Finally, experimental results on several synthetic datasets and a real-world dataset demonstrate the performance of our method.

The aim is to identify both the moments at which significant changes occur in the Ising model, as well as the underlying graph structures. For this purpose, we propose to estimate the neighborhood of each node by maximizing a penalized version of its conditional log-likelihood. The objective of the penalization is twofold: it imposes sparsity in the learned graphs and, thanks to a fused-type penalty, it also enforces them to evolve piece-wise constantly. paragraphs: This paper studies an Ising model whose graph structure changes over time but stays constant between change points. The learning problem has two connected parts: identifying when significant changes happen and recovering the graph within each stable interval. The number of change points is unknown, making it part of what must be inferred.

The method estimates each node's neighborhood by maximizing a penalized conditional log-likelihood. One part of the penalty promotes sparse graphs, favoring a limited set of connections. A fused-type penalty encourages the estimated structure to remain unchanged across stretches of time. Together, these penalties encode the desired combination of sparse relationships and piecewise constant evolution.

Under assumptions described as few, the authors establish two consistency theorems for change-point estimation. They identify these as the first such results for detecting an unknown number of changes in time-varying Ising models. Experiments on several synthetic datasets and one real-world dataset demonstrate the method's performance. The contribution combines a concrete estimation procedure with theoretical support for locating changes in the stated model.
summary.tldr: Penalized neighborhood estimation jointly learns sparse Ising graphs and unknown change points, with consistency guarantees under stated assumptions.

title: Learning the piece-wise constant graph structure of a varying Ising model

abstract: Given data with noisy labels, over-parameterized deep networks can gradually memorize the data, and fit everything in the end. Although equipped with corrections for noisy labels, many learning methods in this area still suffer overfitting due to undesired memorization. In this paper, to relieve this issue, we propose stochastic integrated gradient underweighted ascent (SIGUA): in a mini-batch, we adopt gradient descent on good data as usual, and learning-rate-reduced gradient ascent on bad data; the proposal is a versatile approach where data goodness or badness is w.r.t. desired or undesired memorization given a base learning method. Technically, SIGUA pulls optimization back for generalization when their goals conflict with each other; philosophically, SIGUA shows forgetting undesired memorization can reinforce desired memorization. Experiments demonstrate that SIGUA successfully robustifies two typical base learning methods, so that their performance is often significantly improved.

Although equipped with corrections for noisy labels, many learning methods in this area still suffer overfitting due to undesired memorization. In this paper, to relieve this issue, we propose stochastic integrated gradient underweighted ascent (SIGUA): in a mini-batch, we adopt gradient descent on good data as usual, and learning-rate-reduced gradient ascent on bad data; the proposal is a versatile approach where data goodness or badness is w.r.t. desired or undesired memorization given a base learning method. Technically, SIGUA pulls optimization back for generalization when their goals conflict with each other; philosophically, SIGUA shows forgetting undesired memorization can reinforce desired memorization. Experiments demonstrate that SIGUA successfully robustifies two typical base learning methods, so that their performance is often significantly improved.

paragraphs: Deep networks with many parameters can eventually memorize noisy labels, even when the training method includes corrections for label noise. SIGUA addresses this unwanted memorization by changing how selected examples influence each training update. The approach treats forgetting as an active part of learning when fitting particular data would undermine generalization.

Within a mini-batch, SIGUA applies ordinary gradient descent to data considered good and gradient ascent with a reduced learning rate to data considered bad. The underlying learning method determines these categories according to desired and undesired memorization. This makes SIGUA a versatile modification whose behavior depends on how the base method identifies examples to learn from or partially unlearn.

Experiments apply SIGUA to two representative base learning methods and show improved robustness, often with significant performance gains. The findings support the idea that weakening undesirable memorization can reinforce useful learning. Its central mechanism is the combination of ordinary fitting and smaller opposing updates within the same training process.
summary.tldr: SIGUA combines gradient descent on desirable data with reduced-rate ascent on undesirable data to curb noisy-label memorization.

title: SIGUA: Forgetting May Make Learning with Noisy Labels More Robust

abstract: We introduce a self-supervised approach for learning node and graph level representations by contrasting structural views of graphs. We show that unlike visual representation learning, increasing the number of views to more than two or contrasting multi-scale encodings do not improve performance, and the best performance is achieved by contrasting encodings from first-order neighbors and a graph diffusion. We achieve new state-of-the-art results in self-supervised learning on 8 out of 8 node and graph classification benchmarks under the linear evaluation protocol. For example, on Cora (node) and Reddit-Binary (graph) classification benchmarks, we achieve 86.8% and 84.5% accuracy, which are 5.5% and 2.4% relative improvements over previous state-of-the-art. When compared to supervised baselines, our approach outperforms them in 4 out of 8 benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper learns representations of individual nodes and entire graphs through self-supervision. Its training signal comes from contrasting different structural views of the same graph. The central question is which views provide useful information for learning features that later support classification, without relying on classification labels to learn those features.

The strongest reported configuration contrasts an encoding based on immediate neighbors with one based on graph diffusion, which reflects connectivity beyond those immediate neighbors. In the authors’ experiments, adding more than two views or contrasting encodings across multiple scales does not improve performance. These findings identify a particular pairing as effective within the evaluated graph-learning setting.

Under linear evaluation, the method achieves the best reported self-supervised results on all eight node and graph classification benchmarks. It reaches 86.8% accuracy on Cora and 84.5% on Reddit-Binary, corresponding to relative improvements of 5.5% and 2.4%. It also exceeds supervised baselines on four benchmarks. The results show that carefully chosen structural views can yield features useful even to a linear classifier.
summary.tldr: Contrasting immediate-neighbor and diffusion views learns graph representations that achieve leading self-supervised results on all eight evaluated classification benchmarks.

title: Contrastive Multi-View Representation Learning on Graphs

abstract: Evidence suggests that networks trained on large datasets generalize well not solely because of the numerous training examples, but also class diversity which encourages learning of enriched features. This raises the question of whether this remains true when data is scarce - is there an advantage to learning with additional labels in low-data regimes? In this work, we consider a task that requires difficult-to-obtain expert annotations: tumor segmentation in mammography images. We show that, in low-data settings, performance can be improved by complementing the expert annotations with seemingly uninformative labels from non-expert annotators, turning the task into a multi-class problem. We reveal that these gains increase when less expert data is available, and uncover several interesting properties through further studies. We demonstrate our findings on CSAW-S, a new dataset that we introduce here, and confirm them on two public datasets.

paragraphs: Large training datasets offer both many examples and a variety of classes. The paper asks whether class diversity can also help when training data are scarce. It studies tumor segmentation in mammography images, where the expert annotations needed to identify tumors are difficult to obtain and therefore valuable.

The proposed approach supplements expert annotations with seemingly uninformative labels supplied by non-experts. Adding these labels turns the learning problem into a multi-class task. The key change is therefore the variety of labels available during training, with the extra annotations complementing the expert information already present. The study tests whether that additional supervision can improve the original segmentation task.

The authors report improved performance in low-data settings, with larger gains as the amount of expert data decreases. They demonstrate the finding on their newly introduced CSAW-S dataset and confirm it on two public datasets. These results suggest that inexpensive annotations can have useful training value even when they initially appear to contribute little to the expert task.
summary.tldr: Supplementing scarce expert mammography annotations with non-expert labels improves segmentation in the studied low-data settings.

title: Adding seemingly uninformative labels helps in low data regimes

abstract: This paper studies how neural network architecture affects the speed of training. We introduce a simple concept called gradient confusion to help formally analyze this. When gradient confusion is high, stochastic gradients produced by different data samples may be negatively correlated, slowing down convergence. But when gradient confusion is low, data samples interact harmoniously, and training proceeds quickly. Through theoretical and experimental results, we demonstrate how the neural network architecture affects gradient confusion, and thus the efficiency of training. Our results show that, for popular initialization techniques, increasing the width of neural networks leads to lower gradient confusion, and thus faster model training. On the other hand, increasing the depth of neural networks has the opposite effect. Our results indicate that alternate initialization techniques or networks using both batch normalization and skip connections help reduce the training burden of very deep networks.

paragraphs: This paper examines how neural network architecture affects training speed through a concept called gradient confusion. Gradients computed from different examples may point in conflicting directions, expressed as negative correlation. When that conflict is high, stochastic gradient descent can converge more slowly. Lower confusion means the updates from different samples interact more cooperatively.

The authors use theoretical analysis and experiments to connect this behavior to network shape. Under popular initialization techniques, increasing width reduces gradient confusion and leads to faster training. Increasing depth has the opposite effect in their results. This distinguishes two ways of enlarging a network that can have different consequences for optimization.

The findings also identify ways to ease the training burden of very deep networks. Alternative initialization methods, or architectures combining batch normalization with skip connections, help reduce that burden. The contribution provides a shared explanation for these architectural and initialization effects by examining how individual training examples influence one another through their gradients.
summary.tldr: Gradient confusion links architecture to training speed: under popular initializations, greater width reduces conflicting gradients while greater depth increases them.

title: The Impact of Neural Network Overparameterization on Gradient Confusion and Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: This paper studies the lower bound complexity for minimax optimization problem whose objective function is the average of $n$ individual smooth convex-concave functions. We consider the algorithm which gets access to gradient and proximal oracle for each individual component. For the strongly-convex-strongly-concave case, we prove such an algorithm can not reach an $\varepsilon$-suboptimal point in fewer than $\Omega\left((n+\kappa)\log(1/\varepsilon)\right)$ iterations, where $\kappa$ is the condition number of the objective function. This lower bound matches the upper bound of the existing incremental first-order oracle algorithm stochastic variance-reduced extragradient. We develop a novel construction to show the above result, which partitions the tridiagonal matrix of classical examples into $n$ groups. This construction is friendly to the analysis of incremental gradient and proximal oracle and we also extend the analysis to general convex-concave cases.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much work an algorithm must perform to solve a finite-sum minimax problem. The objective averages n smooth component functions, each convex in the variables being minimized and concave in those being maximized. Algorithms access individual components through gradient and proximal oracles.

For strongly convex–strongly concave objectives, the authors prove a lower bound of Ω((n + κ) log(1/ε)) iterations to reach ε-suboptimality, where κ is the condition number. This expresses an unavoidable worst-case dependence on the number of components, the conditioning of the objective, and the requested accuracy within the considered oracle model.

The bound matches an existing upper bound for stochastic variance-reduced extragradient, establishing that its complexity cannot generally be improved in this setting. The proof uses a new construction that partitions a classical tridiagonal matrix into n groups, making componentwise oracle analysis possible. The authors also extend their analysis to general convex–concave problems. The contribution identifies computational limits and shows where an existing algorithm already reaches them.
summary.tldr: The paper proves a finite-sum minimax lower bound that matches stochastic variance-reduced extragradient in the strongly convex–strongly concave setting.

title: Lower Complexity Bounds for Finite-Sum Convex-Concave Minimax Optimization Problems

abstract: We consider a single-product dynamic pricing problem under a specific non-stationary setting, where the underlying demand process grows over time in expectation and also possibly in the level of random fluctuation. The decision maker sequentially sets price in each time period and learns the unknown demand model, with the goal of maximizing expected cumulative revenue over a time horizon $T$. We prove matching upper and lower bounds on regret and provide near-optimal pricing policies, showing how the growth rate of random fluctuation over time affects the best achievable regret order and the near-optimal policy design. In the analysis, we show that whether the seller knows the length of time horizon $T$ in advance or not surprisingly render different optimal regret orders. We then extend the demand model such that the optimal price may vary with time and present a novel and near-optimal policy for the extended model. Finally, we consider an analogous non-stationary setting in the canonical multi-armed bandit problem, and points out that knowing or not knowing the length of time horizon $T$ render the same optimal regret order, in contrast to the non-stationary dynamic pricing problem.

paragraphs: This paper studies pricing a single product when demand grows over time in expectation and may also become more variable. The seller sequentially chooses prices while learning an unknown demand model, seeking to maximize expected cumulative revenue. The non-stationary setting makes both the growth of demand and the evolution of its random fluctuations relevant to learning.

The authors prove matching upper and lower regret bounds and provide near-optimal pricing policies. Their analysis shows how the rate of growth in demand fluctuations affects achievable regret and policy design. It also finds that knowing the time horizon in advance can change the optimal regret order, making advance knowledge of the selling period theoretically consequential.

An extension permits the optimal price itself to vary with time and supplies a near-optimal policy for that model. The paper also analyzes an analogous growing, non-stationary multi-armed bandit setting. There, knowing the horizon does not change the optimal regret order. This contrast identifies a meaningful difference between the pricing problem and its bandit analogue.
summary.tldr: For growing, increasingly noisy demand, optimal pricing regret depends on fluctuation growth and whether the seller knows the time horizon.

title: When Demands Evolve Larger and Noisier: Learning and Earning in a Growing Environment

abstract: We consider training models on private data that are distributed across user devices. To ensure privacy, we add on-device noise and use secure aggregation so that only the noisy sum is revealed to the server. We present a comprehensive end-to-end system, which appropriately discretizes the data and adds discrete Gaussian noise before performing secure aggregation. We provide a novel privacy analysis for sums of discrete Gaussians and carefully analyze the effects of data quantization and modular summation arithmetic. Our theoretical guarantees highlight the complex tension between communication, privacy, and accuracy. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our solution is essentially able to match the accuracy to central differential privacy with less than 16 bits of precision per value.

paragraphs: The paper addresses private model training when data remains distributed across user devices. Its system adds noise on each device and uses secure aggregation so that the server receives only the noisy sum. The aim is to make the privacy mechanism work together with the numerical representation and aggregation process used in the system.

The method discretizes data and adds discrete Gaussian noise before aggregation. The authors develop a privacy analysis for sums of these noise variables. They also analyze quantization, which maps values to finite precision, and modular arithmetic, which governs how represented values are summed within a bounded numerical range.

These components matter jointly because communication, privacy, and accuracy impose competing demands. The theoretical guarantees characterize that tension rather than treating numerical implementation as separate from privacy. Extensive experiments show that the system can essentially match the accuracy of central differential privacy while using fewer than sixteen bits per value. This is an empirical accuracy comparison supported by an end-to-end analysis of the distributed mechanism.
summary.tldr: A distributed discrete-Gaussian privacy system combines on-device noise and secure aggregation while empirically approaching central-private accuracy below sixteen bits per value.

title: The Distributed Discrete Gaussian Mechanism for Federated Learning with Secure Aggregation

abstract: Inhomogeneous Poisson point processes are widely used models of event occurrences. We address \emph{adaptive sensing of Poisson Point processes}, namely, maximizing the number of captured events subject to sensing costs. We encode prior assumptions on the rate function by modeling it as a member of a known \emph{reproducing kernel Hilbert space} (RKHS). By partitioning the domain into separate small regions, and using heteroscedastic linear regression, we propose a tractable estimator of Poisson process rates for two feedback models: \emph{count-record}, where exact locations of events are observed, and \emph{histogram} feedback, where only counts of events are observed. We derive provably accurate anytime confidence estimates for our estimators for sequentially acquired Poisson count data. Using these, we formulate algorithms based on optimism that provably incur sublinear count-regret. We demonstrate the practicality of the method on problems from crime modeling, revenue maximization as well as environmental monitoring.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose where to sense events when observation has a cost. Events follow an inhomogeneous Poisson point process, whose rate can vary across the domain. The objective is to capture as many events as possible subject to sensing costs while learning about the unknown event rate from sequential observations.

The authors assume the rate function belongs to a known reproducing kernel Hilbert space, encoding prior structure on that function. They partition the domain into small regions and use heteroscedastic linear regression to estimate rates. The estimator accommodates both feedback that includes exact event locations and feedback that supplies only event counts.

The analysis provides accurate confidence estimates valid throughout sequential data collection. Algorithms then use optimism based on those estimates and achieve provably sublinear count-regret, meaning the accumulated regret grows more slowly than the decision horizon. Applications to crime modeling, revenue maximization, and environmental monitoring demonstrate practicality. The guarantees connect adaptive sensing decisions to the assumed rate-function structure and uncertainty estimates.
summary.tldr: Structured rate estimation and confidence-based exploration yield adaptive Poisson-event sensing algorithms with provably sublinear count-regret.

title: No-regret Algorithms for Capturing Events in Poisson Point Processes

abstract: A recent study has shown that graph matching models are vulnerable to adversarial manipulation of their input which is intended to cause a mismatching. Nevertheless, there is still a lack of a comprehensive solution for further enhancing the robustness of graph matching against adversarial attacks. In this paper, we identify and study two types of unique topology attacks in graph matching: inter-graph dispersion and intra-graph assembly attacks. We propose an integrated defense model, IDRGM, for resilient graph matching with two novel defense techniques to defend against the above two attacks simultaneously. A detection technique of inscribed simplexes in the hyperspheres consisting of multiple matched nodes is proposed to tackle inter-graph dispersion attacks, in which the distances among the matched nodes in multiple graphs are maximized to form regular simplexes. A node separation method based on phase-type distribution and maximum likelihood estimation is developed to estimate the distribution of perturbed graphs and separate the nodes within the same graphs over a wide space, for defending intra-graph assembly attacks, such that the interference from the similar neighbors of the perturbed nodes is significantly reduced. We evaluate the robustness of our IDRGM model on real datasets against state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: Graph matching seeks correspondences between nodes in different graphs, but adversarial input changes can cause incorrect matches. This paper identifies two topology-based attack types: inter-graph dispersion and intra-graph assembly. It introduces an integrated defense, IDRGM, with separate techniques designed to address both forms of manipulation simultaneously.

The defense against inter-graph dispersion uses geometric detection involving simplexes inscribed in hyperspheres formed from multiple matched nodes. Its construction spreads matched nodes across graphs into regular-simplex arrangements. The technique uses the geometry of a group of corresponding nodes as part of the defense against this attack type.

For intra-graph assembly, the method estimates the distribution of perturbed graphs using a phase-type distribution and maximum likelihood estimation. It then separates nodes within a graph over a wider space, significantly reducing interference from similar neighbors of perturbed nodes. The authors evaluate IDRGM's robustness on real datasets against state-of-the-art algorithms. The contribution is an integrated treatment of two distinct attack mechanisms through geometric detection and distribution-based node separation.
summary.tldr: IDRGM combines geometric detection and distribution-based node separation to defend graph matching against two topology-based attack types.

title: Integrated Defense for Resilient Graph Matching

abstract: Recommendation models can effectively estimate underlying user interests and predict one’s future behaviors by factorizing an observed user-item rating matrix into products of two sets of latent factors. However, the user-specific embedding factors can only be learned in a transductive way, making it difficult to handle new users on-the-fly. In this paper, we propose an inductive collaborative filtering framework that contains two representation models. The first model follows conventional matrix factorization which factorizes a group of key users’ rating matrix to obtain meta latents. The second model resorts to attention-based structure learning that estimates hidden relations from query to key users and learns to leverage meta latents to inductively compute embeddings for query users via neural message passing. Our model enables inductive representation learning for users and meanwhile guarantees equivalent representation capacity as matrix factorization. Experiments demonstrate that our model achieves promising results for recommendation on few-shot users with limited training ratings and new unseen users which are commonly encountered in open-world recommender systems.

paragraphs: Matrix-factorization recommenders represent users and items with latent factors learned from observed ratings. Their user-specific factors are learned transductively, making it difficult to accommodate newly arriving users immediately. This paper develops an inductive collaborative-filtering framework that can compute representations for query users through relationships with a group of key users.

The framework contains two representation models. The first factorizes the key users' rating matrix to obtain shared meta latents. The second uses attention-based structure learning to estimate hidden relationships between query users and key users. Neural message passing then uses those relationships and meta latents to compute embeddings for the query users.

The authors establish that the framework retains representation capacity equivalent to matrix factorization while enabling inductive user representations. Experiments report promising recommendations for users with few training ratings and for previously unseen users. These findings address two common open-world situations, showing how learned relationships to existing users can support representation construction as the user population expands.
summary.tldr: An inductive recommender builds user embeddings through learned relationships to key users while retaining matrix factorization's representation capacity.

title: Towards Open-World Recommendation: An Inductive Model-based Collaborative Filtering Approach

abstract: An extractive rationale explains a language model’s (LM’s) prediction on a given task instance by highlighting the text inputs that most influenced the prediction. Ideally, rationale extraction should be faithful (reflective of LM’s actual behavior) and plausible (convincing to humans), without compromising the LM’s (i.e., task model’s) task performance. Although attribution algorithms and select-predict pipelines are commonly used in rationale extraction, they both rely on certain heuristics that hinder them from satisfying all three desiderata. In light of this, we propose UNIREX, a flexible learning framework which generalizes rationale extractor optimization as follows: (1) specify architecture for a learned rationale extractor; (2) select explainability objectives (\ie faithfulness and plausibility criteria); and (3) jointly train the task model and rationale extractor on the task using selected objectives. UNIREX enables replacing prior works’ heuristic design choices with a generic learned rationale extractor in (1) and optimizing it for all three desiderata in (2)-(3). To facilitate comparison between methods w.r.t. multiple desiderata, we introduce the Normalized Relative Gain (NRG) metric. On five English text classification datasets, our best UNIREX configuration outperforms baselines by an average of 32.9% NRG. Plus, UNIREX rationale extractors’ faithfulness can even generalize to unseen datasets and tasks.

paragraphs: An extractive rationale highlights input text to explain a language model’s prediction. A useful rationale should reflect the model’s actual behavior, make sense to people, and preserve task performance. These goals are distinct: an explanation can appear convincing without faithfully identifying what influenced the prediction.

UNIREX treats rationale extraction as a learning problem with configurable components. Users choose an extractor architecture and objectives for faithfulness and plausibility, then jointly train the extractor and task model. This replaces heuristic design choices with a learned extractor that can be optimized alongside predictive performance. The authors also introduce Normalized Relative Gain, or NRG, to compare methods across the desired properties.

On five English text-classification datasets, the best UNIREX configuration exceeds the baselines by an average of 32.9% NRG. This is a gain in the proposed comparison metric, not a stated increase of that size in classification accuracy. The authors further find that extractor faithfulness can transfer to unseen datasets and tasks, suggesting that learned explanation behavior can extend beyond its training setting.
summary.tldr: UNIREX jointly learns predictions and text rationales to balance faithfulness, human plausibility, and task performance.

title: UNIREX: A Unified Learning Framework for Language Model Rationale Extraction

abstract: Local differential privacy (LDP) can be adopted to anonymize richer user data attributes that will be input to sophisticated machine learning (ML) tasks. However, today’s LDP approaches are largely task-agnostic and often lead to severe performance loss – they simply inject noise to all data attributes according to a given privacy budget, regardless of what features are most relevant for the ultimate task. In this paper, we address how to significantly improve the ultimate task performance with multi-dimensional user data by considering a task-aware privacy preservation problem. The key idea is to use an encoder-decoder framework to learn (and anonymize) a task-relevant latent representation of user data. We obtain an analytical near-optimal solution for the linear setting with mean-squared error (MSE) task loss. We also provide an approximate solution through a gradient-based learning algorithm for general nonlinear cases. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our task-aware approach significantly improves ultimate task accuracy compared to standard benchmark LDP approaches with the same level of privacy guarantee.

paragraphs: Local differential privacy protects user data by randomizing information before it is used. For data with many attributes, task-agnostic methods can substantially harm prediction because they add noise without considering which features matter to the eventual task. This paper makes that task relevance part of the privacy mechanism’s design.

The proposed encoder-decoder framework learns a hidden representation of user data that is relevant to the task and anonymizes that representation. This ties the information being protected to the information needed for prediction. The authors obtain an analytical near-optimal solution for a linear setting with mean-squared-error task loss.

For general nonlinear settings, they provide an approximate solution learned with gradients. Experiments show significant gains in final task accuracy over standard local-differential-privacy benchmarks at the same level of privacy guarantee. The findings support adapting the representation to the task as a way to improve utility within a fixed privacy requirement. The near-optimal analytical claim applies specifically to the linear, mean-squared-error setting.
summary.tldr: Learning and anonymizing task-relevant representations improves prediction accuracy at the same local differential privacy guarantee.

title: Task-aware Privacy Preservation for Multi-dimensional Data

abstract: We investigate graph neural networks on graphs with heterophily. Some existing methods amplify a node’s neighborhood with multi-hop neighbors to include more nodes with homophily. However, it is a significant challenge to set personalized neighborhood sizes for different nodes. Further, for other homophilous nodes excluded in the neighborhood, they are ignored for information aggregation. To address these problems, we propose two models GloGNN and GloGNN++, which generate a node’s embedding by aggregating information from global nodes in the graph. In each layer, both models learn a coefficient matrix to capture the correlations between nodes, based on which neighborhood aggregation is performed. The coefficient matrix allows signed values and is derived from an optimization problem that has a closed-form solution. We further accelerate neighborhood aggregation and derive a linear time complexity. We theoretically explain the models’ effectiveness by proving that both the coefficient matrix and the generated node embedding matrix have the desired grouping effect. We conduct extensive experiments to compare our models against 11 other competitors on 15 benchmark datasets in a wide range of domains, scales and graph heterophilies. Experimental results show that our methods achieve superior performance and are also very efficient.

To address these problems, we propose two models GloGNN and GloGNN++, which generate a node’s embedding by aggregating information from global nodes in the graph. In each layer, both models learn a coefficient matrix to capture the correlations between nodes, based on which neighborhood aggregation is performed. The coefficient matrix allows signed values and is derived from an optimization problem that has a closed-form solution. We further accelerate neighborhood aggregation and derive a linear time complexity. We theoretically explain the models’ effectiveness by proving that both the coefficient matrix and the generated node embedding matrix have the desired grouping effect. We conduct extensive experiments to compare our models against 11 other competitors on 15 benchmark datasets in a wide range of domains, scales and graph heterophilies. Experimental results show that our methods achieve superior performance and are also very efficient.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks face a challenge when connected nodes are dissimilar, a situation called heterophily. Expanding a node's neighborhood can bring in more similar nodes, but choosing the right expansion separately for each node is difficult. Similar nodes outside the chosen neighborhood also remain unavailable for aggregation.

GloGNN and GloGNN++ instead construct node embeddings using information from across the graph. At each layer, they learn a matrix of correlations that determines how node information is combined. The coefficients can be positive or negative, and the matrix comes from an optimization problem with a closed-form solution. An accelerated aggregation procedure has linear time complexity.

The authors prove a desired grouping effect for both the coefficient matrix and the resulting embeddings, providing a theoretical account of the models' effectiveness. Experiments compare the methods with 11 competitors on 15 datasets covering varied domains, sizes, and heterophily levels. The reported results show superior performance and efficiency, supporting global aggregation as an alternative to selecting increasingly large local neighborhoods.
summary.tldr: GloGNN and GloGNN++ learn signed global aggregation weights to exploit useful node relationships beyond local neighborhoods.

title: Finding Global Homophily in Graph Neural Networks When Meeting Heterophily

abstract: Recent work has found that adversarially-robust deep networks used for image classification are more interpretable: their feature attributions tend to be sharper, and are more concentrated on the objects associated with the image’s ground- truth class. We show that smooth decision boundaries play an important role in this enhanced interpretability, as the model’s input gradients around data points will more closely align with boundaries’ normal vectors when they are smooth. Thus, because robust models have smoother boundaries, the results of gradient- based attribution methods, like Integrated Gradients and DeepLift, will capture more accurate information about nearby decision boundaries. This understanding of robust interpretability leads to our second contribution: boundary attributions, which aggregate information about the normal vectors of local decision bound- aries to explain a classification outcome. We show that by leveraging the key fac- tors underpinning robust interpretability, boundary attributions produce sharper, more concentrated visual explanations{—}even on non-robust models.

This paper investigates a geometric explanation for that observation. It focuses on decision boundaries, the surfaces where a classifier’s predicted class changes, and on the directions perpendicular to those surfaces.

The authors show that smoother boundaries make nearby input gradients align more closely with boundary normal vectors. Because robust models have smoother boundaries, gradient-based methods such as Integrated Gradients and DeepLift can capture more accurate information about those nearby boundaries. This connects the appearance of an attribution map to the local geometry of the classifier.

The paper then introduces boundary attributions, which aggregate local boundary-normal information to explain a classification. These produce sharper, more concentrated visual explanations even for non-robust models. The findings suggest that the geometric factors associated with robust interpretability can also guide explanation methods directly, extending their usefulness beyond models specifically trained for adversarial robustness.
summary.tldr: Smooth decision boundaries help explain robust models’ clearer attributions and motivate sharper boundary-based explanations even for non-robust models.

title: Robust Models Are More Interpretable Because Attributions Look Normal

abstract: Coordination graph is a promising approach to model agent collaboration in multi-agent reinforcement learning. It conducts a graph-based value factorization and induces explicit coordination among agents to complete complicated tasks. However, one critical challenge in this paradigm is the complexity of greedy action selection with respect to the factorized values. It refers to the decentralized constraint optimization problem (DCOP), which and whose constant-ratio approximation are NP-hard problems. To bypass this systematic hardness, this paper proposes a novel method, named Self-Organized Polynomial-time Coordination Graphs (SOP-CG), which uses structured graph classes to guarantee the accuracy and the computational efficiency of collaborated action selection. SOP-CG employs dynamic graph topology to ensure sufficient value function expressiveness. The graph selection is unified into an end-to-end learning paradigm. In experiments, we show that our approach learns succinct and well-adapted graph topologies, induces effective coordination, and improves performance across a variety of cooperative multi-agent tasks.
