paragraphs: Coordination graphs help cooperating reinforcement-learning agents represent how their choices interact. They factor a value function according to a graph, but choosing the best joint action from those factors can be computationally difficult. The paper identifies this selection problem, and even its constant-ratio approximation, as NP-hard in the general setting.

Self-Organized Polynomial-time Coordination Graphs addresses this difficulty by using structured graph classes that guarantee accurate and computationally efficient coordinated action selection. Restricting the graph structure makes the selection problem tractable. To retain sufficient expressiveness in the value function, the method allows the graph topology to change rather than committing to one fixed coordination pattern.

Graph selection is integrated into end-to-end learning, so learning the coordination structure becomes part of learning the agents’ behavior. Experiments show compact, well-adapted graph topologies, effective coordination, and improved performance across varied cooperative tasks. The contribution balances the computational benefits of structured graphs with flexibility in choosing which graph to use as part of the learned system.
summary.tldr: Learned, changing coordination graphs use tractable graph structures to support efficient joint-action selection and effective multi-agent cooperation.

title: Self-Organized Polynomial-Time Coordination Graphs

abstract: The notion of omnipredictors (Gopalan, Kalai, Reingold, Sharan and Wieder ITCS 2022), suggested a new paradigm for loss minimization. Rather than learning a predictor based on a known loss function, omnipredictors can easily be post-processed to minimize any one of a rich family of loss functions compared with the loss of hypotheses in a class $\mathcal C$. It has been shown that such omnipredictors exist and are implied (for all convex and Lipschitz loss functions) by the notion of multicalibration from the algorithmic fairness literature. In this paper, we introduce omnipredictors for constrained optimization and study their complexity and implications. The notion that we introduce allows the learner to be unaware of the loss function that will be later assigned as well as the constraints that will be later imposed , as long as the subpopulations that are used to define these constraints are known. We show how to obtain omnipredictors for constrained optimization problems, relying on appropriate variants of multicalibration. We also investigate the implications of this notion when the constraints used are so-called group fairness notions.

paragraphs: An omnipredictor is designed to remain useful when the loss function is chosen after training. Through post-processing, its predictions can support different objectives, with performance compared against hypotheses in a specified class. This paper extends that idea to optimization problems that include constraints as well as a loss.

The new formulation allows both the eventual loss and the eventual constraints to be unknown to the learner during training. It retains a specific requirement: the subpopulations used to define those constraints must already be known. This makes it possible to study flexibility in later decision-making while specifying which population structure the learning stage needs.

The authors show how suitable variants of multicalibration can produce omnipredictors for constrained optimization and examine the complexity and implications of this construction. They also study constraints expressing group fairness. The contribution is a theoretical framework for preparing predictions that can be adapted to later objectives and restrictions, subject to the stated population knowledge, rather than tailoring training to one fully specified constrained problem.
summary.tldr: The paper extends omnipredictors to later-chosen losses and constraints, provided the subpopulations defining the constraints are known during learning.

title: Omnipredictors for Constrained Optimization

abstract: Recent successful generative models are trained by fitting a neural network to an a-priori defined tractable probability density path taking noise to training examples. In this paper we investigate the space of Gaussian probability paths, which includes diffusion paths as an instance, and look for an optimal member in some useful sense. In particular, minimizing the Kinetic Energy (KE) of a path is known to make particles’ trajectories simple, hence easier to sample, and empirically improve performance in terms of likelihood of unseen data and sample generation quality. We investigate Kinetic Optimal (KO) Gaussian paths and offer the following observations: (i) We show the KE takes a simplified form on the space of Gaussian paths, where the data is incorporated only through a single, one dimensional scalar function, called the data separation function . (ii) We characterize the KO solutions with a one dimensional ODE. (iii) We approximate data-dependent KO paths by approximating the data separation function and minimizing the KE. (iv) We prove that the data separation function converges to $1$ in the general case of arbitrary normalized dataset consisting of $n$ samples in $d$ dimension as $n/\sqrt{d}\rightarrow 0$. A consequence of this result is that the Conditional Optimal Transport (Cond-OT) path becomes kinetic optimal as $n/\sqrt{d}\rightarrow 0$. We further support this theory with empirical experiments on ImageNet.

paragraphs: Many generative models learn a prescribed probability path from noise to data. This paper studies how to choose such a path within the Gaussian family, which includes diffusion paths. It focuses on minimizing kinetic energy, a criterion associated with simpler particle trajectories, easier sampling, and empirical improvements in generation quality and unseen-data likelihood.

The authors show that kinetic energy simplifies so that the data enters through one scalar function, called the data separation function. They characterize optimal paths using a one-dimensional ordinary differential equation. They also approximate data-dependent optimal paths by estimating that function and minimizing the resulting kinetic energy.

Consequently, the Conditional Optimal Transport path becomes kinetic optimal in that limit. Experiments on ImageNet support the theory. The optimality claim is therefore tied to the stated asymptotic regime, while the broader framework offers a way to investigate data-dependent paths.
summary.tldr: The paper reduces kinetic-optimal Gaussian path design to a scalar function and proves Conditional Optimal Transport becomes optimal in a specified limit.

title: On Kinetic Optimal Probability Paths for Generative Models

abstract: We propose an ensemble clustering framework to uncover latent cluster labels in functional data generated from a Gaussian process mixture. Our method exploits the fact that the projection coefficients of the functional data onto any given projection function follow a univariate Gaussian mixture model (GMM). By conducting multiple one-dimensional projections and learning a univariate GMM for each, we create an ensemble of GMMs. Each GMM serves as a base clustering, and applying ensemble clustering yields a consensus clustering. Our approach significantly reduces computational complexity compared to state-of-the-art methods, and we provide theoretical guarantees on the identifiability and learnability of Gaussian process mixtures. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets confirm the superiority of our method over existing techniques.

By conducting multiple one-dimensional projections and learning a univariate GMM for each, we create an ensemble of GMMs. Each GMM serves as a base clustering, and applying ensemble clustering yields a consensus clustering. Our approach significantly reduces computational complexity compared to state-of-the-art methods, and we provide theoretical guarantees on the identifiability and learnability of Gaussian process mixtures. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets confirm the superiority of our method over existing techniques.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering functional data generated by a mixture of Gaussian processes. The goal is to recover the hidden group associated with each observed function. Its approach turns that problem into a collection of simpler clustering problems and then combines their answers.

The key observation is that projecting a function onto a chosen projection function produces a coefficient following a one-dimensional Gaussian mixture model. The method repeats this operation with multiple projections and fits a separate mixture model to each set of coefficients. Each fitted model supplies one clustering, and ensemble clustering merges these into a consensus assignment. Multiple views therefore contribute to the final grouping.

The authors report a substantial computational reduction relative to leading methods and provide theoretical guarantees for identifying and learning Gaussian process mixtures. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets also favor the proposed approach over existing techniques. The contribution combines a distributional property of projections with ensemble clustering, making a potentially costly functional-data problem accessible through many simpler one-dimensional models.
summary.tldr: The method clusters Gaussian-process-mixture data by combining Gaussian mixture clusterings from multiple one-dimensional projections.

title: Learning Mixtures of Gaussian Processes through Random Projection

abstract: The performance of optimization methods is often tied to the spectrum of the objective Hessian. Yet, conventional assumptions, such as smoothness, do often not enable us to make finely-grained convergence statements—particularly not for non-convex problems. Striving for a more intricate characterization of complexity, we introduce a unique concept termed graded non-convexity. This allows to partition the class of non-convex problems into a nested chain of subclasses. Interestingly, many traditional non-convex objectives, including partially convex problems, matrix factorizations, and neural networks, fall within these subclasses. As a second contribution, we propose gradient methods with spectral preconditioning, which employ inexact top eigenvectors of the Hessian to address the ill-conditioning of the problem, contingent on the grade. Our analysis reveals that these new methods provide provably superior convergence rates compared to basic gradient descent on applicable problem classes, particularly when large gaps exist between the top eigenvalues of the Hessian. Our theory is validated by numerical experiments executed on multiple practical machine learning problems.

paragraphs: Optimization speed depends partly on the objective’s curvature, represented by the Hessian and its eigenvalues. Broad assumptions such as smoothness can hide distinctions between non-convex problems that matter for convergence. This paper introduces graded non-convexity to organize such problems into nested subclasses and make those distinctions more explicit.

The subclasses include familiar objectives arising in partially convex problems, matrix factorization, and neural networks. Building on this classification, the authors propose gradient methods with spectral preconditioning. These methods use approximate leading eigenvectors of the Hessian to address ill-conditioning in a way that depends on the problem’s grade.

For the applicable problem classes, the analysis proves better convergence rates than basic gradient descent. The improvements are especially relevant when there are large gaps between the leading Hessian eigenvalues. Numerical experiments on multiple practical machine-learning problems support the theory. The contribution connects a finer description of non-convex structure to an optimization method that can exploit that structure, giving more specific guidance than a single broad smoothness assumption.
summary.tldr: Graded non-convexity identifies problem classes where Hessian-based spectral preconditioning provably improves convergence over basic gradient descent.

title: Spectral Preconditioning for Gradient Methods on Graded Non-convex Functions

abstract: Canonicalization provides an architecture-agnostic method for enforcing equivariance, with generalizations such as frame-averaging recently gaining prominence as a lightweight and flexible alternative to equivariant architectures. Recent works have found an empirical benefit to using probabilistic frames instead, which learn weighted distributions over group elements. In this work, we provide strong theoretical justification for this phenomenon: for commonly-used groups, there is no efficiently computable choice of frame that preserves continuity of the function being averaged. In other words, unweighted frame-averaging can turn a smooth, non-symmetric function into a discontinuous, symmetric function. To address this fundamental robustness problem, we formally define and construct weighted frames, which provably preserve continuity, and demonstrate their utility by constructing efficient and continuous weighted frames for the actions of $SO(d)$, $O(d)$, and $S_n$ on point clouds.

paragraphs: Canonicalization and frame averaging offer ways to enforce symmetry without designing a specialized equivariant architecture. They use transformations of an input to build a symmetry-respecting function. This paper examines whether that process also preserves continuity, so that small input changes do not produce abrupt output changes.

The authors establish a theoretical obstruction for commonly used groups: no efficiently computable choice of unweighted frame preserves continuity in the setting studied. As a result, averaging can transform a smooth function without symmetry into a symmetric function with discontinuities. This gives a theoretical explanation for empirical benefits previously observed with probabilistic frames that weight different group elements.

To address the problem, the paper formally defines weighted frames and constructs examples that provably preserve continuity. It supplies efficient, continuous weighted frames for the actions of SO(d), O(d), and S_n on point clouds. The contribution makes continuity an explicit design requirement alongside symmetry and shows how weighting can satisfy that requirement in these cases.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies continuity barriers for unweighted frame averaging and constructs weighted frames that preserve continuity for point-cloud symmetries.

title: Equivariant Frames and the Impossibility of Continuous Canonicalization

abstract: Federated compositional optimization has been actively studied in the past few years. However, existing methods mainly focus on the two-level compositional optimization problem, which cannot be directly applied to the multi-level counterparts. Moreover, the convergence rate of existing federated two-level compositional optimization learning algorithms fails to achieve linear speedup with respect to the number of workers under heterogeneous settings. After identifying the reason for this failure, we developed a novel federated stochastic multi-level compositional optimization algorithm by introducing a novel Jacobian-vector product estimator. This innovation mitigates both the heterogeneity issue and the communication efficiency issue simultaneously. We then theoretically proved that our algorithm can achieve the level-independent and linear speedup convergence rate for nonconvex problems. To our knowledge, this is the first time that a federated learning algorithm can achieve such a favorable convergence rate for multi-level compositional problems. Moreover, experimental results confirm the efficacy of our algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies federated optimization problems whose objectives contain several nested levels of computation. Earlier approaches mainly handle two levels, and extending them to deeper compositions is not straightforward. Another difficulty is that workers can have different data distributions: existing two-level methods fail to obtain a convergence speedup proportional to the number of workers in that setting.

The authors identify the source of this failure and introduce a stochastic algorithm for multi-level objectives. Its central contribution is a new estimator for Jacobian-vector products, the quantities needed to propagate optimization information through composed functions. The estimator addresses differences between workers alongside communication efficiency, making these two concerns part of the same algorithmic design.

For nonconvex problems, the authors prove a convergence rate that is independent of composition depth and achieves linear speedup with the number of workers. This describes a theoretical convergence benefit, rather than a promise about elapsed runtime. Experiments also support the algorithm’s effectiveness, complementing the analysis of deeper federated objectives.
summary.tldr: A new gradient estimator enables federated optimization of nested objectives with depth-independent convergence rates and linear speedup across workers.

title: A Doubly Recursive Stochastic Compositional Gradient Descent Method for Federated Multi-Level Compositional Optimization

abstract: We investigate model assessment and selection in a changing environment, by synthesizing datasets from both the current time period and historical epochs. To tackle unknown and potentially arbitrary temporal distribution shift, we develop an adaptive rolling window approach to estimate the generalization error of a given model. This strategy also facilitates the comparison between any two candidate models by estimating the difference of their generalization errors. We further integrate pairwise comparisons into a single-elimination tournament, achieving near-optimal model selection from a collection of candidates. Theoretical analyses and empirical experiments underscore the adaptivity of our proposed methods to the non-stationarity in data.

paragraphs: Assessing a model becomes difficult when the data distribution changes over time. Historical observations provide evidence about performance, but their relevance depends on how the environment has changed. This paper studies how to use datasets from the current period and earlier periods to estimate generalization error under unknown, potentially arbitrary temporal distribution shifts.

The authors develop an adaptive rolling window approach that adjusts the historical span used for assessment. They extend the same strategy to compare two candidate models by estimating the difference between their generalization errors. This makes relative model quality a direct target of estimation and supplies a comparison procedure for choosing among alternatives.

To select from a larger collection, the method organizes pairwise comparisons into a single-elimination tournament. The paper establishes near-optimal model selection and supports the approach through theoretical analysis and empirical experiments. Together, the contributions link adaptive use of historical data to both performance estimation and model choice, with the reported results emphasizing responsiveness to non-stationary data.
summary.tldr: Adaptive rolling windows estimate model performance under temporal shift and support near-optimal selection through pairwise tournaments.

title: Model Assessment and Selection under Temporal Distribution Shift

abstract: In recent years, denoising problems have become intertwined with the development of deep generative models. In particular, diffusion models are trained like denoisers, and the distribution they model coincide with denoising priors in the Bayesian picture. However, denoising through diffusion-based posterior sampling requires the noise level and covariance to be known, preventing blind denoising. We overcome this limitation by introducing Gibbs Diffusion (GDiff), a general methodology addressing posterior sampling of both the signal and the noise parameters. Assuming arbitrary parametric Gaussian noise, we develop a Gibbs algorithm that alternates sampling steps from a conditional diffusion model trained to map the signal prior to the class of noise distributions, and a Monte Carlo sampler to infer the noise parameters. Our theoretical analysis highlights potential pitfalls, guides diagnostic usage, and quantifies errors in the Gibbs stationary distribution caused by the diffusion model. We showcase our method for 1) blind denoising of natural images involving colored noises with unknown amplitude and exponent, and 2) a cosmology problem, namely the analysis of cosmic microwave background data, where Bayesian inference of "noise" parameters means constraining models of the evolution of the Universe.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can provide prior knowledge about clean signals for Bayesian denoising. However, diffusion-based posterior sampling ordinarily requires the noise level and covariance to be known. Blind denoising must infer those noise properties as well as the clean signal, so treating them as fixed inputs leaves an important part of the problem unresolved.

Gibbs Diffusion addresses this by alternating between two sampling steps. A conditional diffusion model samples the signal, while a Monte Carlo sampler infers the noise parameters. The method assumes a parametric Gaussian noise model. Within that setting, it targets joint posterior inference over the signal and the parameters describing its corruption.

The theoretical analysis identifies potential pitfalls, informs diagnostics, and quantifies how diffusion-model errors affect the Gibbs stationary distribution. Demonstrations include natural images with colored noise of unknown amplitude and exponent, and cosmic microwave background analysis. In the cosmology application, inferring the quantities treated as noise parameters constrains models of the Universe's evolution, making noise estimation itself scientifically meaningful.
summary.tldr: Gibbs Diffusion alternates signal and noise-parameter sampling to enable blind denoising under parametric Gaussian noise.

title: Listening to the noise: Blind Denoising with Gibbs Diffusion

abstract: Mixed integer linear programs (MILP) are flexible and powerful tools for modeling and solving many difficult real-world combinatorial optimization problems. In this paper, we propose a novel machine learning (ML)-based framework ConPaS that learns to predict solutions to MILPs with contrastive learning. For training, we collect high-quality solutions as positive samples. We also collect low-quality or infeasible solutions as negative samples using novel optimization-based or sampling approaches. We then learn to make discriminative predictions by contrasting the positive and negative samples. During testing, we predict and fix the assignments for a subset of integer variables and then solve the resulting reduced MILP to find high-quality solutions. Empirically, ConPaS achieves state-of-the-art results compared to other ML-based approaches in terms of the quality of and the speed at which solutions are found.

paragraphs: Mixed integer linear programs express optimization problems in which some decisions must take integer values. ConPaS uses machine learning to help solve these problems by learning distinctions between promising assignments and poor ones. Its training signal includes both high-quality solutions and examples that are low-quality or violate the problem’s constraints.

The authors construct negative examples through optimization-based and sampling procedures, then train with a contrastive objective. Contrasting positive and negative examples encourages discriminative predictions about solution assignments. This makes unsuccessful or infeasible candidates useful training evidence alongside successful solutions, rather than learning only from examples of good outcomes.

At test time, the model predicts values for a subset of integer variables and fixes those choices. A solver then handles the reduced optimization problem to find a high-quality solution. This division of work combines learned predictions with subsequent optimization. Empirical results report state-of-the-art solution quality and speed compared with other machine-learning approaches, supporting the usefulness of contrastive training for guiding this predict-and-search process.
summary.tldr: ConPaS learns from good and bad MILP solutions, fixes selected integer decisions, and solves the reduced problem to improve solution quality and speed.

title: Contrastive Predict-and-Search for Mixed Integer Linear Programs

abstract: There are a thousand ways to caption an image. Contrastive Language Pretraining (CLIP) on the other hand, works by mapping an image and its caption to a single vector – limiting how well CLIP-like models can represent the diverse ways to describe an image. In this work, we introduce Llip, Latent Language Image Pretraining, which models the diversity of captions that could match an image. Llip’s vision encoder outputs a set of visual features that are mixed into a final representation by conditioning on information derived from the text. We show that Llip outperforms non-contextualized baselines like CLIP and SigLIP on a variety of tasks even with large-scale encoders. Llip improves zero-shot classification by an average of 2.9% zero-shot classification benchmarks with a ViT-G/14 encoder. Specifically, Llip attains a zero-shot top-1 accuracy of 83.5% on ImageNet outperforming a similarly sized CLIP by 1.4%. We also demonstrate improvement on zero-shot retrieval on MS-COCO by 6.0%. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the components introduced by the method and demonstrate that Llip leads to richer visual representations.

paragraphs: An image can support many descriptions, each emphasizing different content. Contrastive image-language models such as CLIP map an image to a single vector, which limits their ability to represent this diversity. The paper introduces Latent Language Image Pretraining, or Llip, to make visual representations responsive to different possible captions.

Llip's vision encoder produces a set of visual features. Information derived from the text then determines how those features are mixed into the final representation. This gives the model a way to represent the same image differently depending on the description being considered, directly incorporating caption diversity into image-language matching.

The authors report improvements over non-contextualized CLIP and SigLIP baselines across tasks, including with large encoders. With a ViT-G/14 encoder, the reported average zero-shot classification improvement is 2.9%. ImageNet top-1 accuracy reaches 83.5%, exceeding a similarly sized CLIP by 1.4%, and zero-shot MS-COCO retrieval improves by 6.0%. Component analyses further support the claim that the method learns richer visual representations.
summary.tldr: Llip mixes multiple visual features using text context to model caption diversity and improve zero-shot classification and retrieval.

title: Modeling Caption Diversity in Contrastive Vision-Language Pretraining

abstract: Decision Transformer (DT) is an innovative algorithm leveraging recent advances of the transformer architecture in reinforcement learning (RL). However, a notable limitation of DT is its reliance on recalling trajectories from datasets, losing the capability to seamlessly stitch sub-optimal trajectories together. In this work we introduce a general sequence modeling framework for studying sequential decision making through the lens of Hierarchical RL. At the time of making decisions, a high-level policy first proposes an ideal prompt for the current state, a low-level policy subsequently generates an action conditioned on the given prompt. We show DT emerges as a special case of this framework with certain choices of high-level and low-level policies, and discuss the potential failure of these choices. Inspired by these observations, we study how to jointly optimize the high-level and low-level policies to enable the stitching ability, which further leads to the development of new offline RL algorithms. Our empirical results clearly show that the proposed algorithms significantly surpass DT on several control and navigation benchmarks. We hope our contributions can inspire the integration of transformer architectures within the field of RL.

paragraphs: Decision Transformer uses sequence modeling for reinforcement learning, but this paper identifies a weakness in combining useful portions of imperfect recorded trajectories. Recalling trajectories from a dataset does not necessarily provide the ability to stitch those portions into better behavior. The authors examine this issue through hierarchical reinforcement learning.

Their general framework separates each decision into two stages. A high-level policy proposes a prompt suited to the current state, and a low-level policy chooses an action conditioned on that prompt. They show that Decision Transformer is a special case under particular choices of these policies and discuss how those choices can fail.

The authors then study joint optimization of the two policies to enable trajectory stitching, leading to new offline reinforcement learning algorithms. Experiments show significant improvements over Decision Transformer on several control and navigation benchmarks. The contribution is both an explanation of an existing limitation and a design route: learning what to ask the action policy to do can improve how stored experience is combined.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical view of Decision Transformer leads to jointly trained prompt and action policies that better combine useful parts of offline trajectories.

title: Rethinking Decision Transformer via Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Local feature selection in machine learning provides instance-specific explanations by focusing on the most relevant features for each prediction, enhancing the interpretability of complex models. However, such methods tend to produce misleading explanations by encoding additional information in their selections. In this work, we attribute the problem of misleading selections by formalizing the concepts of label and feature leakage. We rigorously derive the necessary and sufficient conditions under which we can guarantee no leakage, and show existing methods do not meet these conditions. Furthermore, we propose the first local feature selection method that is proven to have no leakage called SUWR. Our experimental results indicate that SUWR is less prone to overfitting and combines state-of-the-art predictive performance with high feature-selection sparsity. Our generic and easily extendable formal approach provides a strong theoretical basis for future work on interpretability with reliable explanations.

paragraphs: Local feature selection explains a prediction by showing a small set of relevant inputs. But the pattern of selected features can itself encode extra information, making an apparently sparse explanation misleading. This paper formalizes that issue as label leakage and feature leakage within the selection process.

The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for avoiding leakage and show that existing methods fail those conditions. They then introduce SUWR, a local feature-selection method with a proof of no leakage. The formal framework is intended to support reliable explanations by ensuring the selection mechanism does not secretly communicate information beyond the selected values.

Experiments find less overfitting and a combination of strong predictive performance with sparse selections. The contribution is therefore both a diagnostic theory and a method satisfying it. The no-leakage property addresses a specific failure mode in feature-based explanations; it does not by itself certify that every selected feature is causally responsible for the underlying outcome.
summary.tldr: SUWR provides provably leakage-free local feature selection, making sparse prediction explanations less prone to hidden information encoding.

title: Local Feature Selection without Label or Feature Leakage for Interpretable Machine Learning Predictions

abstract: Modern advancements in large-scale machine learning would be impossible without the paradigm of data-parallel distributed computing. Since distributed computing with large-scale models imparts excessive pressure on communication channels, significant recent research has been directed toward co-designing communication compression strategies and training algorithms with the goal of reducing communication costs. While pure data parallelism allows better data scaling, it suffers from poor model scaling properties. Indeed, compute nodes are severely limited by memory constraints, preventing further increases in model size. For this reason, the latest achievements in training giant neural network models also rely on some form of model parallelism. In this work, we take a closer theoretical look at Independent Subnetwork Training (IST), which is a recently proposed and highly effective technique for solving the aforementioned problems. We identify fundamental differences between IST and alternative approaches, such as distributed methods with compressed communication, and provide a precise analysis of its optimization performance on a quadratic model.

paragraphs: Distributed training faces two related pressures: moving information between compute nodes and fitting a large model into each node's memory. Data parallelism helps process more data, but memory constraints limit how far it can scale model size. Communication compression addresses another part of the problem by reducing what nodes exchange.

This paper gives a theoretical examination of Independent Subnetwork Training, or IST, a previously proposed technique for addressing these scaling challenges. The authors identify fundamental differences between IST and alternative distributed approaches, including methods that compress communication. Their focus is on understanding the optimization behavior of the method, rather than treating these approaches as interchangeable ways to reduce communication.

The main analytical result is a precise account of IST's optimization performance on a quadratic model. That setting defines the scope of the stated analysis. The contribution provides a mathematical basis for reasoning about IST and distinguishing it from other distributed strategies, helping clarify the optimization consequences of changing how training is divided across subnetworks.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes Independent Subnetwork Training on a quadratic model and explains its fundamental differences from communication-compressed distributed optimization.

title: Towards a Better Theoretical Understanding of Independent Subnetwork Training

abstract: In digital markets comprised of many competing services, each user chooses between multiple service providers according to their preferences, and the chosen service makes use of the user data to incrementally improve its model. The service providers’ models influence which service the user will choose at the next time step, and the user’s choice, in return, influences the model update, leading to a feedback loop. In this paper, we formalize the above dynamics and develop a simple and efficient decentralized algorithm to locally minimize the overall user loss. Theoretically, we show that our algorithm asymptotically converges to stationary points of of the overall loss almost surely. We also experimentally demonstrate the utility of our algorithm with real world data.

paragraphs: In a market with competing services, each provider learns from the users who choose it. Better or different models can change which provider a user selects next, which in turn changes the data available for future learning. This paper formalizes that feedback loop between user choice and incremental model updates.

The authors develop a simple, efficient decentralized algorithm aimed at locally minimizing overall user loss. Its target reflects outcomes across users, while its decentralized structure allows learning to proceed across the competing providers. The formulation treats the evolving allocation of users as part of the learning problem, because the models themselves influence which data each service receives.

The theoretical result establishes that the algorithm converges asymptotically to stationary points of overall loss almost surely. This is a convergence statement about stationary points, rather than a guarantee of reaching a global optimum. Experiments using real-world data also demonstrate the algorithm’s utility. Together, the analysis and evaluation address learning in markets where the stream of training data is shaped by users’ responses to the current services.
summary.tldr: A decentralized learning algorithm accounts for user-choice feedback and converges almost surely to stationary points of overall user loss.

title: Learning from Streaming Data when Users Choose

abstract: We use (multi)modal deep neural networks (DNNs) to probe for sites of multimodal integration in the human brain by predicting stereoencephalography (SEEG) recordings taken while human subjects watched movies. We operationalize sites of multimodal integration as regions where a multimodal vision-language model predicts recordings better than unimodal language, unimodal vision, or linearly-integrated language-vision models. Our target DNN models span different architectures (e.g., convolutional networks and transformers) and multimodal training techniques (e.g., cross-attention and contrastive learning). As a key enabling step, we first demonstrate that trained vision and language models systematically outperform their randomly initialized counterparts in their ability to predict SEEG signals. We then compare unimodal and multimodal models against one another. Because our target DNN models often have different architectures, number of parameters, and training sets (possibly obscuring those differences attributable to integration), we carry out a controlled comparison of two models (SLIP and SimCLR), which keep all of these attributes the same aside from input modality. Using this approach, we identify a sizable number of neural sites (on average 141 out of 1090 total sites or 12.94%) and brain regions where multimodal integration seems to occur. Additionally, we find that among the variants of multimodal training techniques we assess, CLIP-style training is the best suited for downstream prediction of the neural activity in these sites.

paragraphs: The paper uses neural networks to investigate where the human brain may integrate visual and language information. It predicts stereoencephalography recordings collected while people watched movies. A site counts as evidence of integration when a multimodal model predicts its activity better than vision-only, language-only, or linearly combined vision-and-language models.

They then compare models spanning different architectures and multimodal training methods. Using this approach, they identify an average of 141 out of 1,090 recording sites, or 12.94%, where multimodal integration appears to occur. Among the assessed training approaches, CLIP-style training best predicts activity at these sites. The findings locate candidate integration sites through comparative predictive performance; the evidence rests on that operational definition of integration and the accompanying controlled model comparison.
summary.tldr: Comparing neural models’ predictions of brain recordings identifies candidate sites of vision-language integration during movie watching.

title: Revealing Vision-Language Integration in the Brain with Multimodal Networks

abstract: We seek to enable classic processing of continuous ultra-sparse spatiotemporal data generated by event-based sensors with dense machine learning models. We propose a novel hybrid pipeline composed of asynchronous sensing and synchronous processing that combines several ideas: (1) an embedding based on PointNet models – the ALERT module – that can continuously integrate new and dismiss old events thanks to a leakage mechanism, (2) a flexible readout of the embedded data that allows to feed any downstream model with always up-to-date features at any sampling rate, (3) exploiting the input sparsity in a patch-based approach inspired by Vision Transformer to optimize the efficiency of the method. These embeddings are then processed by a transformer model trained for object and gesture recognition. Using this approach, we achieve performances at the state-of-the-art with a lower latency than competitors. We also demonstrate that our asynchronous model can operate at any desired sampling rate.

paragraphs: Event-based sensors generate sparse streams of changes across space and time, creating a mismatch with dense machine learning models. ALERT-Transformer addresses this mismatch by separating continuous updates from the timing of downstream processing. Its pipeline combines asynchronous sensing with synchronous computation so that conventional models can work with features representing the current event stream.

The central ALERT module uses a PointNet-based embedding that continuously incorporates incoming events. A leakage mechanism removes the influence of older events. A flexible readout then supplies updated features whenever a downstream model needs them, at a chosen sampling rate. The pipeline also uses a patch-based design inspired by Vision Transformers to exploit sparsity and improve computational efficiency.

The authors feed these embeddings into a transformer trained for object and gesture recognition. They report state-of-the-art performance with lower latency than competing methods and demonstrate operation at arbitrary desired sampling rates. The approach matters because it lets the event representation evolve continuously while leaving the timing of downstream decisions flexible.
summary.tldr: ALERT-Transformer continuously embeds sparse sensor events for flexible downstream processing, achieving state-of-the-art recognition with lower latency.

title: ALERT-Transformer: Bridging Asynchronous and Synchronous Machine Learning for Real-Time Event-based Spatio-Temporal Data

abstract: Sample efficiency remains a crucial challenge in applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to real-world tasks. While recent algorithms have made significant strides in improving sample efficiency, none have achieved consistently superior performance across diverse domains. In this paper, we introduce EfficientZero V2, a general framework designed for sample-efficient RL algorithms. We have expanded the performance of EfficientZero to multiple domains, encompassing both continuous and discrete actions, as well as visual and low-dimensional inputs. With a series of improvements we propose, EfficientZero V2 outperforms the current state-of-the-art (SoTA) by a significant margin in diverse tasks under the limited data setting. EfficientZero V2 exhibits a notable advancement over the prevailing general algorithm, DreamerV3, achieving superior outcomes in 50 of 66 evaluated tasks across multiple benchmarks, including Atari 100k, Proprio Control, and Vision Control.

We have expanded the performance of EfficientZero to multiple domains, encompassing both continuous and discrete actions, as well as visual and low-dimensional inputs. With a series of improvements we propose, EfficientZero V2 outperforms the current state-of-the-art (SoTA) by a significant margin in diverse tasks under the limited data setting. EfficientZero V2 exhibits a notable advancement over the prevailing general algorithm, DreamerV3, achieving superior outcomes in 50 of 66 evaluated tasks across multiple benchmarks, including Atari 100k, Proprio Control, and Vision Control.

paragraphs: EfficientZero V2 targets a practical reinforcement-learning problem: learning useful behavior from limited interaction data across different kinds of tasks. The paper builds on EfficientZero and broadens its reach to settings with discrete or continuous actions. It also covers both visual observations and low-dimensional inputs, making breadth across environments a central part of the contribution.

These combinations matter because a generally useful learning framework must handle variation in both what an agent observes and how it acts. The authors introduce a series of improvements intended to make that broader coverage sample-efficient. Their evaluation asks whether the resulting framework performs strongly when the amount of available training data is restricted.

The reported results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in the evaluated limited-data tasks. Against DreamerV3, EfficientZero V2 achieves better outcomes in 50 of 66 tasks across benchmarks including Atari 100k, Proprio Control, and Vision Control. This supports its empirical breadth while preserving the distinction between strong performance across many tasks and superiority on every evaluated task.
summary.tldr: EfficientZero V2 extends sample-efficient reinforcement learning across action and observation types, outperforming DreamerV3 on 50 of 66 evaluated tasks.

title: EfficientZero V2: Mastering Discrete and Continuous Control with Limited Data

abstract: Koufogiannis et al. (2016) showed a $\textit{gradual release}$ result for Laplace noise-based differentially private mechanisms: given an $\varepsilon$-DP release, a new release with privacy parameter $\varepsilon’ > \varepsilon$ can be computed such that the combined privacy loss of both releases is at most $\varepsilon’$ and the distribution of the latter is the same as a single release with parameter $\varepsilon’$. They also showed gradual release techniques for Gaussian noise, later also explored by Whitehouse et al. (2022). In this paper, we consider a more general $\textit{multiple release}$ setting in which analysts hold private releases with different privacy parameters corresponding to different access/trust levels. These releases are determined one by one, with privacy parameters in arbitrary order. A multiple release is $\textit{lossless}$ if having access to a subset $S$ of the releases has the same privacy guarantee as the least private release in $S$, and each release has the same distribution as a single release with the same privacy parameter. Our main result is that lossless multiple release is possible for a large class of additive noise mechanisms. For the Gaussian mechanism we give a simple method for lossless multiple release with a short, self-contained analysis that does not require knowledge of the mathematics of Brownian motion. We also present lossless multiple release for the Laplace and Poisson mechanisms. Finally, we consider how to efficiently do gradual release of sparse histograms, and present a mechanism with running time independent of the number of dimensions.

paragraphs: Different analysts may be allowed to receive differentially private releases at different privacy levels. This paper asks how to construct those releases sequentially when their privacy parameters can arrive in any order. The aim is to prevent access to several releases from adding privacy loss beyond the least private release among them.

The authors call a multiple-release scheme lossless when every subset has that privacy guarantee and each individual release has the same distribution as a standalone release at its assigned privacy level. Both conditions matter: coordinating releases must preserve their individual distributions while controlling what their combination reveals. The main result establishes that this is possible for a large class of additive-noise mechanisms.

The paper provides constructions for Gaussian, Laplace, and Poisson mechanisms. Its Gaussian method comes with a short, self-contained analysis that avoids Brownian-motion mathematics. It also addresses gradual release for sparse histograms, presenting a mechanism whose running time does not depend on the number of dimensions, extending the contribution to efficient release of high-dimensional summaries.
summary.tldr: Coordinated noisy releases can preserve standalone distributions while limiting any subset’s privacy loss to its least private release.

title: Private Lossless Multiple Release

abstract: Existing symmetry discovery methods predominantly focus on global transformations across the entire system or space, but they fail to consider the symmetries in local neighborhoods. This may result in the reported symmetry group being a misrepresentation of the true symmetry. In this paper, we formalize the notion of local symmetry as atlas equivariance. Our proposed pipeline, automatic local symmetry discovery (AtlasD), recovers the local symmetries of a function by training local predictor networks and then learning a Lie group basis to which the predictors are equivariant. We demonstrate AtlasD is capable of discovering local symmetry groups with multiple connected components in top-quark tagging and partial differential equation experiments. The discovered local symmetry is shown to be a useful inductive bias that improves the performance of downstream tasks in climate segmentation and vision tasks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/AtlasD.

This may result in the reported symmetry group being a misrepresentation of the true symmetry. In this paper, we formalize the notion of local symmetry as atlas equivariance. Our proposed pipeline, automatic local symmetry discovery (AtlasD), recovers the local symmetries of a function by training local predictor networks and then learning a Lie group basis to which the predictors are equivariant. We demonstrate AtlasD is capable of discovering local symmetry groups with multiple connected components in top-quark tagging and partial differential equation experiments. The discovered local symmetry is shown to be a useful inductive bias that improves the performance of downstream tasks in climate segmentation and vision tasks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/AtlasD.

paragraphs: Symmetries describe transformations under which a function behaves in a consistent way. Existing discovery methods commonly search for transformations that apply throughout an entire space. The paper argues that this can misrepresent systems whose symmetries differ between local neighborhoods, and introduces a formal description of local symmetry called atlas equivariance.

AtlasD discovers this structure in two stages. It first trains predictor networks for local regions, then learns a Lie group basis describing transformations to which those predictors are equivariant. In plain terms, it seeks organized families of transformations whose effects on inputs correspond consistently to effects on predictions. The local formulation allows the discovered structure to reflect neighborhood-specific behavior.

Experiments involving top-quark tagging and partial differential equations demonstrate discovery of local symmetry groups with multiple connected components. The authors also use the recovered symmetries as an inductive bias, meaning structural guidance for learning, and report improved performance in climate segmentation and vision tasks. These findings connect symmetry discovery to practical downstream prediction improvements.
summary.tldr: AtlasD learns local symmetries and uses the discovered structure to improve downstream climate and vision tasks.

title: AtlasD: Automatic Local Symmetry Discovery

abstract: Model merging seeks to integrate task-specific expert models into a unified architecture while preserving multi-task generalization capabilities, yet parameter interference between constituent models frequently induces performance degradation. Although prior work has explored many merging strategies, resolving interference without additional data for retraining or test-time computation remains challenging. In this paper, we theoretically demonstrate that the task vectors of the linear layer constitute an approximate linear subspace for its corresponding input. Therefore, we can minimize interference under the guidance of task vectors. Based on this insight, we propose WUDI-Merging (Whoever started the interference shoUld enD It), a simple yet effective model merging method that eliminates interference without any additional data or rescaling coefficients. Comprehensive empirical evaluations across vision and language benchmarks demonstrate our method’s superiority, achieving state-of-the-art performance in data-free model merging scenarios (average 10.9% improvement versus baseline methods) while even outperforming mainstream test-time adaptation approaches by 3.3%, and only very few computing resources are required. The source code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/nathanielyvo/WUDI-Merging.

paragraphs: Model merging combines task-specific experts into one model, but their parameters can interfere and degrade performance. Addressing this without additional training data or test-time computation is difficult. WUDI-Merging uses information in task vectors to guide how that interference is resolved.

The theoretical starting point is that a linear layer’s task vectors form an approximate linear subspace for its corresponding input. The authors use this relationship to guide interference minimization. Their resulting merging method is described as eliminating interference without additional data or rescaling coefficients, with low computational requirements. The approximate nature of the subspace relationship is part of the underlying theoretical claim.

Across the evaluated vision and language benchmarks, WUDI-Merging achieves reported state-of-the-art results for data-free merging. The abstract reports an average 10.9% improvement over baseline methods and a 3.3% improvement over mainstream test-time adaptation approaches. These findings support task vectors as useful guidance for combining experts while avoiding the additional data and computation associated with other adaptation strategies.
summary.tldr: WUDI-Merging uses task-vector geometry to address interference when combining expert models without additional data or rescaling coefficients.

title: Whoever Started the interference Should End It: Guiding Data-Free Model Merging via Task Vectors

abstract: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) has demonstrated success in online planning for deterministic environments, yet significant challenges remain in adapting it to stochastic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), particularly in continuous state-action spaces. Existing methods, such as HOOT, which combines MCTS with the Hierarchical Optimistic Optimization (HOO) bandit strategy, address continuous spaces but rely on a logarithmic exploration bonus that lacks theoretical guarantees in non-stationary, stochastic settings. Recent advancements, such as POLY-HOOT, introduced a polynomial bonus term to achieve convergence in deterministic MDPs, though a similar theory for stochastic MDPs remains undeveloped. In this paper, we propose a novel MCTS algorithm, Stochastic-Power-HOOT, designed for continuous, stochastic MDPs. Stochastic-Power-HOOT integrates a power mean as a value backup operator, alongside a polynomial exploration bonus to address the non-stationarity inherent in continuous action spaces. Our theoretical analysis establishes that Stochastic-Power-HOOT converges at a polynomial rate of $\mathcal{O}(n^{-\zeta})$, $\zeta \in (0,1/2)$, where $ n $ is the number of visited trajectories, thereby extending the non-asymptotic convergence guarantees of POLY-HOOT to stochastic environments. Experimental results on stochastic tasks validate our theoretical findings, demonstrating the effectiveness of Stochastic-Power-HOOT in continuous, stochastic domains.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo Tree Search becomes harder to analyze when actions and states are continuous and outcomes are stochastic. Existing approaches combine tree search with hierarchical exploration, but the paper identifies a gap in convergence guarantees for this setting. In particular, guarantees developed for deterministic environments do not supply the corresponding stochastic theory.

The proposed Stochastic-Power-HOOT algorithm combines a power-mean value backup with a polynomial exploration bonus. The backup determines how values from explored branches are aggregated. The exploration bonus addresses the non-stationarity that arises in continuous-action search, where the estimation problem changes as exploration proceeds. These components are designed together for continuous, stochastic Markov decision processes.

The authors establish a non-asymptotic polynomial convergence rate of O(n^(-zeta)), with zeta between zero and one-half and n denoting visited trajectories. This extends the type of convergence guarantee provided by POLY-HOOT to stochastic environments. Experiments on stochastic tasks support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the proposed algorithm's effectiveness in the continuous, uncertain domains it targets.
summary.tldr: Stochastic-Power-HOOT combines power-mean backups and polynomial exploration bonuses to obtain convergence guarantees for continuous, stochastic tree search.

title: Power Mean Estimation in Stochastic Continuous Monte-Carlo Tree Search

abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful approach to extract semantically meaningful concepts from the internals of large language models (LLMs) trained mainly in the text domain. In this work, we explore whether DL can extract meaningful concepts from less human-interpretable scientific data, such as vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images, where limited prior knowledge exists about which high-level concepts should arise. We propose a novel combination of a sparse DL algorithm, Iterative Codebook Feature Learning (ICFL), with a PCA whitening pre-processing step derived from control data. Using this combined approach, we successfully retrieve biologically meaningful concepts, such as cell types and genetic perturbations. Moreover, we demonstrate how our method reveals subtle morphological changes arising from human-interpretable interventions, offering a promising new direction for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability in bioimaging.

paragraphs: Sparse dictionary learning has been used to extract meaningful concepts from language model internals. This paper asks whether it can also reveal useful concepts in microscopy foundation models. The challenge differs from interpreting ordinary text because scientific images are less directly understandable, and researchers may have limited prior knowledge of the high-level concepts a model represents.

The proposed method combines Iterative Codebook Feature Learning, a sparse dictionary learning algorithm, with PCA whitening based on control data. This preprocessing and feature-learning combination is applied to representations from models trained on cell microscopy images. The aim is to extract interpretable biological structure from the model’s internal features.

The researchers recover concepts associated with cell types and genetic perturbations. They also show how the method reveals subtle changes in cell morphology arising from interpretable interventions. These results support dictionary learning as a promising tool for mechanistic interpretation in bioimaging, with potential to aid scientific discovery by exposing biologically meaningful distinctions already encoded in learned representations.
summary.tldr: Sparse dictionary learning with control-derived PCA whitening extracts biological concepts and subtle morphological changes from microscopy model representations.

title: Towards scientific discovery with dictionary learning: Extracting biological concepts from microscopy foundation models

abstract: Estimating causal effects is crucial for decision-makers in many applications, but it is particularly challenging with observational network data due to peer interactions. Some algorithms have been proposed to estimate causal effects involving network data, particularly peer effects, but they often fail to tell apart diverse peer effects. To address this issue, we propose a general setting which considers both peer direct effects and peer indirect effects, and the effect of an individual’s own treatment, and provide the identification conditions of these causal effects. To differentiate these effects, we leverage causal mediation analysis and tailor it specifically for network data. Furthermore, given the inherent challenges of accurately estimating effects in networked environments, we propose to incorporate attention mechanisms to capture the varying influences of different neighbors and to explore high-order neighbor effects using multi-layer graph neural networks (GNNs). Additionally, we employ the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to further enhance the model’s robustness and accuracy. Extensive experiments on two semi-synthetic datasets derived from real-world networks and on a dataset from a recommendation system confirm the effectiveness of our approach. Our findings have the potential to improve intervention strategies in networked systems, particularly in social networks and public health.

paragraphs: In network data, an individual’s outcome can depend on their own treatment and on interactions with peers. This makes causal estimation difficult, especially when different peer effects are combined. The paper introduces a setting that distinguishes direct peer effects, indirect peer effects, and the effect of the individual’s own treatment.

The authors provide identification conditions for these effects and adapt causal mediation analysis to network data. Their estimation approach uses attention to represent differences in how strongly neighbors influence an individual. Multiple graph neural network layers capture higher-order neighbor effects. The method also incorporates the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion to improve robustness and accuracy.

Experiments use two semi-synthetic datasets derived from real networks and a recommendation-system dataset, supporting the approach’s effectiveness. Separating different pathways of influence could help decision-makers design interventions in connected populations. The identification conditions are central to the causal interpretation: the framework specifies when the distinct effects can be identified, while the model addresses the practical challenge of estimating them in networks.
summary.tldr: A network-specific causal mediation framework separates direct and indirect peer effects from own-treatment effects, with identification conditions and empirical support.

title: Telling Peer Direct Effects from Indirect Effects in Observational Network Data

abstract: This work examines average-reward reinforcement learning with general policy parametrization. Existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) guarantees for this problem are either suboptimal or hindered by several challenges, including poor scalability with respect to the size of the state-action space, high iteration complexity, and a significant dependence on knowledge of mixing times and hitting times. To address these limitations, we propose a Multi-level Monte Carlo-based Natural Actor-Critic (MLMC-NAC) algorithm. Our work is the first to achieve a global convergence rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/\sqrt{T})$ for average-reward Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) (where $T$ is the horizon length), using an Actor-Critic approach. Moreover, the convergence rate does not scale with the size of the state space, therefore even being applicable to infinite state spaces.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when the objective is the average reward earned over continuing interaction. It considers general policy parametrization and asks how quickly an actor-critic method can converge globally. Previous guarantees face several obstacles: unfavorable dependence on the number of states and actions, many required iterations, or substantial reliance on knowledge of mixing and hitting times.

The proposed algorithm, MLMC-NAC, combines a natural actor-critic approach with multilevel Monte Carlo. The central contribution is a sharper convergence analysis for this combination. The authors establish a global convergence rate proportional to one over the square root of the interaction horizon, with logarithmic factors suppressed. They identify this as the first actor-critic guarantee of that order for average-reward Markov decision processes.

A particularly consequential feature is that the stated rate does not grow with the size of the state space. This makes the analysis applicable even to infinite state spaces. The result concerns a theoretical convergence guarantee, explaining how the proposed approach improves the scaling of guarantees for this learning objective.
summary.tldr: MLMC-NAC achieves a sharper global convergence guarantee for average-reward reinforcement learning without dependence on state-space size.

title: A Sharper Global Convergence Analysis for Average Reward Reinforcement Learning via an Actor-Critic Approach

abstract: This paper introduces $k$-Dynamic Time Warping ($k$-DTW), a novel dissimilarity measure for polygonal curves. $k$-DTW has stronger metric properties than Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) and is more robust to outliers than the Fréchet distance, which are the two gold standards of dissimilarity measures for polygonal curves. We show interesting properties of $k$-DTW and give an exact algorithm as well as a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for $k$-DTW by a parametric search for the $k$-th largest matched distance. We prove the first dimension-free learning bounds for curves and further learning theoretic results. $k$-DTW not only admits smaller sample size than DTW for the problem of learning the median of curves, where some factors depending on the curves’ complexity $m$ are replaced by $k$, but we also show a surprising separation on the associated Rademacher and Gaussian complexities: $k$-DTW admits strictly smaller bounds than DTW, by a factor $\tilde\Omega(\sqrt{m})$ when $k\ll m$. We complement our theoretical findings with an experimental illustration of the benefits of using $k$-DTW for clustering and nearest neighbor classification.

paragraphs: Comparing polygonal curves requires a dissimilarity measure that handles how points along different curves correspond. The paper introduces k-Dynamic Time Warping, or k-DTW, as an alternative to Dynamic Time Warping and Fréchet distance. It establishes stronger metric properties than DTW and greater robustness to outliers than Fréchet distance.

The authors provide exact and approximate algorithms based on parametric search for the kth-largest matched distance. Beyond computation, they prove dimension-free learning bounds for curves. For learning a median curve, some sample-size factors that depend on curve complexity m under DTW are replaced by k, making the choice of dissimilarity consequential for statistical learning.

They also establish strictly smaller bounds on associated Rademacher and Gaussian complexities, with an improvement factor of approximately the square root of m, up to logarithmic factors, when k is much smaller than m. Experiments illustrate benefits for clustering and nearest-neighbor classification. The work thus combines a new curve comparison measure, algorithms for evaluating it, and learning guarantees explaining advantages in particular parameter regimes.
summary.tldr: k-DTW offers improved curve-comparison properties and dimension-free learning bounds, with statistical advantages over DTW when k is small relative to curve complexity.

title: Improved Learning via k-DTW: A Novel Dissimilarity Measure for Curves

abstract: Given how large parts of publicly available text are crawled to pretrain large language models (LLMs), data creators increasingly worry about the inclusion of their proprietary data for model training without attribution or licensing. Their concerns are also shared by benchmark curators whose test-sets might be compromised. In this paper, we present STAMP, a framework for detecting dataset membership—i.e., determining the inclusion of a dataset in the pretraining corpora of LLMs. Given an original piece of content, our proposal involves first generating multiple rephrases, each embedding a watermark with a unique secret key. One version is to be released publicly, while others are to be kept private. Subsequently, creators can compare model likelihoods between public and private versions using paired statistical tests to prove membership. We show that our framework can successfully detect contamination across four benchmarks which appear only once in the training data and constitute less than 0.001% of the total tokens, outperforming several contamination detection and dataset inference baselines. We verify that STAMP preserves both the semantic meaning and utility of the original data. We apply STAMP to two real-world scenarios to confirm the inclusion of paper abstracts and blog articles in the pretraining corpora.

paragraphs: STAMP helps content creators and benchmark curators determine whether their material entered a language model’s pretraining data. Its approach requires preparing content before publication. For each original item, the framework creates several rephrasings with distinct secret-key watermarks, releases one version publicly, and retains the others as private comparison material.

Later, the creator compares the model’s likelihoods for the public and private versions using paired statistical tests. The comparison uses related versions of the same content to assess dataset membership. STAMP outperforms several contamination-detection and dataset-inference baselines. Two real-world applications also confirm inclusion of paper abstracts and blog articles, supporting the method’s usefulness beyond the benchmark contamination experiments.
summary.tldr: STAMP compares model likelihoods for public and private watermarked rephrasings to detect whether a dataset was included in pretraining.

title: STAMP Your Content: Proving Dataset Membership via Watermarked Rephrasings

abstract: We propose DocVXQA, a novel framework for visually self-explainable document question answering, where the goal is not only to produce accurate answers to questions but also to learn visual heatmaps that highlight critical regions, offering interpretable justifications for the model decision. To integrate explanations into the learning process, we quantitatively formulate explainability principles as explicit learning criteria. Unlike conventional relevance map methods that solely emphasize regions relevant to the answer, our context-aware DocVXQA delivers explanations that are contextually sufficient yet representation-efficient. This fosters user trust while achieving a balance between predictive performance and interpretability in document visual question answering applications. Extensive experiments, including human evaluation, provide strong evidence supporting the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: A document question-answering system can return an answer without making clear which parts of the document justify it. DocVXQA aims to produce both an accurate answer and a visual explanation. Its heatmaps highlight important document regions so that a user can inspect the visual basis offered for the system's decision.

The central design choice is to make explanation quality part of learning. The authors translate explainability principles into explicit quantitative training criteria. Their approach goes beyond emphasizing regions associated with the answer: it seeks enough surrounding context to support the explanation while keeping the representation efficient. This balances the need to show supporting information with the need for a focused, interpretable explanation.

The paper reports extensive experiments, including human evaluation, that provide strong evidence for the method's effectiveness. Its contribution is therefore both a document-answering framework and a way to train for the quality of accompanying visual explanations. The stated goal is to balance predictive performance and interpretability while helping users understand and trust model decisions.
summary.tldr: DocVXQA learns to answer document questions while highlighting compact, contextually sufficient visual evidence for its answers.

title: DocVXQA: Context-Aware Visual Explanations for Document Question Answering

abstract: Comprehensive evaluations of language models (LM) during both development and deployment phases are necessary because these models are thought to possess numerous capabilities as well as safety risks. The average score across a wide range of benchmarks provides a signal that helps guide the use of these LMs in practice. Currently, holistic evaluations are costly due to the large volume of benchmark questions, making frequent evaluations impractical. A popular attempt to lower the cost is to compute the average score on a subset of the benchmark. This approach, unfortunately, often renders an unreliable measure of LM performance because the average score is often confounded with the difficulty of the questions in the benchmark subset. Item response theory (IRT) was designed to address this challenge, providing a reliable measurement by careful controlling for question difficulty. Unfortunately, question difficulty is expensive to estimate. Facing this challenge, we train a model that predicts question difficulty from its content, enabling a reliable measurement at a fraction of the cost. In addition, we leverage this difficulty predictor to further improve the evaluation efficiency through training a question generator given a difficulty level. This question generator is essential in adaptive testing, where, instead of using a random subset of the benchmark questions, informative questions are adaptively chosen based on the current estimation of LLM performance. Experiments on 22 common natural language benchmarks and 183 LMs show that this approach is more reliable and efficient compared to the current common practice.

paragraphs: Evaluating a language model on many benchmark questions is expensive, but evaluating a small subset introduces another problem: its average score can depend strongly on how difficult those particular questions are. This paper uses item response theory to account for question difficulty when measuring model performance, while addressing the expense of estimating that difficulty.

The authors train a predictor to infer a question’s difficulty from its content. This makes difficulty information available at lower cost. They also use that predictor to train a question generator conditioned on a requested difficulty level. The generator supports adaptive testing, where questions are chosen to be informative given the current estimate of a model’s performance.

Experiments cover twenty-two natural language benchmarks and 183 language models. The approach is reported to be more reliable and efficient than current common practice. Its two components address complementary sources of evaluation cost: estimating how challenging questions are and selecting useful questions rather than relying on a random subset.
summary.tldr: Predicting question difficulty and generating questions for adaptive testing makes language-model evaluation more reliable and efficient in the reported experiments.

title: Reliable and Efficient Amortized Model-based Evaluation

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have demonstrated remarkable potential across many domains, including computer vision and natural language processing, owing to their energy efficiency and biological plausibility. However, their application in long-term prediction tasks remains underexplored, which is primarily due to two critical challenges: (1) current SNN encoding methods are unable to effectively encode long temporal information, leading to increased computational complexity and energy consumption; (2) though Transformer-based models have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy in temporal prediction tasks, the absence of proper positional encoding for spiking self-attention restricts Spiking Transformer from effectively utilizing positional information, resulting in performance degradation. To address these challenges, we introduce an attention-free framework, Spiking Fourier Network (SpikF), that encodes input sequences in patches and employs an innovative frequency domain selection mechanism to effectively utilize the sequential properties of time-series data. Extensive evaluations on eight well-established long-term prediction datasets demonstrate that SpikF achieves an averaged $1.9\%$ reduction in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) compared to state-of-the-art models, while lowering total energy consumption by $3.16\times$. Our code is available at https://github.com/WWJ-creator/SpikF.
