paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer potential energy benefits, but long-term prediction poses challenges for encoding extended sequences. The paper also identifies a problem for spiking Transformers: inadequate positional encoding can limit how effectively their self-attention uses sequence position. SpikF addresses these issues with an attention-free forecasting architecture.

The model encodes input sequences in patches and uses a frequency-domain selection mechanism to exploit the sequential properties of time-series data. These choices connect the representation of long inputs with the way the model processes temporal information. The approach avoids relying on spiking self-attention, whose positional-information difficulties are one motivation for the design.

Across eight established long-term prediction datasets, SpikF achieves an average 1.9% reduction in mean absolute error compared with state-of-the-art models. The paper also reports a 3.16-fold reduction in total energy consumption. Together, these findings support the possibility of improving forecasting accuracy and energy efficiency at the same time in the evaluated setting, using patch encoding and frequency-based processing within a spiking network.
summary.tldr: SpikF uses patch encoding and frequency-domain selection for attention-free spiking forecasts, improving reported accuracy and energy efficiency.

title: SpikF: Spiking Fourier Network for Efficient Long-term Prediction

abstract: This paper studies a range of AI/ML trust concepts, including memorization, data poisoning, and copyright, which can be modeled as constraints on the influence of data on a (trained) model, characterized by the outcome difference from a processing function (training algorithm). In this realm, we show that provable trust guarantees can be efficiently provided through a new framework termed Data-Specific Indistinguishability (DSI) to select trust-preserving randomization tightly aligning with targeted outcome differences, as a relaxation of the classic Input-Independent Indistinguishability (III). We establish both the theoretical and algorithmic foundations of DSI with the optimal multivariate Gaussian mechanism. We further show its applications to develop trustworthy deep learning with black-box optimizers. The experimental results on memorization mitigation, backdoor defense, and copyright protection show both the efficiency and effectiveness of the DSI noise mechanism.

paragraphs: This paper connects several machine-learning trust concerns through a shared question: how much can particular data influence a trained model? It treats memorization, data poisoning, and copyright-related constraints in terms of differences in the outputs of a processing function, such as a training algorithm, when the relevant data influence changes.

The proposed framework, Data-Specific Indistinguishability, selects randomization tailored to the outcome differences being constrained. It relaxes classic Input-Independent Indistinguishability and aims to align the added noise closely with the specific trust requirement. The authors establish theoretical and algorithmic foundations using an optimal multivariate Gaussian mechanism.

They also show how to apply the framework to deep learning with black-box optimizers. Experiments on memorization mitigation, backdoor defense, and copyright protection support the efficiency and effectiveness of the noise mechanism. The contribution is a common mathematical approach for these data-influence constraints, together with a way to choose targeted randomization that provides provable guarantees within that formulation.
summary.tldr: Data-Specific Indistinguishability tailors Gaussian randomization to particular data influences, providing a unified framework for several machine-learning trust guarantees.

title: Trustworthy Machine Learning through Data-Specific Indistinguishability

abstract: We employ a game-theoretic framework to study the impact of a specific strategic behavior among creators—group behavior—on recommendation platforms. In this setting, creators within a group collaborate to maximize their collective utility. We show that group behavior has a limited effect on the game’s equilibrium when the group size is small. However, when the group size is large, group behavior can significantly alter content distribution and user welfare. Specifically, in a top-$K$ recommendation system with exposure-based rewards, we demonstrate that user welfare can suffer a significant loss due to group strategies, and user welfare does not necessarily increase with larger values of $K$ or more random matching, contrasting sharply with the individual creator case. Furthermore, we investigate user welfare guarantees through the lens of the Price of Anarchy (PoA). In the general case, we establish a negative result on the bound of PoA with exposure rewards, proving that it can be arbitrarily large. We then investigate a user engagement rewarding mechanism, which mitigates the issues caused by large group behavior, showing that $\text{PoA}\leq K+1$ in the general case and $\text{PoA}\leq 2$ in the binary case. Empirical results from simulations further support the effectiveness of the user engagement rewarding mechanism.

Furthermore, we investigate user welfare guarantees through the lens of the Price of Anarchy (PoA). We then investigate a user engagement rewarding mechanism, which mitigates the issues caused by large group behavior, showing that $\text{PoA}\leq K+1$ in the general case and $\text{PoA}\leq 2$ in the binary case. Empirical results from simulations further support the effectiveness of the user engagement rewarding mechanism.

paragraphs: Recommendation platforms influence what creators produce by deciding which content receives attention and rewards. This paper studies what happens when creators coordinate as a group to maximize their combined benefit. Its game-theoretic analysis finds that small groups have limited effects on equilibrium, while large groups can substantially change content distribution and user welfare.

The reward mechanism matters. In a system recommending the top K items and rewarding exposure, group strategies can cause substantial welfare losses. Increasing K or introducing more random matching does not necessarily improve welfare. The authors also analyze the Price of Anarchy, a measure of how unfavorable strategic outcomes can be relative to the best outcome, and show that it can become arbitrarily large under exposure rewards.

Rewarding user engagement instead provides stronger guarantees in the studied framework: the Price of Anarchy is at most K + 1 generally and at most 2 in the binary case. Simulations support this mechanism. The findings show why accounting for coordinated creators can materially change conclusions about platform incentives.
summary.tldr: Coordinated creator groups can harm user welfare under exposure rewards, while engagement rewards provide stronger theoretical welfare guarantees.

title: Beyond Self-Interest: How Group Strategies Reshape Content Creation in Recommendation Platforms?

abstract: We study a setting in which two players play a (possibly approximate) Nash equilibrium of a bimatrix game, while a learner observes only their actions and has no knowledge of the equilibrium or the underlying game. A natural question is whether the learner can rationalize the observed behavior by inferring the players’ payoff functions. Rather than producing a single payoff estimate, inverse game theory aims to identify the entire set of payoffs consistent with observed behavior, enabling downstream use in, e.g., counterfactual analysis and mechanism design across applications like auctions, pricing, and security games. We focus on the problem of estimating the set of feasible payoffs with high probability and up to precision $\epsilon$ on the Hausdorff metric. We provide the first minimax-optimal rates for both exact and approximate equilibrium play, in zero-sum as well as general-sum games. Our results provide learning-theoretic foundations for set-valued payoff inference in multi-agent environments.

paragraphs: Observing players’ actions does not directly reveal the incentives behind them. This paper studies a learner who sees two players’ actions while they play an exact or approximate Nash equilibrium of a bimatrix game. The learner knows neither the underlying game nor the equilibrium and seeks payoffs that could explain the observed behavior.

The target is the entire set of compatible payoffs. This set-valued formulation retains the range of incentive structures consistent with the evidence. The authors measure estimation accuracy using Hausdorff distance, which compares sets through how closely their points can be matched, and seek guarantees that hold with high probability at a chosen precision.

The paper establishes the first minimax-optimal rates for this problem, covering exact and approximate equilibrium play in both zero-sum and general-sum games. Minimax optimality characterizes the best achievable worst-case estimation rate. These results give learning-theoretic foundations for inferring incentives from behavior, supporting downstream uses such as counterfactual analysis and mechanism design that need to account for multiple plausible payoff functions.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes minimax-optimal rates for estimating all payoff functions consistent with observed exact or approximate equilibrium behavior.

title: Optimal Rates for Feasible Payoff Set Estimation in Games

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) offers a compelling approach to offline RL by enabling value learning on imagined on-policy trajectories. However, it often suffers from compounding errors due to repeated model inference on self-generated states. While geometric horizon models (GHM) alleviate this issue through direct prediction over a discounted infinite-horizon future, they remain challenged in accurately modeling distant future states. To this end, we introduce universal horizon models (UHM), a generalization of GHM that directly predicts future states under arbitrary horizons. Leveraging this flexibility, we propose a scalable value learning method that employs a winsorized horizon distribution to stabilize training by capping excessively large horizons. Experimental results on 100 challenging OGBench tasks demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms competitive baselines, particularly on tasks with highly suboptimal datasets and those requiring long-horizon reasoning. Project page: https://rllab-snu.github.io/projects/UHM/

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning can use a learned model to imagine trajectories and estimate the value of actions. However, repeatedly feeding predicted states back into that model can compound errors. Geometric horizon models reduce this repeated prediction by directly modeling a discounted future, but accurately representing distant states remains difficult.

Universal horizon models generalize that approach by directly predicting future states for arbitrary horizons. This gives the learning procedure flexibility over how far ahead it asks the model to predict. The proposed value-learning method uses a winsorized horizon distribution, which caps excessively large horizons to stabilize training while retaining a range of prediction distances.

Across 100 challenging OGBench tasks, the method outperforms competitive baselines, with particular strengths on highly suboptimal datasets and tasks requiring long-horizon reasoning. These results support flexible direct future prediction as a useful approach to offline value learning. The horizon cap is an integral part of the method: it manages the difficulty of distant predictions while the model supports different look-ahead distances.
summary.tldr: Universal horizon models predict future states at flexible horizons, with capped training horizons improving offline reinforcement learning across 100 OGBench tasks.

title: Offline Reinforcement Learning with Universal Horizon Models

abstract: While video generation holds promise for embodied intelligence, current video models struggle with physical realism, and progress is hindered by the lack of standardized benchmarks. To address this gap, we introduce a comprehensive robotics benchmark, RBench, designed to evaluate robot-oriented video generation across five task domains and four distinct embodiments. By assessing task correctness and visual fidelity through reproducible metrics, our evaluation of 25 models reveals significant deficiencies in generating physically realistic robot behaviors. Furthermore, the benchmark achieves a 0.96 Spearman correlation with human judgment, validating its effectiveness. While RBench provides the necessary lens to identify these deficiencies, achieving physical realism requires moving beyond evaluation to address the critical shortage of high-quality training data. Driven by these insights, we introduce a refined four-stage data pipeline, resulting in RoVid-X, the largest open-source robotic dataset for video generation with 4 million annotated video clips, covering thousands of tasks and enriched with physical property annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that finetuning on RoVid-X yields consistent performance gains. Collectively, this synergistic ecosystem of evaluation and data establishes a robust foundation for rigorous assessment and scalable training of video models, accelerating the evolution of embodied AI toward physical intelligence. The code and video demos are available in the supplementary materials.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether generated robot videos depict correct tasks and physically realistic behavior. It introduces RBench, an evaluation resource spanning five task domains and four robot embodiments. Reproducible metrics assess task correctness alongside visual fidelity, making the benchmark useful for examining more than how convincing a video looks.

An evaluation of 25 models reveals substantial shortcomings in physical realism. RBench's reported Spearman correlation of 0.96 with human judgment indicates strong agreement in ranking within that evaluation. The benchmark therefore supplies evidence of deficiencies and a standardized way to measure progress toward addressing them.

The authors also tackle training-data scarcity with a four-stage pipeline that produces RoVid-X, containing four million annotated robotic video clips across thousands of tasks, including physical-property annotations. They describe it as the largest open-source robotic dataset for video generation. Fine-tuning on RoVid-X produces consistent gains in the reported experiments. Together, the benchmark and dataset connect measurement of robot-video quality with a resource for improving it.
summary.tldr: RBench exposes physical-realism gaps in robot video generation, while the four-million-clip RoVid-X dataset supports consistent fine-tuning gains.

title: Rethinking Video Generation Model for the Embodied World

abstract: There is growing interest in utilizing flow-based models as decision-making policies in reinforcement learning due to their high expressive capacity. However, effectively leveraging this expressivity for value maximization remains challenging, as naive gradient-based optimization requires backpropagating through numerical solvers and often leads to instability. Existing approaches typically address this issue by restricting the expressive capacity of flow-based policies, resulting in a trade-off between optimization stability and representational flexibility. To resolve this, we introduce Q-Flow, a framework that leverages the deterministic nature of flow dynamics to explicitly propagate terminal trajectory value to intermediate latent states along the policy-induced flow. This formulation enables stable policy optimization using intermediate value gradients without unrolling the numerical solver, effectively bridging the gap between stability and expressivity. We evaluate Q-Flow in the offline learning setting on the challenging OGBench suite, where it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by an average of 10.6 percentage points, while also enabling stable online adaptation within the same framework.

paragraphs: Flow-based policies can represent flexible action distributions, but optimizing them for high value is difficult. A direct gradient approach must backpropagate through the numerical solver that generates actions, which can create instability. Existing methods often respond by limiting policy expressiveness, leaving a tradeoff between representing complex behavior and training reliably.

Q-Flow uses the deterministic dynamics of the flow to assign terminal trajectory value to intermediate latent states. Those intermediate states then provide value gradients for policy optimization. This avoids unrolling the numerical solver during the update and gives the framework a way to improve the policy without imposing the same restrictions on representational flexibility.

On the OGBench suite in offline reinforcement learning, Q-Flow consistently exceeds state-of-the-art baselines, with an average advantage of 10.6 percentage points. The framework also supports stable online adaptation. Together, these findings suggest that moving value information inside the policy’s generative trajectory can make its expressiveness easier to optimize, both when learning from existing data and when subsequently adapting through interaction.
summary.tldr: Q-Flow propagates value to intermediate flow states, enabling stable policy optimization without backpropagating through an unrolled numerical solver.

title: Q-Flow: Stable and Expressive Reinforcement Learning with Flow-based Policy

abstract: Dynamic relational data arise in many machine learning applications, yet their evolving structure poses challenges for learning representations that remain consistent and interpretable over time. A common approach is to learn time varying node embeddings, whose usefulness depends on well defined stability properties across nodes and across time. We introduce Unfolded Laplacian Spectral Embedding (ULSE), a principled extension of unfolded adjacency spectral embedding to normalized Laplacian operators, a setting where stability guarantees have remained out of reach. We prove that ULSE satisfies both cross-sectional and longitudinal stability under a dynamic stochastic block model. Moreover, the Laplacian formulation yields a dynamic Cheeger-type inequality linking the spectrum of the unfolded normalized Laplacian to worst case conductance over time, providing structural insight into the embeddings. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world dynamic networks validate the theory.

paragraphs: Representing an evolving network requires more than producing useful coordinates for each snapshot. The coordinates also need consistent meaning across nodes and across time, so that comparisons reflect the network's behavior. This paper introduces Unfolded Laplacian Spectral Embedding, or ULSE, to address those stability requirements.

ULSE extends unfolded adjacency spectral embedding to normalized Laplacian operators. Under a dynamic stochastic block model, the authors prove both cross-sectional and longitudinal stability. These guarantees address consistency along the two axes relevant to dynamic node representations: comparing different nodes and comparing positions across time. The model assumption supplies the setting in which the stability statements hold.

The Laplacian formulation also yields a dynamic Cheeger-type inequality. It links spectral information from the unfolded normalized Laplacian to worst-case conductance over time, connecting the embedding mathematics to network connectivity and bottlenecks. Experiments on synthetic and real dynamic networks validate the theory. The contribution combines a representation method with both stability guarantees and a structural interpretation of the spectral quantities it uses.
summary.tldr: ULSE provides stable dynamic-network embeddings under a block-model assumption and links their spectrum to connectivity over time.

title: Unfolded Laplacian Spectral Embedding: A Theoretically Grounded Approach to Dynamic Network Representation

abstract: Preference alignment is a crucial post-training step for large language models (LLMs) to ensure their outputs align with human values. However, post-training on real human preference data raises privacy concerns, as these datasets often contain sensitive user prompts and human judgments. To address this, we propose DPPrefSyn, a novel algorithm for generating differentially private (DP) synthetic preference data to enable privacy-preserving preference alignment. DPPrefSyn is a principled framework grounded in the Bradley–Terry preference model and the intrinsic geometric structure of pairwise human preference data. It first learns an underlying preference model from private data with formal differential privacy guarantees, and then leverages the learned model together with public prompts to synthesize high-quality preference data. It exploits the shared linear structure of per-cluster reward models to effectively capture heterogeneous human preferences in private datasets, and leverages DP Principal Component Analysis (DP-PCA) to improve learning accuracy. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that DPPrefSyn achieves competitive alignment performance under strong DP guarantees. These findings highlight the potential of synthetic preference data as a practical alternative for privacy-preserving preference alignment across a broad range of applications. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to generate DP synthetic preference data for LLM alignment.

paragraphs: Preference alignment trains language models using judgments about which responses people prefer. Real preference datasets can contain sensitive prompts and judgments, creating privacy concerns during post-training. DPPrefSyn addresses this by learning from private preferences and producing synthetic preference data that can support subsequent alignment.

The framework first fits a preference model with formal differential privacy guarantees, then combines that learned model with public prompts to generate synthetic comparisons. Its design uses the Bradley–Terry model for pairwise preferences and the geometric structure of the data. Cluster-specific reward models share a linear structure, allowing the method to represent heterogeneous preferences while exploiting common information. Differentially private principal component analysis improves learning accuracy.

Experiments show competitive alignment performance under strong differential privacy guarantees. The findings support synthetic preferences as a practical route to privacy-preserving alignment: the private learning stage captures preference patterns, and public prompts provide inputs for synthesis. The paper’s central contribution is a structured method for producing useful preference data while formally protecting the private data used to learn those patterns.
summary.tldr: DPPrefSyn learns a differentially private preference model and uses public prompts to synthesize data for competitive language-model alignment.

title: Differentially Private Preference Data Synthesis for Large Language Model Alignment

abstract: Social recruitment offers a solution to worker scarcity in Spatial Crowdsourcing (SC) but faces challenges that are often ignored in traditional Influence Maximization. First, task heterogeneity arising from offline execution constraints breaks the “interest-implies-participation” assumption, as social influence often fails to translate into physical presence. Second, finite task demand creates a “saturation trap”, a non-submodular setting in which utility drops sharply to zero once demand is met. To bridge these gaps, we propose GKD-Recruiter, a Task-Aware framework designed to maximize Effective Task Satisfaction (ETS). We explicitly model the complex worker-task affinity via a heterogeneous graph and capture directional social influence using a novel Influential GAT. To robustly fuse these distinct signals, we introduce a Graph Knowledge Distillation mechanism. Furthermore, we employ Rainbow DQN to navigate the non-submodular combinatorial search space, avoiding the local optima that trap greedy heuristics. Extensive experiments on the real-world dataset demonstrate that GKD-Recruiter significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both solution quality and inference efficiency. The code is available at https://github.com/GaoYucen/GKD-Recruiter.

paragraphs: Recruiting workers through social connections is complicated when tasks require physical attendance. Someone influenced to take interest may still be unable to participate. Tasks also have finite demand, so attracting more workers ceases to add value once that demand is met. These features make social reach alone an inadequate recruitment objective.

GKD-Recruiter targets effective task satisfaction by combining two kinds of information. A heterogeneous graph models worker-task compatibility, while a directional graph attention mechanism models social influence. Graph knowledge distillation combines these signals. The framework then uses Rainbow DQN to search recruitment choices in a setting where demand saturation creates difficulties for greedy selection.

Experiments on a real-world dataset report better solution quality and faster inference than state-of-the-art baselines. The results support considering actual task fulfillment throughout recruitment, including compatibility and saturation. The approach matters because recruitment choices interact: the value of reaching another worker depends on which tasks still need people, as well as whether that worker is socially reachable and able to execute the task.
summary.tldr: GKD-Recruiter combines worker-task compatibility and social influence to improve recruitment under physical participation constraints and finite task demand.

title: GKD-Recruiter: Jointly Modeling Social and Task Heterogeneity for Spatial Crowdsourcing via Graph Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Generalization in generative modeling is defined as the ability to learn an underlying distribution from a finite dataset and produce novel samples, with evaluation largely driven by held-out performance and perceived sample quality. In practice, training is often stopped at the minimum of the test loss, taken as an operational indicator of generalization. We challenge this viewpoint by identifying a phase of biased generalization during training, in which the model continues to decrease the test loss while favoring samples with anomalously high proximity to training data. By training the same network on two disjoint datasets and comparing the mutual distances of generated samples and their similarity to training data, we introduce a quantitative measure of bias and demonstrate its presence on real images. We then study the mechanism of bias, using a controlled hierarchical data model where access to exact scores and ground-truth statistics allows us to precisely characterize its onset. We attribute this phenomenon to the sequential nature of feature learning in deep networks, where coarse structure is learned early in a data-independent manner, while finer features are resolved later in a way that increasingly depends on individual training samples. Our results show that early stopping at the test loss minimum, while optimal under standard generalization criteria, may be insufficient for privacy-critical applications.

paragraphs: This paper questions whether improving test loss is enough to establish desirable generalization in diffusion models. It identifies a training phase in which test loss keeps decreasing while generated samples become unusually close to training examples. A model can therefore improve under a standard evaluation criterion while becoming more dependent on the particular data it saw.

To measure this bias, the authors train the same network on two disjoint datasets and compare distances among generated samples and their proximity to training data. They demonstrate the phenomenon on real images. They then investigate its emergence with a controlled hierarchical data model that provides exact scores and known underlying statistics.

The proposed mechanism is sequential feature learning. Broad structure is learned early in a relatively data-independent way, while later learning of finer features increasingly reflects individual training samples. This makes the timing of training relevant beyond the test-loss curve alone. The results suggest that stopping at minimum test loss may be insufficient for privacy-critical applications, even when that stopping point is optimal under conventional generalization criteria.
summary.tldr: Diffusion models can improve test loss while generating samples increasingly close to training data, complicating privacy-sensitive early stopping.

title: Biased Generalization in Diffusion Models

abstract: Recent time series modeling faces a sharp divide between numerical generation and semantic understanding, with research showing that generation models often rely on superficial pattern matching, while understanding-oriented models struggle with high-fidelity numerical output. Although unified multimodal models (UMMs) have bridged this gap in vision, their potential for time series remains untapped. We propose TimeOmni-VL, the first vision-centric framework that unifies time series understanding and generation through two key innovations: (1) Fidelity-preserving bidirectional mapping between time series and images (Bi-TSI), which advances Time Series-to-Image (TS2I) and Image-to-Time Series (I2TS) conversions to ensure near-lossless transformations. (2) Understanding-guided generation. We introduce TSUMM-Suite, a novel dataset consisting of six understanding tasks rooted in time series analytics and coupled with two generation tasks. With a calibrated Chain-of-Thought (CoT), TimeOmni-VL is the first to leverage time series understanding as an explicit control signal for high-fidelity generation. Experiments confirm that this unified approach significantly improves semantic understanding and numerical precision, establishing a new frontier for multimodal time series modeling.

paragraphs: TimeOmni-VL seeks to combine understanding time series with generating accurate numerical sequences. The authors describe a divide between models that generate through superficial pattern matching and models that understand series but struggle to produce faithful numbers. Their approach uses an image-centered framework to bring the two capabilities into a common modeling process.

The first component, Bi-TSI, maps time series to images and images back to time series with near-lossless fidelity. Preserving numerical information through both directions matters because the visual representation must support accurate output as well as interpretation. The second component uses calibrated chain-of-thought reasoning to make understanding an explicit control signal for generation.

The authors also introduce TSUMM-Suite, pairing six time-series understanding tasks with two generation tasks. Their experiments report significant improvements in semantic understanding and numerical precision. These findings support the proposed combination of faithful representation conversion and understanding-guided generation. The framework connects the model's interpretation of a series to the numerical content it subsequently produces.
summary.tldr: TimeOmni-VL uses near-lossless image mappings and understanding-guided reasoning to unify time-series interpretation with accurate numerical generation.

title: TimeOmni-VL: Unified Models for Time Series Understanding and Generation

abstract: Learning discrete neural samplers is challenging due to the lack of gradients and combinatorial complexity. While stochastic optimal control (SOC) and Schrödinger bridge (SB) provide principled solutions, efficient SOC solvers like adjoint matching (AM), which excel in continuous domains, remain unexplored for discrete spaces. We bridge this gap by revealing that the core mechanism of AM is state-space agnostic, and introduce discrete ASBS, a unified framework that extends AM and adjoint Schrödinger bridge sampler (ASBS) to discrete spaces. Theoretically, we analyze the optimality conditions of the discrete SB problem and its connection to SOC, identifying a necessary cyclic group structure on the state space to enable this extension. Empirically, discrete ASBS achieves competitive sample quality with significant advantages in training efficiency and scalability. Our code is available at https://github.com/AlexandreGUO2001/DASBS.

While stochastic optimal control (SOC) and Schrödinger bridge (SB) provide principled solutions, efficient SOC solvers like adjoint matching (AM), which excel in continuous domains, remain unexplored for discrete spaces. We bridge this gap by revealing that the core mechanism of AM is state-space agnostic, and introduce discrete ASBS, a unified framework that extends AM and adjoint Schrödinger bridge sampler (ASBS) to discrete spaces. Theoretically, we analyze the optimality conditions of the discrete SB problem and its connection to SOC, identifying a necessary cyclic group structure on the state space to enable this extension. Empirically, discrete ASBS achieves competitive sample quality with significant advantages in training efficiency and scalability. Our code is available at https://github.com/AlexandreGUO2001/DASBS.

paragraphs: Learning to sample discrete objects is difficult because discrete choices do not provide ordinary gradients and their combinations can be numerous. Stochastic optimal control and Schrödinger bridges offer principled formulations for sampling, but an efficient solver called adjoint matching had primarily been explored in continuous spaces. This paper develops its discrete counterpart.

The key argument is that adjoint matching’s central mechanism does not inherently depend on whether the state space is continuous or discrete. Building on that observation, the authors introduce discrete ASBS, extending both adjoint matching and the adjoint Schrödinger bridge sampler. Their analysis connects discrete bridge optimality conditions with stochastic optimal control.

The extension has a stated structural requirement: the analysis identifies a necessary cyclic group structure on the state space. Thus, the generality of the central mechanism does not imply an unrestricted extension to every discrete setting. Empirically, discrete ASBS delivers competitive sample quality together with substantial training-efficiency and scalability advantages, supporting the usefulness of this theoretically motivated transfer.
summary.tldr: Discrete ASBS extends adjoint-based sampling to discrete spaces with a required cyclic group structure, achieving competitive quality and efficient training.

title: Discrete Adjoint Schrödinger Bridge Sampler

abstract: Unsupervised dense retrievers offer scalability by learning semantic similarity from unlabeled documents via contrastive learning, but they struggle to capture the temporal relevance, retrieving semantically related but temporally misaligned documents-an important aspect when a document collection spans multiple time periods (e.g., retrieving documents from 2018-2025 for "Who is the president in 2019?" introduces temporal ambiguity). Existing methods rely on supervised training with explicit timestamps, which are not always feasible. We propose TPOUR (Temporal Preference Optimization for Unsupervised Retriever), which uses our novel training method Temporal Retrieval Preference Optimization (TRPO). TRPO reinterprets preference learning in the temporal dimension, guiding the retriever to favor temporally aligned documents. TPOUR further generalizes to unseen time periods via interpolation in a learned time embedding, enabling continuous temporal alignment. Experiments on temporal information retrieval (T-IR), TPOUR outperforms both unsupervised and supervised baselines. Compared to Qwen-Embedding-8B, despite being about 72.7$\times$ smaller, TPOUR Contriever improves average nDCG@5 by +4.04 (+12.15%) on explicit and +4.98 (+15.21%) on implicit queries. Existing methods rely on supervised training with explicit timestamps, which are not always feasible. TRPO reinterprets preference learning in the temporal dimension, guiding the retriever to favor temporally aligned documents. TPOUR further generalizes to unseen time periods via interpolation in a learned time embedding, enabling continuous temporal alignment. Experiments on temporal information retrieval (T-IR), TPOUR outperforms both unsupervised and supervised baselines. Compared to Qwen-Embedding-8B, despite being about 72.7$\times$ smaller, TPOUR Contriever improves average nDCG@5 by +4.04 (+12.15%) on explicit and +4.98 (+15.21%) on implicit queries. title: Temporal Preference Optimization for Unsupervised Retrieval

abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) generation aims to synthesize videos with high visual quality and temporal consistency that are semantically aligned with input text. Reward-based post-training has emerged as a promising direction to improve the quality and semantic alignment of generated videos. However, recent methods either rely on large-scale human preference annotations or operate on misaligned embeddings from pre-trained vision-language models, leading to limited scalability or suboptimal supervision. We present PISCES, an annotation-free post-training algorithm that addresses these limitations via a novel Dual Optimal Transport (OT)-aligned Rewards module. To align reward signals with human judgment, PISCES uses OT to bridge text and video embeddings at both distributional and discrete token levels, enabling reward supervision to fulfill two objectives: (i) a Distributional OT-aligned Quality Reward that captures overall visual quality and temporal coherence; and (ii) a Discrete Token-level OT-aligned Semantic Reward that enforces semantic, spatio-temporal correspondence between text and video tokens. To our knowledge, PISCES is the first to improve annotation-free reward supervision in generative post-training through the lens of OT. Experiments on both short- and long-video generation show that PISCES outperforms both annotation-based and annotation-free methods on VBench across Quality and Semantic scores, with human preference studies further validating its effectiveness. We show that the Dual OT-aligned Rewards module is compatible with multiple optimization paradigms, including direct backpropagation and reinforcement learning fine-tuning.

This division gives the training process signals for both how a video looks and how its content relates to the requested description.

Experiments on short and long videos show improvements over evaluated annotation-based and annotation-free methods on VBench Quality and Semantic scores. Human preference studies further support effectiveness. The reward module also works with direct backpropagation and reinforcement learning fine-tuning, indicating that the alignment approach can serve more than one optimization procedure for generative post-training.
summary.tldr: PISCES uses optimal-transport-aligned rewards to improve video quality and prompt alignment without human training annotations.

title: PISCES: Annotation-free Text-to-Video Post-Training via Optimal Transport-Aligned Rewards

abstract: Scene graph generation (SGG) aims to parse an image into a structured graph of objects and their predicates, enabling explicit relational reasoning for visual understanding. However, prevailing methods often over-predict geometric predicates, resulting in scene graphs that are factually correct yet semantically shallow. While recent works effectively attribute this phenomenon to the long-tailed data distribution, we identify another critical factor driving such biased prediction: co-occurrence-induced representation entanglement, where geometric and non-geometric predicates that frequently co-occur are encoded into overly similar representations. To this end, we introduce Dual-stream Synergistic Network (DS-Net) that models geometric and non-geometric predicates with two specialized streams, coupled with a bidirectional cross-stream fusion mechanism. The space stream focuses on spatial and structural cues, while the vision stream captures fine-grained visual evidence and semantic priors. Extensive experiments show that DS-Net consistently improves predicate inference, achieving 1.3% $\sim$ 6.1% absolute gains in mR@100 on the SGGen task when integrated into existing SGG methods. These results highlight the importance of synergistic modeling of geometric and non-geometric predicates for generating semantically richer scene graphs.

paragraphs: Scene graph generation describes an image through objects and the relationships between them. Existing methods often favor geometric relationships, producing descriptions that can be correct yet semantically limited. Beyond imbalanced training frequencies, this paper identifies another source of bias: geometric and non-geometric relationships that frequently appear together can acquire overly similar internal representations.

DS-Net addresses this entanglement with two specialized processing streams. A space stream handles spatial and structural cues, while a vision stream handles detailed visual evidence and semantic priors. A bidirectional fusion mechanism allows information to pass between them. This design gives the two kinds of evidence distinct representations while retaining their ability to support each other during relationship prediction.

When integrated into existing scene graph generation methods, DS-Net consistently improves predicate inference in the reported experiments. On the SGGen task, the authors report absolute gains of 1.3% to 6.1% in mR@100. The results support treating representation entanglement as a useful intervention point for producing scene graphs that capture richer relationships.
summary.tldr: DS-Net separates and reconnects spatial and visual processing to improve relationship prediction in scene graphs.

title: Synergistic Space-Vision Processing for Predicate Inference

abstract: The trustworthiness of evaluation is critical to reliable model comparison and deployment in Video Anomaly Understanding (VAU). However, existing metrics are sensitive to expression styles and normal content, and this field lacks a diagnostic benchmark to validate metric validity and robustness. To bridge this gap, we propose: (1) a Class-Guided Chain-of-Evaluation (CG-CoE) metric, which structures assessment by extracting anomalous events and matching them under a class-specific semantic tolerance boundary, thereby decoupling anomaly semantics from descriptive style; and (2) an anomaly-focused meta-evaluation benchmark with two subsets: Anomalous Event-level Annotations (AEA) for measuring the validity of reflecting VAU models’ anomaly understanding ability and Controlled Variant Pairs (CVP) with fixed anomalies for quantifying robustness to stylistic perturbations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CG-CoE achieves SOTA validity and robustness.

paragraphs: Evaluating a video anomaly explanation should reflect whether it understands the anomalous events. Existing metrics can instead respond strongly to writing style or descriptions of normal content. This paper introduces both an evaluation metric and a benchmark for testing evaluation metrics, addressing how to score model outputs and how to establish that those scores are meaningful.

The proposed Class-Guided Chain-of-Evaluation first extracts anomalous events and then matches them within a semantic tolerance boundary specific to each class. This structures comparison around the meaning of the anomaly while accommodating permitted variation in its description. The aim is to separate the event being understood from the wording used to describe it.

The accompanying meta-benchmark has two parts. Anomalous Event-level Annotations test whether a metric reflects anomaly understanding, while Controlled Variant Pairs keep anomalies fixed and vary expression to test robustness. Experiments report state-of-the-art validity and robustness for the proposed metric. Together, the contributions provide a scoring procedure and targeted checks of whether that procedure measures the intended capability.
summary.tldr: CG-CoE evaluates anomaly-event meaning, and a companion meta-benchmark tests whether scores remain valid and robust to stylistic changes.

title: Towards Trustworthy Video Anomaly Understanding: A Class-Guided Chain-of-Evaluation Metric and An Anomaly-focused Meta-Benchmark

abstract: Recent progress in spatial reasoning with Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly leverages geometric priors from 3D encoders. However, most existing integration strategies remain passive: geometry is exposed as a global stream and fused in an indiscriminate manner, which often induces semantic-geometry misalignment and redundant signals. We propose GeoThinker, a framework that shifts the paradigm from passive fusion to active perception. Instead of feature mixing, GeoThinker enables the model to selectively retrieve geometric evidence conditioned on its internal reasoning demands. GeoThinker achieves this through Spatial-Grounded Fusion applied at carefully selected VLM layers, where semantic visual priors selectively query and integrate task-relevant geometry via frame-strict cross-attention, further calibrated by Importance Gating that biases per-frame attention toward task-relevant structures. Comprehensive evaluation results show that GeoThinker sets a new state-of-the-art in spatial intelligence, achieving a peak score of 72.6 on the VSI-Bench. Furthermore, GeoThinker demonstrates robust generalization and significantly improved spatial perception across complex downstream scenarios, including embodied referring and autonomous driving. Our results indicate that the ability to actively integrate spatial structures is essential for next-generation spatial intelligence.

paragraphs: Adding 3D features to a multimodal language model does not guarantee that it uses the right geometry for a question. Indiscriminate fusion can introduce redundancy or misalign spatial and semantic information. GeoThinker lets the model retrieve geometric evidence according to its current reasoning needs.

Spatial-Grounded Fusion is inserted at selected layers, where visual-semantic representations query task-relevant geometry through frame-specific cross-attention. The results suggest that access to geometric information is only part of the problem: the model also needs a way to choose and use that information at the appropriate reasoning stage.
summary.tldr: GeoThinker selectively retrieves task-relevant geometry inside a multimodal model, improving spatial reasoning and downstream generalization.

title: Thinking with Geometry: Active Geometry Integration for Spatial Reasoning

abstract: Existing approaches for analyzing neural network activations, such as PCA and sparse autoencoders, rely on strong structural assumptions. Generative models offer an alternative: they can uncover structure without such assumptions and act as priors that improve intervention fidelity. We explore this direction by training diffusion models on one billion residual stream activations, creating "meta-models" that learn the distribution of a network’s internal states. We find that diffusion loss decreases smoothly with compute and reliably predicts downstream utility. In particular, applying the meta-model’s learned prior to steering interventions improves fluency, with larger gains as loss decreases. Moreover, the meta-model’s neurons increasingly isolate concepts into individual units, with sparse probing scores that scale as loss decreases. These results suggest generative meta-models offer a scalable path toward interpretability without restrictive structural assumptions.

paragraphs: Methods for interpreting neural activations often assume a particular structure, as in principal component analysis or sparse autoencoders. This paper explores learning the distribution of internal states with a generative model instead. The authors train diffusion models on one billion residual-stream activations, creating meta-models of another network’s internal activity.

The learned distribution serves as a prior for interventions that steer the underlying language model. Applying this prior improves fluency, and the improvements increase as diffusion loss falls. The authors also find that loss decreases smoothly with compute and reliably predicts downstream usefulness, connecting the meta-model’s training progress to the quality of its interventions.

A second finding concerns interpretability inside the meta-model itself. As loss decreases, individual neurons increasingly isolate concepts, with corresponding improvements in sparse probing scores. Together, these results suggest that generative modeling of activations could provide a scalable route to interpretation and more faithful interventions. The claim is a promising direction supported by the observed scaling behavior, rather than a complete account of the original model’s computation.
summary.tldr: Diffusion models trained on LLM activations learn useful priors for fluent steering and increasingly isolate concepts as training loss improves.

title: Learning a Generative Meta-Model of LLM Activations

abstract: Test-time scaling strategies have effectively leveraged inference-time compute to enhance the reasoning abilities of Autoregressive Large Language Models. In this work, we demonstrate that Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) are inherently amenable to advanced search strategies, owing to their iterative and non-autoregressive generation process. To leverage this, we propose UnMaskFork (UMF), a framework that formulates the unmasking trajectory as a search tree and employs Monte Carlo Tree Search to optimize the generation path. In contrast to standard scaling methods relying on stochastic sampling, UMF explores the search space through deterministic partial unmasking actions performed by multiple MDLMs. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that UMF consistently outperforms existing test-time scaling baselines on complex coding benchmarks, while also exhibiting strong scalability on mathematical reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Spending additional computation at inference time can improve language-model reasoning, but search strategies must fit the model's generation process. Masked diffusion language models generate through iterative unmasking rather than a strictly left-to-right sequence. UnMaskFork uses that structure to search over alternative paths through generation.

The framework treats an unmasking trajectory as a tree and applies Monte Carlo Tree Search to optimize the path. Its branches come from deterministic partial-unmasking actions performed by multiple masked diffusion models. This makes the choice of how to reveal a partial answer an explicit search decision, providing an alternative to expanding candidates through stochastic sampling alone.

These findings support using the iterative, non-autoregressive structure of masked diffusion as a basis for more advanced search. The contribution concerns organizing additional inference computation around generation trajectories, with the reported benefits demonstrated on coding and mathematical reasoning.
summary.tldr: UnMaskFork searches deterministic partial-unmasking trajectories to improve masked-diffusion reasoning with additional inference computation.

title: UnMaskFork: Test-Time Scaling for Masked Diffusion via Deterministic Action Branching

abstract: Researchers have shown that neural similarity among humans predicts social closeness and cooperative success, whereas innovation often emerges from interactions among dissimilar individuals. We investigate whether these principles extend to artificial intelligence by examining interactions between large language models. In our experiments, 276 model pairs interact across eight games spanning both cooperation and novelty. We find that pairs with more similar representation spaces achieve significantly higher cooperation but exhibit reduced novelty and creativity. The effects of representational similarity on cooperation and novelty remain robust even after controlling for other factors such as performance disparity and model size. We also find that similarity in the early layers consistently shows the strongest association with cooperation and novelty, compared to the middle and later layers. This suggests that a central factor underlying these patterns could be the extent to which the two models share lexical and semantic grounding. Overall, representational similarity can be an important consideration in multi-agent system design.

paragraphs: When language models interact, their internal representations may help explain how well they cooperate and how much novelty they produce. The motivation comes from human studies linking neural similarity to social closeness and cooperation, while associating dissimilarity with innovation.

The results therefore identify an association that is not explained away by those particular differences between the paired models.

Similarity in early layers has the strongest association with both cooperation and novelty, compared with similarity in middle or later layers. The authors suggest that shared grounding in words and meanings could help account for this pattern. For multi-agent design, the findings make representational similarity a potentially useful consideration when choosing between stronger coordination and greater novelty, without establishing that similarity alone causes either outcome.
summary.tldr: Language-model pairs with more similar internal representations cooperate better but produce less novelty in the evaluated games.

title: Representational Similarity and Model Behavior in Multi-Agent Interaction

abstract: Large language models generate text by sampling tokens at random, a process now widely used for inference-time watermarking that verifies AI-generated content. We present an information-theoretic framework that captures the trade-off between robustness to text edits and detectability by observers who lack the watermark key or a keyless detector. The bounds we derive hold regardless of computational power, and what a keyless detector can actually achieve depends on what it can observe about the model and its outputs. At the heart of the analysis is an additive, Kullback-Leibler (KL) information measure that quantifies how well a hypothesis test can distinguish watermarked from unwatermarked text while the watermark remains stealthy. The measure remains zero for distribution-preserving schemes and increases with text length for token-level and sentence-level probability-modifying schemes. When edits are modeled as noise, the KL measure shrinks quadratically with the edit rate for token-level schemes and with an induced semantic flip rate for sentence-level schemes. This shrinkage exposes an unavoidable trilemma among robustness, stealth, and reliable verification. Guided by these limits, we propose a hybrid watermarking strategy that selects the Pareto-optimal scheme among distribution-preserving, semantic-level, and token-level methods based on the expected editing regime at deployment. Experiments on Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B under paraphrasing attacks corroborate these theoretical predictions and confirm that the hybrid strategy lies near the Pareto frontier across the edit regimes we evaluate.

title: Catch-22: On the Fundamental Tradeoff Between Detectability and Robustness in LLM Watermarking

abstract: Scaling test-time compute with multi-path chain-of-thought can improve reasoning accuracy, but its gains hinge on an effective exploration–exploitation trade-off. Existing methods handle this trade-off in rigid ways: tree-structured search hard-codes exploration via brittle expansion rules that disrupt post-trained reasoning, while parallel reasoning over-explores redundant hypothesis paths and relies on a weak answer selection strategy. Driven by the insight that the optimal balance is phase-dependent and that correct vs. incorrect paths often diverge only at late stages, we reconceptualize test-time scaling as a dynamic expand–reduce control problem over a pool of hypothesis paths. We introduce HyPER, a training-free online control policy for MoE multi-path decoding that reallocates compute under a fixed budget using lightweight path statistics. HyPER features (i) an online controller that shifts from exploration to exploitation as the hypothesis pool evolves, (ii) an MoE-based token-level refinement primitive for efficient generation-time exploitation without full-path resampling, and (iii) a length- and confidence-aware aggregation rule to bridge the existence–selection gap for reliable answer-time exploitation. Extensive experimental results across four MoE models and diverse benchmarks demonstrate HyPER consistently achieves the accuracy–compute Pareto frontier, outperforming prior-art methods by 8-10% while reducing token consumption by 25-40%.

paragraphs: Generating several reasoning paths can improve language-model accuracy, but the available computation must be divided between exploring alternatives and refining promising ones. HyPER builds on two observations: the useful balance changes during reasoning, and correct and incorrect paths often separate only late in generation. Fixed search rules or excessive parallel sampling can therefore allocate computation poorly.

The method is a training-free controller for multi-path decoding in mixture-of-experts models. It uses lightweight path statistics to expand or reduce the hypothesis pool within a fixed budget. A token-level refinement mechanism supports exploitation during generation without resampling entire paths. A separate answer-aggregation rule considers length and confidence, addressing the gap between generating a correct answer somewhere and selecting it reliably.

Across four mixture-of-experts models and diverse benchmarks, HyPER reports improvements of 8–10% over prior methods while reducing token consumption by 25–40%. Its reported accuracy–compute frontier supports adapting computational allocation throughout reasoning and treating final answer selection as a distinct part of that allocation.
summary.tldr: HyPER dynamically allocates a fixed reasoning budget across exploring, refining, and selecting hypothesis paths in mixture-of-experts language models.

title: HyPER: Bridging Exploration and Exploitation for Scalable LLM Reasoning with Hypothesis Path Expansion and Reduction

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems deployed in sensitive domains must provide interpretable evidence selection and robust safeguards against data poisoning, yet current approaches rely on opaque similarity-based retrieval with arbitrary top-k cutoffs that offer no explanation for their selections and remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulation. We propose METEORA, a rationale-driven RAG framework that addresses these fundamental limitations through interpretable, adaptive evidence retrieval. Our framework introduces three synergistic contributions. First, we preference-tune a general-purpose LLM to generate explicit rationales that articulate why specific evidence is needed for a given query. These rationales then guide adaptive evidence selection through a two-step process: rationale-chunk pairing for query-specific relevance assessment, followed by dynamic cutoff detection that eliminates the need for arbitrary k heuristics. Finally, the same rationales enable a verification stage that filters poisoned or misleading evidence before generation. Evaluation across six datasets demonstrates substantial improvements on three critical dimensions. For retrieval quality, METEORA achieves 21.05% higher precision than the best-performing baseline, while its variant with context expansion achieves 13.41% higher recall. In terms of efficiency, the framework reduces the volume of evidence required to reach comparable recall by 80%, which directly translates to a 33.34% improvement in downstream answer generation accuracy. Finally, the same rationales enable a verification stage that filters poisoned or misleading evidence before generation. In terms of efficiency, the framework reduces the volume of evidence required to reach comparable recall by 80%, which directly translates to a 33.34% improvement in downstream answer generation accuracy. Most notably for adversarial robustness, METEORA increases the F1 score from 0.10 to 0.44 under poisoning attacks, a 4.4$\times$ improvement that makes RAG systems substantially more resilient to adversarial manipulation. Human evaluation with four experienced annotators confirms genuine interpretability, achieving a mean confidence score of 3.64/5 and demonstrating that humans can reliably reconstruct evidence-level decisions with 86% accuracy. The code is available in the anonymous GitHub repository https://anonymous.4open.science/r/METEORA-DC46/README.md

paragraphs: METEORA uses explicit explanations of evidence needs to guide retrieval-augmented generation. Conventional similarity retrieval often takes a fixed number of chunks, leaving the reason for each selection unclear. The proposed framework preference-tunes a general-purpose language model to explain what evidence a query requires and then uses those rationales throughout retrieval.

Selection first assesses relevance by pairing rationales with candidate chunks, then dynamically determines where to stop selecting evidence. The same rationales support a verification stage that filters poisoned or misleading material before answer generation. This gives the explanations a functional role in both evidence selection and checking.

It uses 80% less evidence for comparable recall and reports a 33.34% improvement in answer accuracy. Under poisoning attacks, F1 rises from 0.10 to 0.44. These results support improved retrieval, robustness, and human interpretability in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: METEORA uses query-specific rationales to select and verify evidence, improving reported retrieval quality, interpretability, and resistance to poisoning.

title: Ranking Free RAG: Replacing Re-ranking with Selection in RAG for Sensitive Domains

abstract: Time series forecasting plays a pivotal role in data-driven decision-making across various time series domains. Recently, leveraging their ability to extract semantically rich representations, Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved promising results in time series forecasting. However, existing LLM-based methods struggle to obtain multi-scale retrieval-augmented representations due to entangled multi-scale representations and redundant multi-scale interference. To address this, we propose TimeMRA, an LLM-empowered Time series forecasting framework via Multi-Scale Retrieval-Augmented representations. Specifically, a scale-aware prompt generation (SAPG) module is designed to decompose time series into multiple scales and generate augmented multi-scale representations. Then, a cross-scale disentanglement constraint (CSDC) mechanism with a router network is designed to obtain the disentangled multi-scale semantic representations while mitigating interference from irrelevant scales. Finally, a cross-modality retrieval module is designed to obtain multi-scale retrieval-augmented representations for time series forecasting. Experiments on 10 real-world datasets demonstrate that TimeMRA achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting can benefit from representations that capture patterns at several scales. The paper argues that existing language-model-based approaches struggle to combine such representations with retrieval because information from different scales becomes entangled or introduces redundant interference. TimeMRA organizes the representation process to address those problems.

Its scale-aware prompt generation module first decomposes the time series into multiple scales and produces augmented representations. A cross-scale disentanglement constraint, paired with a router network, then separates the semantic representations and reduces interference from irrelevant scales. This makes scale separation an explicit part of learning, rather than leaving the model to handle all scales together.

A cross-modality retrieval module subsequently produces the multi-scale retrieval-augmented representations used for forecasting. The overall design links decomposition, disentanglement, routing, and retrieval so that information can contribute at appropriate scales. Experiments across ten real-world datasets report state-of-the-art forecasting performance. The findings support managing interactions among scales as an important component of combining language models and retrieval for time-series prediction.
summary.tldr: TimeMRA improves time-series forecasting by separating multi-scale representations and augmenting them through cross-modality retrieval.

title: TimeMRA: LLM-Empowered Time Series Forecasting via Multi-Scale Retrieval-Augmented Representations

abstract: Federated Graph Learning (FGL) enables collaborative training across distributed clients without sharing raw graph data. However, its performance is severely hindered by graph-specific heterogeneity arising from divergent node feature distributions and disparate graph structures. Existing FGL methods primarily focus on aligning or personalizing node features but largely overlook the role of structural knowledge, leading to aggregation-induced representation drift during message passing. We observe that structural heterogeneity often originates from feature-driven connection biases shaped by local data collection practices or user preferences. To address this, we propose Fed-Kalter, a novel FGL framework that integrates Kalman filtering principles into graph neural networks. Fed-Kalter introduces Kalter-Conv, a graph convolution grounded in a Kalman framework with learnable dynamics, which treats structural embeddings as latent states and feature-augmented neighborhoods as noisy observations, thereby filtering feature-induced structural noise in a layer-wise manner. Only structural parameters are aggregated globally, enabling effective cross-client knowledge transfer while preserving local personalization. Extensive experiments on 16 graph classification datasets spanning 4 domains demonstrate that Fed-Kalter consistently outperforms state-of-the-art FGL methods. Further ablation and hyperparameter studies confirm its robustness, efficiency, and effectiveness in mitigating structural heterogeneity.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning trains across clients without exchanging their raw graphs. Clients can differ in both node attributes and connection patterns, making shared training difficult. This paper emphasizes structural differences that existing approaches often overlook, particularly connection biases associated with local features, collection practices, or user preferences.

Fed-Kalter introduces a graph convolution built around Kalman filtering with learned dynamics. It treats structural representations as hidden states and neighborhoods enriched with node features as noisy observations. Each layer filters feature-induced structural noise as information passes through the graph. Global aggregation shares only structural parameters, leaving room for each client to retain local personalization.

This separates the knowledge intended for transfer from aspects that should remain locally adapted. Across 16 graph classification datasets in four domains, Fed-Kalter consistently outperforms the evaluated state-of-the-art federated graph methods. Additional ablation and hyperparameter studies support its efficiency, robustness, and ability to mitigate structural heterogeneity, strengthening the case for explicitly modeling structure during federated aggregation.
summary.tldr: Fed-Kalter uses learned Kalman-style graph filtering and structural parameter sharing to improve federated learning across clients with different graph structures.

title: Federated Graph Learning via Structure-Aware Fusion Using a Kalman Framework with Learnable Dynamics

abstract: 1-bit LLM quantization offers significant advantages in reducing storage and computational costs. However, existing methods typically train 1-bit LLMs from scratch, failing to fully leverage pre-trained models. This results in high training costs and notable accuracy degradation. We identify that the large gap between full precision and 1-bit representations makes naive adaptation difficult. In this paper, we introduce a consistent progressive training for both forward and backward, smoothly converting the full-precision weights into the binarized ones. Additionally, we incorporate binary-aware initialization and dual-scaling compensation to reduce the difficulty of progressive training and improve the performance. Experimental results on LLMs of various sizes demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches. Our results show that high-performance 1-bit LLMs can be achieved using pre-trained models, eliminating the need for expensive training from scratch.

paragraphs: One-bit language models promise lower storage and computation costs, but moving from full-precision weights to binary weights creates a large representational change. This paper argues that the gap makes naive adaptation of an existing model difficult. Training a binary model from scratch avoids that direct transition but incurs substantial training costs and can still suffer accuracy degradation.

The proposed method progressively converts a pretrained model’s weights into binary form. It keeps this transition consistent across both forward computation and backward training updates, making the conversion gradual. Binary-aware initialization and dual-scaling compensation further support the transition, reducing the difficulty of progressive training and improving performance.

Experiments across language models of different sizes report better performance than existing approaches. The stated conclusion is that high-performing one-bit models can be obtained by adapting pretrained models, removing the need for expensive training from scratch in this approach. The contribution therefore concerns the conversion process as much as the compressed representation: it offers a way to retain value from pretraining while making the substantial shift to binary weights.
summary.tldr: A progressive training method converts pretrained language models to one-bit weights and outperforms existing approaches in the reported experiments.

title: Rethinking 1-bit Optimization Leveraging Pre-trained Large Language Models

abstract: While EEG foundation models have shown significant potential in universal neural decoding across tasks, their advancement remains constrained by the inadequacy modeling of complex spatiotemporal topology, as well as the inherent modality gap between low-level physiological signals and high-level textual semantics. To address these challenges, we propose a Knowledge-Anchored Semantically-Dynamic Topology Brain Autoregressive Model (KAST-BAR), which dynamically aligns physiological representations derived from multi-level brain topology with an expert-level semantic space. Specifically, we design a Dual-Stream Hierarchical Attention (DSHA) encoder that accurately captures the brain’s intrinsic non-Euclidean topology by modeling local temporal dynamics with global spatial contexts. On this basis, a Knowledge-Anchored Semantic Profiler (KASP) is proposed to synthesize physically-grounded and instance-level textual profiles, which subsequently drive a Semantic Text-Aware Refiner (STAR) to dynamically reconstruct EEG representations using Latent Expert Queries. By conducting large-scale pre-training on 21 diverse datasets to build a foundation model, KAST-BAR effectively integrates expert-level medical knowledge into EEG signal representations, consistently achieving state-of-the-art performance across six downstream tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/KAST-BAR/KAST-BAR

paragraphs: Interpreting EEG signals requires modeling patterns across time and relationships across brain locations. The paper also identifies a gap between these physiological measurements and the higher-level language used to describe them. KAST-BAR aims to connect both forms of information within a foundation model for neural decoding across tasks.

A Dual-Stream Hierarchical Attention encoder combines local temporal dynamics with global spatial context to represent the brain's complex topology. A Knowledge-Anchored Semantic Profiler then synthesizes textual profiles grounded in physiology and specific to individual instances. The authors pretrain the model on 21 diverse datasets, incorporating expert medical knowledge into its signal representations. They report state-of-the-art results across six downstream tasks. The findings support combining structured spatiotemporal modeling with instance-specific semantic guidance: the text-derived knowledge participates in refining the physiological representation itself, linking the two sources of information within the model.
summary.tldr: KAST-BAR combines EEG topology modeling with expert semantic guidance and reports state-of-the-art performance across six downstream tasks.

title: KAST-BAR: Knowledge-Anchored Semantically-Dynamic Topology Brain Autoregressive Modeling for Universal Neural Interpretation

abstract: Social media platforms enable large-scale cross-lingual communication, but translating user-generated content (UGC) remains challenging due to its informal style, cultural references, and interaction-based expressions. While recent LLMs have improved translation quality, existing benchmarks and metrics often fail to capture whether translations convey intended meaning and cultural resonance in real-world settings. In this work, we introduce CULTURE-MT, a benchmark for social media translation that focuses on both CULtural Transmission and UGC-specific emotion REsonance. CULTURE-MT consists of 1,002 UGC notes across 14 domains, categorized into four types based on culture-loaded symbol and linguistic style features. We also construct UGC-oriented training data to fine-tune Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B as baselines. We propose cultural effectiveness as a new evaluation criterion, focusing on expression accuracy and cultural adaptability. Testing 15 models, including the baselines, we find that traditional metrics fail to capture cultural effectiveness. We also observe that cultural effectiveness on base LLMs correlates with model size. Our work provides a comprehensive evaluation system for UGC translation models and will offers an open evaluation platform to advance research in this area. We release the CULTURE-MT benchmark and provide an online leaderboard where submitted translation results can be evaluated by our trained JUDGER.

paragraphs: Social media translation has to carry more than literal meaning. Informal language, cultural references, and expressions shaped by online interaction can lose their intended effect when translated. This paper introduces CULTURE-MT to evaluate whether translations preserve that meaning and emotional resonance in ways that work for the receiving culture.

The benchmark contains 1,002 user-generated notes across 14 domains. It organizes them into four types using culturally loaded symbols and linguistic style. The authors propose cultural effectiveness as an evaluation criterion combining expression accuracy with cultural adaptability. They also create training data tailored to social media content and fine-tune Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B as baseline translation models.

Testing 15 models, the authors find that traditional metrics do not adequately capture cultural effectiveness. They also observe a correlation between model size and this criterion among base language models. This finding separates a measured association from a guarantee about any particular model. The released benchmark and evaluation platform provide a way to compare translations on qualities that conventional scores can overlook.
summary.tldr: CULTURE-MT evaluates whether social media translations preserve cultural meaning and emotional resonance that conventional translation metrics can miss.

title: Beyond Literal Translation: Evaluating Cultural Effectiveness in Social Media UGC

abstract: We present a mechanism to steer the sampling diversity of denoising diffusion and flow matching models, allowing users to sample from a sharper or broader distribution than the training distribution. We build on the observation that these models leverage (learned) score functions of noisy data distributions for sampling and show that rescaling these allows one to effectively control a ’local’ sampling temperature. Notably, this approach does not require any finetuning or alterations to training strategy, and can be applied to any off-the-shelf model and is compatible with both deterministic and stochastic samplers. We first validate our framework on toy 2D data, and then demonstrate its application for diffusion models trained across five disparate tasks – image generation, pose estimation, depth prediction, robot manipulation, and protein design. We find that across these tasks, our approach allows sampling from sharper (or flatter) distributions, yielding performance gains e.g., depth prediction models benefit from sampling more likely depth estimates, whereas image generation models perform better when sampling a slightly flatter distribution.

paragraphs: A generative model may need to produce either concentrated, likely answers or a broader range of possibilities depending on the task. This paper introduces a sampling-time mechanism for controlling that diversity in diffusion and flow matching models. It aims to make the sampled distribution sharper or flatter than the distribution used for training.
