Across these tasks, rescaling changes distribution concentration and can improve performance. The preferred direction depends on the application: more likely depth estimates help depth prediction, while a slightly flatter distribution helps image generation in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Rescaling scores during sampling controls local temperature in diffusion and flow models without retraining, with task-dependent performance benefits.

title: Temporal Score Rescaling for Temperature Sampling in Diffusion and Flow Models

abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across diverse tasks. Existing approaches optimize communication topology, role assignment, or LLM routing in isolation, while treating each agent as a monolithic unit—failing to exploit internal LLM mixtures that can enhance individual role capabilities. We propose HieraMAS, a hierarchical agent collaboration framework with intra-node LLM mixtures and inter-node communication topology. HieraAgent introduces supernodes, where each functional role comprises multiple heterogeneous LLMs in a propose-synthesis structure. The optimization of HieraMAS poses unique credit assignment challenges, as final task performance heavily depends on LLM capabilities, potentially causing erroneous reinforcement of suboptimal configurations. We address this via a two-stage algorithm: (1) multi-level reward attribution providing fine-grained feedback at both node and system levels; and (2) graph classification treating topology selection as a holistic task rather than per-edge optimization. Experiments on reasoning and coding benchmarks demonstrate that HieraMAS significantly outperforms existing methods while achieving better cost-performance trade-offs.

We propose HieraMAS, a hierarchical agent collaboration framework with intra-node LLM mixtures and inter-node communication topology. HieraAgent introduces supernodes, where each functional role comprises multiple heterogeneous LLMs in a propose-synthesis structure. paragraphs: Language-model multi-agent systems must decide both how agents perform their roles and how they communicate. HieraMAS addresses these decisions together. It replaces the assumption that each role belongs to one indivisible agent with a supernode: several different language models contribute proposals that are combined through synthesis.

Optimizing this hierarchy creates a credit-assignment problem. Strong underlying models can produce good final results even when the surrounding configuration is suboptimal, potentially rewarding the wrong design choices. HieraMAS uses a two-stage algorithm: multi-level reward attribution provides feedback at both the node and whole-system levels, while graph classification selects communication structures as complete configurations.

Considering the topology as a whole allows the optimization to assess the arrangement of communication links together instead of making isolated decisions about each link. On reasoning and coding benchmarks, the framework significantly outperforms existing methods and achieves better cost-performance trade-offs. These results support coordinating the mixture within each role with the communication structure between roles when designing collaborative language-model systems.
summary.tldr: HieraMAS jointly organizes model mixtures within agent roles and communication between roles to improve performance and cost trade-offs.

title: HieraMAS: Optimizing Intra-Node LLM Mixtures and Inter-Node Topology for Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: Most visual generative models compress images into a latent space before applying diffusion or autoregressive modelling. Yet, existing approaches such as VAEs and foundation model aligned encoders implicitly constrain the latent space without explicitly shaping its distribution, making it unclear which types of distributions are optimal for modeling. We introduce Distribution-Matching VAE (DMVAE), which explicitly aligns the encoder’s latent distribution with an arbitrary reference distribution via a distribution matching constraint. This generalizes beyond the Gaussian prior of conventional VAEs, enabling alignment with distributions derived from self-supervised features, diffusion noise, or other prior distributions. With DMVAE, we can systematically investigate which latent distributions are more conducive to modeling, and we find that SSL-derived distributions provide an excellent balance between reconstruction fidelity and modeling efficiency, reaching a gFID of 3.2 on ImageNet with only 64 training epochs. Our results suggest that choosing a suitable latent distribution structure (achieved via distribution-level alignment), rather than relying on fixed priors, is key to bridging the gap between easy-to-model latents and high-fidelity image synthesis.

paragraphs: Many image generators first compress images into latent representations and then learn to generate within that space. The distribution of those representations affects the modeling problem. This paper asks how deliberately shaping that distribution can help retain image information while making the latent space easier for a generative model to learn.

Distribution-Matching VAE introduces a constraint that aligns the encoder's latent distribution with a chosen reference distribution. The reference need not be the Gaussian prior associated with conventional VAEs. It can instead come from self-supervised features, diffusion noise, or other priors, providing a framework for comparing different distribution structures within the same general approach.

The authors find that distributions derived from self-supervised learning offer a strong balance between reconstruction fidelity and modeling efficiency. They report a generation FID of 3.2 on ImageNet after 64 training epochs. The broader finding is that distribution-level alignment provides a useful design choice: the structure of the latent distribution can help reconcile faithful image reconstruction with efficient generative modeling.
summary.tldr: DMVAE explicitly matches image latents to chosen reference distributions, finding that self-supervised feature distributions balance reconstruction and generation efficiency.

title: Distribution Matching Variational AutoEncoder

abstract: Current evaluations of spatial intelligence can be systematically invalid under modern vision-language model (VLM) settings. First, many benchmarks derive question-answer (QA) pairs from point-cloud-based 3D annotations originally curated for traditional 3D perception. When such annotations are treated as ground truth for video-based evaluation, reconstruction and annotation artifacts can miss objects that are clearly visible in the video, mislabel object identities, or corrupt geometry-dependent answers (e.g., size), yielding incorrect or ambiguous QA pairs. Second, evaluations often assume full-scene access, while many VLMs operate on sparsely sampled frames (e.g., 16-64), making many questions effectively unanswerable under the actual model inputs. We improve evaluation validity by introducing ReVSI, a benchmark and protocol that ensures each QA pair is answerable and correct under the model’s actual inputs. To this end, we re-annotate object labels and geometry across 413 scenes from 5 datasets to improve data quality, and regenerate all QA pairs with rigorous bias mitigation and human verification using professional 3D visualization and annotation tools. We further enhance evaluation controllability by providing variants across multiple frame budgets (16/32/64/all) and fine-grained object visibility metadata, enabling controlled diagnostic analyses. Evaluations of general and domain-specific VLMs on ReVSI reveal systematic failure modes that are obscured by prior benchmarks, yielding a more reliable and diagnostic assessment of spatial intelligence.

paragraphs: A spatial-reasoning benchmark can give misleading results when its answers do not match what a model can actually see. The paper identifies errors introduced by using point-cloud annotations as ground truth for video questions, including missing objects, mistaken identities, and corrupted geometry. Questions can also become unanswerable when a model receives only a sparse selection of frames.

ReVSI rebuilds both the data and evaluation protocol around correctness and answerability under the actual inputs. The authors re-annotate object labels and geometry in 413 scenes from five datasets, then regenerate question-answer pairs with bias mitigation and human verification using professional 3D tools.

The benchmark provides versions with 16, 32, 64, or all frames, together with detailed object-visibility metadata. These controls enable analysis of how available visual evidence affects performance. Evaluations of general and specialized vision-language models expose systematic failure modes obscured by previous benchmarks. ReVSI therefore improves the interpretability of spatial-reasoning results by aligning the questions, reference answers, and evidence supplied to each model.
summary.tldr: ReVSI rebuilds spatial-reasoning evaluation so questions are correct and answerable from the frames a model actually receives.

title: ReVSI: Rebuilding Visual Spatial Intelligence Evaluation for Accurate Assessment of VLM 3D Reasoning

abstract: Bayesian predictive inference provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, data efficiency, and robust generalization. However, exact inference is often intractable, and scalable approximations may remain computationally expensive or require restrictive modeling assumptions that degrade predictive performance. Prior-Data Fitted and in-context learning networks have recently emerged as an amortized alternative by learning to map datasets directly to predictive distributions, but existing approaches are tightly coupled to the support of the training prior and lack explicit mechanisms for adapting to new priors at test time, resulting in limited robustness under distribution shift. We introduce a multi-task in-context learning framework for amortized hierarchical Bayesian predictive inference that explicitly represents prior information as a prefix of in-context datasets. A transformer trained on sequences of prior and target tasks learns to adapt its predictions across families of priors. On a suite of evaluations with increasing difficulty, including out-of-meta-distribution heavy-tailed priors and priors with high-dimensional latent structures, our method matches oracle Bayesian predictors while being orders of magnitude faster. We further demonstrate its practical relevance on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction benchmark.

paragraphs: Bayesian prediction represents uncertainty by combining prior information with observed data, but computing it can be expensive. Networks that learn to map datasets directly to predictive distributions offer a faster alternative. Their weakness, as described here, is that predictions remain closely tied to the priors encountered during training, limiting adaptation when those priors change.

This paper introduces a multi-task framework that makes prior information an explicit part of the input. A prefix of in-context datasets represents that information, and a Transformer trains on sequences containing prior and target tasks. The resulting model learns to adjust predictions across families of priors within an amortized hierarchical Bayesian inference framework.

Evaluations include challenging priors outside the meta-training distribution, covering heavy-tailed behavior and high-dimensional latent structures. The authors report matching oracle Bayesian predictors while running orders of magnitude faster. They also demonstrate the method on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature-prediction benchmark. These results support task-based context as a practical mechanism for adapting fast Bayesian prediction to changing prior information.
summary.tldr: A Transformer uses prior-task datasets as context to adapt Bayesian predictions across prior families, matching evaluated oracle predictors much faster.

abstract: A novel algorithm for performing Independent Subspace Analysis, the estimation of hidden independent subspaces is introduced. This task is a generalization of Independent Component Analysis. The algorithm works by estimating the multi-dimensional differential entropy. The estimation utilizes minimal geodesic spanning trees matched to the sample points. Numerical studies include (i) illustrative examples, (ii) a generalization of the cocktail-party problem to songs played by bands, and (iii) an example on mixed independent subspaces, where subspaces have dependent sources, which are pairwise independent.
originalAbstract: A novel algorithm for performing Independent Subspace Analysis, the estimation of hidden independent subspaces is introduced. This task is a generalization of Independent Component Analysis. The algorithm works by estimating the multi-dimensional differential entropy. The estimation utilizes minimal geodesic spanning trees matched to the sample points. Numerical studies include (i) illustrative examples, (ii) a generalization of the cocktail-party problem to songs played by bands, and (iii) an example on mixed independent subspaces, where subspaces have dependent sources, which are pairwise independent.

paragraphs: Independent Subspace Analysis seeks hidden groups of variables that are independent of one another, while allowing dependencies inside each group. It generalizes Independent Component Analysis by making an entire subspace the unit of independence. The paper introduces an algorithm for estimating these hidden subspaces from observed sample points.

The algorithm relies on estimating multidimensional differential entropy, a quantity describing uncertainty in a continuous multivariate distribution. It obtains this estimate using minimal geodesic spanning trees fitted to the samples. This gives the method a geometric way to assess multivariate uncertainty as part of identifying the independent subspaces.

Numerical studies include illustrative examples and an extension of the cocktail-party problem involving songs played by bands. Another example mixes independent subspaces whose internal sources are pairwise independent but still jointly dependent. That example highlights the distinction between independence of pairs and independence of a whole collection, which matters when identifying groups that may contain internal statistical relationships.
summary.tldr: Geodesic spanning-tree entropy estimates support an algorithm for recovering independent subspaces that can contain internally dependent sources.

title: Independent subspace analysis using geodesic spanning trees

abstract: We consider the problem of computing the Euclidean projection of a vector of length $n$ onto a closed convex set including the $\ell_1$ ball and the specialized polyhedra employed in (Shalev-Shwartz & Singer, 2006). These problems have played building block roles in solving several $\ell_1$-norm based sparse learning problems. Existing methods have a worst-case time complexity of $O(n \log n)$. In this paper, we propose to cast both Euclidean projections as root finding problems associated with specific auxiliary functions, which can be solved in linear time via bisection. We further make use of the special structure of the auxiliary functions, and propose an improved bisection algorithm. Empirical studies demonstrate that the proposed algorithms are much more efficient than the competing ones for computing the projections.

These problems have played building block roles in solving several $\ell_1$-norm based sparse learning problems. Existing methods have a worst-case time complexity of $O(n \log n)$. In this paper, we propose to cast both Euclidean projections as root finding problems associated with specific auxiliary functions, which can be solved in linear time via bisection. We further make use of the special structure of the auxiliary functions, and propose an improved bisection algorithm. Empirical studies demonstrate that the proposed algorithms are much more efficient than the competing ones for computing the projections.

paragraphs: A Euclidean projection finds the point in a permitted set that is closest to a given vector. This paper studies that operation for sets used in sparse learning, including the l1 ball and particular polyhedra. These projections act as building blocks inside learning algorithms, so improving their cost can improve a repeatedly used computational step.

The authors recast the two projection problems as finding roots of specially constructed auxiliary functions. This changes the computational task from directly searching for a projected vector to solving a root-finding problem. They show that the resulting problems can be solved in linear time using bisection, compared with the stated O(n log n) worst-case complexity of existing methods.

The paper further exploits the structure of the auxiliary functions to develop an improved bisection algorithm. Empirical studies find the proposed algorithms much more efficient than competing projection methods. The contribution concerns the specified projection problems: their mathematical structure makes it possible to accelerate an operation important to several l1-based sparse-learning procedures.
summary.tldr: Reformulating specific sparse-learning projections as root-finding problems yields linear-time algorithms with strong empirical efficiency.

title: Efficient Euclidean projections in linear time

abstract: In many real-world domains, undirected graphical models such as Markov random fields provide a more natural representation of the statistical dependency structure than directed graphical models. Unfortunately, structure learning of undirected graphs using likelihood-based scores remains difficult because of the intractability of computing the partition function. We describe a new Markov random field structure learning algorithm, motivated by canonical parameterization of Abbeel et al. We provide computational improvements on their parameterization by learning per-variable canonical factors, which makes our algorithm suitable for domains with hundreds of nodes. We compare our algorithm against several algorithms for learning undirected and directed models on simulated and real datasets from biology. Our algorithm frequently outperforms existing algorithms, producing higher-quality structures, suggesting that enforcing consistency during structure learning is beneficial for learning undirected graphs.
originalAbstract: In many real-world domains, undirected graphical models such as Markov random fields provide a more natural representation of the statistical dependency structure than directed graphical models. Unfortunately, structure learning of undirected graphs using likelihood-based scores remains difficult because of the intractability of computing the partition function. We describe a new Markov random field structure learning algorithm, motivated by canonical parameterization of Abbeel et al. We provide computational improvements on their parameterization by learning per-variable canonical factors, which makes our algorithm suitable for domains with hundreds of nodes. We compare our algorithm against several algorithms for learning undirected and directed models on simulated and real datasets from biology. Our algorithm frequently outperforms existing algorithms, producing higher-quality structures, suggesting that enforcing consistency during structure learning is beneficial for learning undirected graphs.

paragraphs: Undirected graphical models represent statistical dependencies without assigning a direction to every connection. They can be a natural fit for real-world domains, but learning their structure with likelihood-based scores is difficult. The obstacle highlighted here is the partition function, whose computation can be intractable and thereby complicate comparisons between candidate structures.

The paper introduces a structure learning algorithm for Markov random fields, motivated by canonical parameterization. Its computational improvement is to learn canonical factors for individual variables. This change makes the algorithm suitable for domains with hundreds of nodes, bringing the representation strategy into a more substantial problem scale.

The authors compare the method with algorithms for both directed and undirected models using simulated data and real biological datasets. It frequently produces higher-quality structures than existing algorithms. These results suggest that enforcing consistency during structure learning is beneficial for undirected graphs. The empirical conclusion is qualified by its frequency across the comparisons, while the main methodological contribution is a more computationally practical factor-learning approach.
summary.tldr: Learning per-variable canonical factors enables structure learning for undirected models with hundreds of nodes and frequently improves structural quality in experiments.

title: Learning structurally consistent undirected probabilistic graphical models

abstract: Codebook-based representations are widely employed in the classification of complex objects such as images and documents. Most previous codebook-based methods construct a single codebook via clustering that maps a bag of low-level features into a fixed-length histogram that describes the distribution of these features. This paper describes a simple yet effective framework for learning multiple non-redundant codebooks that produces surprisingly good results. In this framework, each codebook is learned in sequence to extract discriminative information that was not captured by preceding codebooks and their corresponding classifiers. We apply this framework to two application domains: visual object categorization and document classification. Experiments on large classification tasks show substantial improvements in performance compared to a single codebook or codebooks learned in a bagging style.
originalAbstract: Codebook-based representations are widely employed in the classification of complex objects such as images and documents. Most previous codebook-based methods construct a single codebook via clustering that maps a bag of low-level features into a fixed-length histogram that describes the distribution of these features. This paper describes a simple yet effective framework for learning multiple non-redundant codebooks that produces surprisingly good results. In this framework, each codebook is learned in sequence to extract discriminative information that was not captured by preceding codebooks and their corresponding classifiers. We apply this framework to two application domains: visual object categorization and document classification. Experiments on large classification tasks show substantial improvements in performance compared to a single codebook or codebooks learned in a bagging style.

paragraphs: Codebook representations turn collections of low-level features into fixed-length histograms for classifying objects such as images and documents. A conventional approach constructs one codebook through clustering, then uses the histogram to describe how the object's features are distributed. This paper investigates how multiple codebooks can provide additional useful information.

The proposed framework learns codebooks sequentially. Each new codebook targets discriminative information that earlier codebooks and their associated classifiers did not capture. This makes the relationship between codebooks part of the learning procedure: adding a codebook is intended to address what the existing collection has missed, rather than merely create another representation of the same information.

The authors apply the framework to visual object categorization and document classification. On large classification tasks, they report substantial improvements over both a single codebook and codebooks learned in a bagging style. The results support the value of learning complementary representations in sequence. The main contribution is the explicit use of earlier classifiers' uncovered information to guide later codebook construction.
summary.tldr: Sequentially learned codebooks capture information missed by earlier classifiers and improve image and document classification in the reported experiments.

title: Learning non-redundant codebooks for classifying complex objects

abstract: We derive a generalized notion of f-divergences, called (f,l)-divergences. We show that this generalization enjoys many of the nice properties of f-divergences, although it is a richer family. It also provides alternative definitions of standard divergences in terms of surrogate risks. As a first practical application of this theory, we derive a new estimator for the Kulback-Leibler divergence that we use for clustering sets of vectors.
originalAbstract: We derive a generalized notion of f-divergences, called (f,l)-divergences. We show that this generalization enjoys many of the nice properties of f-divergences, although it is a richer family. It also provides alternative definitions of standard divergences in terms of surrogate risks. As a first practical application of this theory, we derive a new estimator for the Kulback-Leibler divergence that we use for clustering sets of vectors.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a broader family of distribution-comparison measures called (f,l)-divergences. These generalize f-divergences while retaining many of their useful properties. The theoretical aim is to expand the available family without losing the properties that make the original measures valuable, although the abstract does not claim that every property carries over.

The framework also gives alternative definitions of familiar divergences in terms of surrogate risks. This connects two ways of describing a comparison: through a divergence and through a risk-based formulation. The contribution is therefore more than a collection of additional measures; it provides a different characterization of established ones within the generalized framework.

As a practical application, the authors derive a new estimator of Kullback-Leibler divergence and use it to cluster sets of vectors. That application connects the theory to an estimation problem and then to a data-analysis task. The stated finding is the construction and use of this estimator. The abstract does not attach a comparative performance claim to the clustering application.
summary.tldr: Risk-based (f,l)-divergences generalize f-divergences and yield a new KL-divergence estimator used to cluster sets of vectors.

title: Risk-Based Generalizations of f-divergences

abstract: We consider a multi-armed bandit problem where the decision maker can explore and exploit different arms at every round. The exploited arm adds to the decision maker's cumulative reward (without necessarily observing the reward) while the explored arm reveals its value. We devise algorithms for this setup and show that the dependence on the number of arms can be much better than the standard square root of the number of arms dependence, according to the behavior of the arms' reward sequences. For the important case of piecewise stationary stochastic bandits, we show a significant improvement over existing algorithms. Our algorithms are based on a non-uniform sampling policy, which we show is essential to the success of any algorithm in the adversarial setup. We finally show some simulation results on an ultra-wide band channel selection inspired setting indicating the applicability of our algorithms.
originalAbstract: We consider a multi-armed bandit problem where the decision maker can explore and exploit different arms at every round. The exploited arm adds to the decision maker's cumulative reward (without necessarily observing the reward) while the explored arm reveals its value. We devise algorithms for this setup and show that the dependence on the number of arms can be much better than the standard square root of the number of arms dependence, according to the behavior of the arms' reward sequences. For the important case of piecewise stationary stochastic bandits, we show a significant improvement over existing algorithms. Our algorithms are based on a non-uniform sampling policy, which we show is essential to the success of any algorithm in the adversarial setup. We finally show some simulation results on an ultra-wide band channel selection inspired setting indicating the applicability of our algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies a bandit setting in which earning a reward and collecting information can involve different choices. On each round, one arm supplies the reward added to the decision maker’s total, while another arm can be explored to reveal its value. The reward from the exploited arm need not itself be observed.

The authors develop algorithms for this separation and show that dependence on the number of arms can improve substantially over the standard square-root dependence. The improvement depends on how the arms’ reward sequences behave. They establish a significant gain over existing algorithms for piecewise stationary stochastic bandits, where reward behavior is stable within segments but can change between them.

The algorithms use non-uniform sampling, assigning different exploration frequencies to different arms. The paper shows that this is essential for success in the adversarial setting considered. Simulations inspired by ultra-wideband channel selection indicate practical applicability. Together, the results show how separating information gathering from reward collection can change the learning problem and the benefits available from targeted exploration.
summary.tldr: Separating exploration from reward collection enables improved bandit guarantees under suitable reward behavior, using non-uniform exploration.

title: Decoupling Exploration and Exploitation in Multi-Armed Bandits
